all.title: A new equilibrium: COVID-19 lockdowns and WFH persistence
institutions: ARC Centre of Excellence for Children and Families over the Life Course
all.abstract: This paper documents a robust link between COVID-19 lockdowns and the uptake and persistence of working from home (WFH) practices. Exploiting rich longitudinal data, we use a difference-in-differences strategy to compare office workers in three heavily locked-down Australian states to similar workers in less affected states. Locked-down workers sustain 43% higher WFH levels through 2023  0.5 days per week  with a monotonic doseresponse relationship. Persistence is driven by adjustments on both sides of the labor market: employers downsize office space and open remote/hybrid positions, while employees relocate away from city centers and invest in home offices and technology.

all.title: Structural Empirical Analysis of Vacancy Referrals with Imperfect Monitoring and the Strategic Use of Sickness Absence
all.abstract: This paper provides a structural analysis of the role of job vacancy referrals (VRs) by public employment agencies in the job search behavior of unemployed individuals, incorporating institutional features of the monitoring of search behavior by the agencies. Notably, rejections of VRs may lead to sanctions (temporary benefits reductions) while workers may report sick to avoid those. We estimate models using German administrative data from social security records linked with caseworker recorded data on VRs, sick reporting and sanctions. The analysis highlights the influence of aspects of the health care system on unemployment durations. We estimate that for around 25% of unemployed workers, removing the channel that enables strategic sick reporting reduces the mean unemployment duration by 4 days.

all.title: Deciphering the slow adoption of HR analytics: a comprehensive exploration of individual, social, and technological factors
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: The growing importance of analytics in management, including Human Resource Management, supports data-driven decisions and strategic objectives. Despite its benefits, HR professionals have been slow to adopt HR analytics. This study aims to identify factors that facilitate and hinder HR analytics adoption among HR professionals, with a focus on the moderating role of organizational culture. Using an integrated model that combines the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), this study examines factors influencing HR analytics readiness and their influence on adoption behavior The validation of model was accomplished through the employment of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), which was conducted using survey data from 305 HR professionals based in India. The findings show significant positive relationships between readiness for HR analytics and factors such as attitude, quantitative self-efficacy, peer influence, superior influence, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and tool trialability, while data availability was insignificant. Individual and social factors positively influence readiness, whereas organizational culture negatively moderates the relationship between readiness and the adoption of HR analytics. The findings emphasize the need for cultural reorientation to foster innovation and effectively implement HR analytics, offering valuable insights for managers, business leaders, and policymakers.

all.title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
all.abstract: Pay range transparency—that is, disclosing the minimum and maximum pay for a job rather than individuals’ actual pay—has become the most prevalent form of pay transparency. Yet, existing theories explain employee reactions to pay information through present-focused, interpersonal comparisons with coworkers’ pay. We theorize that pay range transparency instead directs employees to interpret their structural pay standing—their pay position relative to the disclosed range boundaries—as a forward-looking signal of the organization’s recognition and structural room for pay growth. Drawing on expectancy theory, we propose that structural pay standing has a curvilinear (attenuated-positive) effect on job satisfaction, intention to stay, and job performance, mediated by pay growth uncertainty: pay near the range minimum offers weak evidence that contributions will be recognized, whereas pay near the maximum reveals limited structural room for further growth, a pattern we term a ceiling effect. Pay-related procedural justice attenuates these effects. Four studies—a natural experiment (n = 371), an online experiment (n = 603), a three-wave field study (n = 525), and an experimental-causal-chain study (n = 392)—support our theorizing, establishing structural pay standing as distinct from interpersonal pay standing and revealing an unrecognized trade-off of pay range transparency.

all.title: Beyond speak-up: A multidirectional framework for employee voice issue processing
all.abstract: Employee voice research explains why employees speak up or remain silent and how managers respond when they do. This article develops an organizational-level framework of employee voice issue processing to explain how HRM systems handle voiced concerns and why those concerns lead to different consequences. The framework shifts attention from voice occurrence to the movement, handling, and fate of employee voice issues within HRM voice architecture. It identifies five component pathways—voice up as upward expression, voice down as authoritative response, voice around as lateral voice testing, voice in as inward translation, and voice out as outward escalation—and argues that their consequences depend on how pathways are configured and integrated. The article introduces voice integration capacity as the organization's ability to link, interpret, coordinate, and respond to employee voice issues across these pathways. By connecting voice research with HRM system design, the article explains why opportunities to speak can lead to learning and correction in some settings but pseudo-voice, fragmentation, or external scrutiny in others. It treats employee voice not only as an individual act of expression but also as an HRM issue-processing challenge.

all.title: When shifts matter for hybrid teams: The moderating role of location predictability.
all.abstract: In recent years, changes to the nature of work and evolving employee preferences have led to the rise of hybrid teams. In contrast to traditional teams, hybrid teams frequently shift between remote and face-to-face interaction. This structure raises new questions about how such dynamism impacts team engagement, an emergent state typically thought to develop under long periods of stability and face-to-face interaction. Drawing on the boundary transition theory of dynamic teamwork, we theorize that weekly downshifts in face-to-face interaction (i.e., relative decreases from the prior week) harm weekly team engagement and performance, but only for teams with lower levels of location predictability-an important yet understudied differentiator of hybrid team functioning. To test these ideas, we use a within-team, repeated-measures field survey design with a sample of hybrid sales teams at a large alcohol distributor in China. We surveyed 164 hybrid teams and their supervisors across 6 weeks (648 team-level weekly responses) to capture shifts in team work locations and examine their impact on weekly team engagement and performance. Results supported our hypotheses. By focusing on the role of weekly fluctuations in team structures and how location predictability shapes these effects, we advance our understanding of the unique and dynamic nature of hybrid teams. all.title: The relationship between language ideologies and workplace mistreatment towards North Korean defectors
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: Previous studies on Social Identity Theory (SIT) have revealed the role of social categorisation in power imbalances between languages, linking it to negative acts in workplaces (e.g. discrimination). We focus on subtle social categorisation along the linguistic dimension, investigating whether North Korean Defectors (NKDs) working at South Korean organisations perceive workplace mistreatment as a result of linguistic discrimination. Repeat interviews were conducted with 20 NKDs, and one-off interviews with 6 NKDs. Our study shows that the use of North Korean accents or lexical items has been regarded as illegitimate in South Korean workplaces, leading NKDs to feel mistreated. We also investigate NKDs’ identity formation in response to workplace mistreatment. Our results show that the majority of NKDs hide their North Korean ethnicity in the workplace for fear of being mistreated due to ingrained stereotypes about NKDs.

all.title: Who Will be Assigned Unreasonable Tasks by Supervisors: A Conjoint Survey Experiment
all.abstract: Supervisors sometimes assign employees tasks that employees may perceive as unreasonable because they fall outside their formal job duties. Prior research has mostly focused on the negative effects of unreasonable tasks on employee outcomes, without examining the fundamental question of who is more likely to be assigned such tasks by their supervisors. To answer this question, we examined three distinct logics underlying the assignment of unreasonable tasks based on employee attributes (i.e., age, gender, task performance, helping behavior, recent workload, and relationship closeness): stereotype‐driven logic, efficiency‐driven logic, and exchange‐driven logic. In a fully randomized conjoint survey experiment, we asked 464 supervisors to allocate an unreasonable task based on evaluations of 4640 hypothetical employee profiles, with profiles varying randomly on six employee attributes. Results show that supervisors are more likely to assign unreasonable tasks to younger employees who perform better on tasks, exhibit more helping behavior, currently have lighter workloads, and maintain closer relationships with their supervisor. The relatively stronger effects of employees' recent workload, task performance, and helping behavior suggest that the efficiency‐driven logic plays the most influential role in shaping supervisors' unreasonable task assignments. We discuss the theoretical, methodological, and practical implications of our findings.

all.title: ‘Flying under the radar’: job crafting when menopause disrupts neurodivergent coping
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: Human Resource Management increasingly recognises the importance of job crafting, which relies on personal structures of coping. This study foregrounds workplace job crafting using a critical case approach, focusing on neurodivergent individuals whose coping mechanisms may be destabilised during menopause. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 45 neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms (UK and US) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings provide insight into how intersecting vulnerabilities shape person-led workplace adaptation. Specifically, neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms were found to engage in different forms of avoidance job crafting (behavioural avoidance demand crafting, behavioural avoidance resource crafting, cognitive avoidance demand crafting). Moreover, a newly identified preservation orientation drives a combination of avoidance and approach job crafting, evidenced by crafting strategies that primarily focus preservation, or maintaining the status quo, to align personal resources within maintaining job performance. This article contributes to the job crafting literature by demonstrating distinctive job crafting practices of individuals whose life-long coping strategies (of neurodivergence) are temporarily and transitionally destabilised (by menopause symptoms). Organisations have a critical role to support potentially stigmatised employees, thereby nurturing inclusive human resources support policies that provide support to individuals experiencing multiple stigmas.

all.title: From exclusive to inclusive? Exploring the barriers of i-deals for functionally diverse (FD) workers
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: Idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) have traditionally been granted exclusively to the ‘stars’ of organisations, promoting the ‘Matthew effect’ (the more you have, the more you get), while other workers are denied access to this contemporary HR practice that takes accommodation requests one step further. This practice has led to perceptions of unfairness among co-workers, particularly minorities, who encounter obstacles and discrimination when seeking to access or benefit from i-deals. Through a scoping review, we explore the barriers that arise when functionally diverse workers (FD workers) negotiate i-deals, shedding light on whether, and how, it is possible to move beyond an exclusionary, opportunistic approach toward an inclusive, strategic use of i-deals as a tool for inclusion. By explicitly applying a workplace dignity framework, the study supports a genuine concern for equity in i-deal negotiations, as opposed to a mere practice of ‘social washing’ and self-serving hypocrisy regarding the inclusion of FD workers in organisations. Recommendations for organizations to eliminate the barriers and the inclusive application of i-deals are discussed, as well as the paper’s theoretical and practical contributions.

all.title: Examining Negative Asymmetry in Employee Social Networks: A Meta-Analysis
institutions: University at Buffalo, State University of New York
all.abstract: Two decades have passed since Labianca and Brass introduced social ledger theory with its focal assumption of negative asymmetry—that the social liabilities created by negative workplace ties are more strongly related to employee outcomes than the social assets created by positive workplace ties. Yet widespread conclusions that negative workplace ties are more consequential have exceeded a surprisingly limited base of empirical tests. This article uses meta-analysis to examine this largely untested assumption by offering 22 original meta-analytic estimates drawn from 248 effect sizes across 71 samples representing 13,369 employees. At the bivariate level, both positive and negative ties have significant relationships with employee outcomes. However, evidence consistent with negative asymmetry emerged only for out-degree ties predicting task performance. In contrast, evidence more consistent with positive asymmetry emerged for in-degree ties predicting task performance and for both in-degree and out-degree ties predicting organizational attachment, although the relationships between in-degree ties and attachment are relatively small. Considerable variation exists around the effect sizes constituting these patterns, suggesting that future research is needed to consider moderating factors that may shift the relative importance of negative versus positive ties. We discuss the implications for refining social ledger theory and for helping practitioners managing social assets and liabilities in organizations.

all.title: Generative AI collaboration and expatriate career adaptability: a career construction perspective on sustainable career development
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.

all.title: Confident and Well‐Connected: The Interplay of Line Managers' HR Self‐Efficacy, Brokerage, and HRM Implementation
institutions: University of Doha for Science and Technology
all.abstract: HRM implementation, defined as line managers' execution of core HRM tasks, has been identified as a key challenge in realizing the competitive advantages associated with HRM. Integrating social cognitive and social network theories, we investigate the joint effect of line managers' HR self‐efficacy (i.e., their confidence in their ability to effectively perform HRM‐related tasks) and their positions as brokers (i.e., their role as intermediaries between otherwise disconnected contacts) in HR advice networks on HRM implementation and establish a link to team performance. Multilevel analyses were conducted using multisource survey data from 88 line managers, their 325 subordinates, and 69 of the line managers' direct superiors across six Indonesian firms. The findings reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, with medium levels of self‐efficacy linked to more effective HRM implementation than either low or high levels. Moreover, line managers' positions as HR information brokers moderate the inverted U‐shaped relationship: The curve remains steeper at low levels of brokerage, but becomes shallower at high levels. Finally, HRM implementation mediates the joint effect of self‐efficacy and HR information brokerage on team performance. Taken together, these findings challenge the assumption of a linear relationship between HR self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, enrich understanding of the social foundations of line managers' HRM implementation, and contribute to broader discussions on the enablers and effects of HRM implementation.

all.title: HR Pacesetter: Workday’s AI Transformation Demands A New Model for Leadership
all.abstract: How is Workday driving its own AI transformation? The answer is a nine-month Change Leadership Program , designed for a critical audience that bridges strategy and execution: 300 key leaders in pivotal business areas. In this episode, we speak with Michael Campbell , Director of Talent Development, and Kristen Hartley , Senior Principal of Executive Development at Workday — a 2026 HR Pacesetter Award winner — about how their team designed the Change Leadership Program, not as a traditional theory-based leadership course but as a dynamic learning experience built around real work application. And the results speak for themselves: measurable behavior change, stronger strategic alignment, and high goal achievement. Among many innovations, Workday’s internal research identified five new leadership dimensions (these are highlighted in our Supermanager work): Directors must lead change , instead of reacting to change Lead in changing the business , not just executing for growth Change leaders need cross-functional connections , not just within their domain Leaders should focus on building scale and lift, not just output. Michael is the Director of Talent Development at Workday, where he leads a team focused on leadership and executive development for enterprise talent. He brings over 20 years of experience, including previous roles as research and custom solution faculty at the Center for Creative Leadership. all.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
all.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: This work was supported by the Bijzonder Onderzoeksfonds UGent [Grant BOF/STA/202009/047]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00955 .

all.title: Queer Social Television: an empowering consumption assemblage explored through RuPaul’s Drag Race
authors: André Luiz Maranhão de Souza Leão
all.abstract: Purpose Social Television (STV) describes the digital engagement of consumers with TV shows. Marketing studies have used this term to investigate how transmedia strategies broaden reach, engagement and co-productive consumption experiences. However, its managerial potential within contexts of gender and sexual dissidence remains overlooked. To explore this gap, this study aims to understand how queer fandom practices (re)configure the STV phenomenon toward the digital engagement of dissident identities. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a year-long netnography on Twitter/X with Brazilian fans of RuPaul’s Drag Race. Findings The findings suggest how discourses and practices are enacted through four interconnected categories of queering work that happen through broadcast, social media, fandom and activism. Social implications Four managerial strategies capable of promoting inclusion and social change are proposed, linking the study to Sustainable Development Goal 10 (Reduced Inequalities). Originality/value This study conceptualizes Queer Social Television and theorize it as an empowering consumption assemblage, explaining its nuances through a Global South perspective. In doing so, it contributes to both STV and Consumer Culture Theory (CCT) scholarships.

all.title: How and when do green HRM practices foster organizational citizenship behavior for the environment? A multilevel approach
all.abstract: Purpose Organizational citizenship behavior for the environment (OCBE) is essential for sustainable development. This study aims to examine how and when green human resource management (GHRM) practices contribute to OCBE. Design/methodology/approach Two waves of multisource data were collected from 737 employees and 84 HR directors in the Chinese hospitality industry. Data were analyzed using robust maximum likelihood estimators in Mplus 7.4. Findings The results show that green organizational climate (GOC) and employee environmental commitment (EEC) serially mediate the GHRM practices–OCBE relationship. Moreover, line managers’ environmental support (LMES) moderates the GHRM practices–GOC relationship. Practical implications The current study suggests that organizations can improve OCBE by implementing GHRM practices and recognizing LMES’s significant role. Social implications Specifically, the authors’ findings offer actionable insights for Global South organizations to support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 12 and SDG 13) by fostering voluntary pro-environmental behaviors. Originality/value This study explains how and when GHRM practices contribute to OCBE.

all.title: How does servant leadership make work meaningful across different societies? A situational strength perspective
all.abstract: Purpose Although prior research has linked servant leadership (SL) with job crafting and organizational identification, its relationship with work meaningfulness (WM) remains underexplored. The purpose of this study is to examine this relationship across ethnically dissimilar cultural contexts to advance situational strength theory (SST). Design/methodology/approach Data from 327 academics at private universities in China and Malaysia were collected via a self-administered questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares path modeling (SmartPLS). Findings The study revealed that job crafting mediates the relationship between SL and WM only in a heterogeneous, but not a homogeneous, society. Moreover, it was observed that organizational identification mediates the relationship between SL and WM in both homogeneous and heterogeneous societies. The findings indicate that ethnic dissimilarity moderates the hypothesized relationships in the research model. Social implications This study provides empirical evidence of how SL fosters decent work (Sustainable Development Goals [SDG] 8) and well-being (SDG 3) among academics, particularly within informal and under-resourced labor markets in the Global South. Originality/value This study offers originality by extending the SL literature to the underexplored outcome of WM, particularly within ethnically dissimilar cultural contexts where leadership effects may vary according to situational cues and cultural diversity. In doing so, the study advances SST by demonstrating how contextual and cultural conditions shape employees’ interpretation of SL behaviors and their experience of meaningful work.

all.title: Gender narratives and female leadership in the Turkish logistics sector
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how and why women in the Turkish logistics sector remain strategically marginalized despite their central contribution to operational continuity. It develops the Operational Core-Margin Paradox (OCMP) as a diagnostic lens for understanding how female leaders’ relational coordination, emotional labor, crisis management and operational intelligence are absorbed into core logistics work while remaining insufficiently recognized as strategic leadership. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a feminist qualitative methodology grounded in feminist standpoint theory and paradox theory. It analyzes publicly available interview narratives of 20 female logistics managers in Turkey, supplemented by two semi-structured interviews, field observation notes and media analysis. A directed qualitative content analysis and feminist discourse analytical approach are used to identify gendered mechanisms of exclusion, recognition gaps and justice-related tensions. Findings The analysis identifies eight interrelated themes: gender-based inequality and discrimination, emotional and strategic competence, visibility and recognition challenges, structural and systemic obstacles, leadership and role modeling, work-family balance and motherhood, internalized masculinity and adaptation, and organizational transformation efforts. The findings show that women’s operational centrality does not automatically translate into strategic authority. Instead, their contributions are often naturalized as care, intuition or support work, producing recognition, procedural, distributive and interactional injustices. The OCMP explains this paradox through the mechanism of functional absorption, whereby women become indispensable to operational resilience while remaining excluded from formal strategic power. Research limitations/implications The study is based on a qualitative sample from the Turkish logistics sector and therefore does not aim for statistical generalization. However, it offers analytical generalizability for other operations-intensive and masculinized sectors where relational coordination and tacit knowledge are essential but undervalued. Future research could operationalize the OCMP quantitatively by measuring the gap between operational centrality and strategic marginality across larger samples. Practical implications The findings suggest that logistics firms should move beyond symbolic diversity initiatives and embed justice-oriented mechanisms into core organizational processes. These include recognizing invisible labor in performance evaluations, auditing promotion and pay systems, expanding mentoring and reverse mentoring structures, supporting flexible work arrangements, and institutionalizing DEI benchmarks. Social implications The study links gender justice in logistics to broader social sustainability goals, particularly Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 5 on gender equality and SDG 10 on reduced inequalities. It argues that inclusive leadership is not only a moral concern but also a condition for sustainable and resilient operations and supply chain management. Originality/value The study contributes to the justice conversation in Operations and Supply Chain Management by introducing the OCMP as a novel analytical framework. It extends gendered organization theory, feminist standpoint theory, and paradox theory by showing how women’s epistemic and operational contributions can be simultaneously utilized and devalued within logistics systems.

all.title: Workplace gender discrimination: key insights, emerging trends, and future research directions
all.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
all.abstract: Workplace gender discrimination has been extensively examined across disciplines, yet its evolving research landscape remains fragmented. This study applies Structural Topic Modelling (STM) to 1,091 peer-reviewed articles published between 1975 and 2024, identifying six major themes: wage gaps, performance evaluation bias, work-family conflict, unequal working conditions, professional inequality, and structural masculinity. Temporal analysis reveals a shift from concerns about pay and promotion towards broader discussions of identity, mental health, intersectionality, and inclusivity. Integrating these findings with related literature, the study develops the Inclusive Impact Matrix, a conceptual framework connecting workplace culture, formal policies, and everyday organisational practices to outcomes including reduced stereotyping, equitable career advancement, work-life balance, professional support, and employee well-being. The matrix illustrates how cultural, policy-based, and practice-based mechanisms can jointly address distinct dimensions of gender inequality, emphasising their alignment rather than isolated interventions. The study contributes by synthesising fragmented research streams and identifying intersectionality and women’s self-neglect under sustained workplace and care-related pressures as areas warranting further investigation. It offers organisational leaders, HR practitioners, and policymakers an evidence-informed framework for advancing workplace equity and inclusion.

all.title: Using AI to Guide Workers
all.abstract: New research shows how LLMs can balance organizational performance with individual priorities. Listen to this article: If AI is integrated into operational and decision-making systems within organizations, it could in effect start to act like a manager. Think of AI in charge of assigning workers to tasks, sequencing work, or distributing resources. Executives who oversee […] The post Using AI to Guide Workers appeared first on Harvard Business School AI Institute .

all.title: AI Transforms Healthcare at Providence: Pacesetter Winner
all.abstract: The healthcare industry is no stranger to challenges around hiring and retaining critical talent. But for Providence , a not-for-profit healthcare system with over 119,000 caregivers, the challenge wasn’t demand—employees wanted to stay and grow. The internal transfer process, however, was getting in the way. In this episode, we speak with Carol McDaniel, Vice President of Talent Acquisition at Providence, a 2026 HR Pacesetter Award winner — about how her team reimagined the internal transfer experience from the ground up, not by patching an existing process, but by rebuilding it entirely through human-centered design. The result is RITA — the Requisition and Internal Transfer Assistant — an AI-powered tool that has not only made transfers seamless—it has also given leaders time back to reinvest in patient care. Carol McDaniel is Vice President of Talent Acquisition at Providence where she focuses on driving hiring innovation, operational effectiveness, and a culture of excellence. She brings more than two decades of experience to her work, with previous roles at Randstad, Delta Airlines, and Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital. You can apply to win a 2027 Pacesetter award , celebrated at Irresistible 2027, May 17-19 in Los Angeles.
