all.title: The Search for Parental Leave and the Early-Career Gender Wage Gap
all.abstract: Gender differences in preferences for parental leave contribute to the early-career growth in the gender wage gap among highly educated millennial Americans. Estimating a hedonic job-search model, I show that, while both men and women experience wage growth by entering firms offering better pay and benefits, the wage gap increases as women accept lower wages upon receiving job offers from employers providing parental leave. The wage-gap growth could decline by 60% if preferences for paid parental leave did not differ by gender. It could also decline if mandating and subsidizing the provision of paid leave muted workers’ leave-wage trade-off.

all.title: LLM time machines: Valuing digital goods over time
all.abstract: Digital goods generate substantial consumer welfare, but their valuations are difficult to estimate because many are free to consumers. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct these valuations over time using incentive-compatible binary choice experiments. We benchmark predictions against eight waves of representative US survey data collected between 2016 and 2024. Calibrating GPT-4-Turbo on one year, we find that it approximates the magnitude and temporal patterns of median human valuations in other years. Newer models do not necessarily improve predictions, tending to favor monetary compensation. Our findings suggest opportunities and limitations for longitudinal valuations using LLMs.

all.title: Automation and Gender: Implications for Occupational Segregation and the Gender Skill Gap
all.abstract: We examine the differential effects of automation on the labor market and educational outcomes of women relative to men over the past four decades. Although women were disproportionately employed in occupations with a high risk of automation in 1980, they were more likely to shift to high-skill, high-wage occupations than men in over time. We provide a causal link by exploiting variation in local labor market exposure to automation attributable to historical differences in local industry structure. For a given change in the exposure to automation across commuting zones, women were more likely than men to shift out of routine task-intensive occupations to high-skill, high wage occupations over the subsequent decade. The net effect is that initially routine-intensive local labor markets experienced greater occupational gender integration. College attainment among younger workers, particularly women, also rose signicantly more in areas more exposed to automation. We propose a model of occupational choice with endogenous skill investments, where social skills and routine tasks are q-complements, and women have a comparative advantage in social skills, to explain the observed patterns. Supporting the model mechanisms, areas with greater exposure to automation experienced a greater movement of women into occupations with high social skill (and high cognitive) requirements than men.

all.title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
institutions: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
all.abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. Zhang is partly supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) [Grant 72394361] and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Mathematical Foundations for Artificial Intelligence [2023B1212010001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01346 .

all.title: Digital drains: the role of IT-related mental fatigue in the relationship between remote work stressors and psychological detachment
institutions: Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design Institute (Group) Co., Ltd (China)
Swinburne University of Technology Sarawak Campus
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effects of information and communication technology (ICT) use during work hours, ICT use after work hours and multitasking on mental fatigue, as well as the impact of mental fatigue on employees’ psychological detachment while working at home. The moderating effect of physical isolation on the relationship between mental fatigue and psychological detachment is also investigated. Design/methodology/approach A self-administered questionnaire was used to collect data from employees in Malaysian firms across various industries; 324 questionnaires were collected and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings The results indicated that ICT use during work hours, ICT use after work hours and multitasking lead to mental fatigue and subsequently contribute to psychological detachment. Physical isolation was not significant in moderating the relationship between mental fatigue and psychological detachment. Research limitations/implications Three limitations are identified. First, this study is industry-neutral and uses data from one country. Therefore, the results may not be generalized. Second, the study did not consider individual differences in the psychological detachment process, which may influence how employees recover from work demands. Third, the study used self-reports, which may have introduced bias and affected the results. Practical implications The findings can guide workplace policies to reduce mental fatigue and manage employees’ psychological detachment during remote work. Social implications If a remote work arrangement is not implemented appropriately, it can lead to work−family conflict and decreased organizational performance. Originality/value While prior research highlights the benefits of psychological detachment for employee well-being, increased psychological detachment resulting from increased mental fatigue in the context of working from home may have both positive and negative effects on employees and organizations.

all.title: Digital leadership and sustainability as catalysts of the dynamic capability cluster: evidence from Central Java’s industrial ecosystem
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to test and bound the orchestration architecture through which technological, cognitive, strategic and behavioural enablers converge into a dynamic capability cluster associated with digital innovation performance. Design/methodology/approach Anchored in the orchestration dimension of dynamic capabilities theory, with resource-based and knowledge-based perspectives serving as input logics, the model was tested using covariance-based structural equation modelling on 312 manufacturing, logistics, technology and service firms in Central Java, Indonesia. Findings Digital infrastructure, algorithmic intelligence, sustainability orientation and digital leadership each predict the capability cluster, with leadership carrying the largest point estimate. The cluster carries every enabler effect to innovation performance; no direct path reached significance. The configuration is indirect-only rather than additive. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, single-informant design constrains temporal inference; the leadership-substitution interpretation remains bounded to institutionally fragile settings pending replication where institutional quality varies. Practical implications Leadership routines and explicit digital decision rights warrant funding alongside the first wave of infrastructure procurement rather than after it. Sustainability criteria belong in project stage-gates. Social implications Building coordinative capacity within firms offers regional programmes a more accessible route to industrial upgrading than infrastructure subsidy. Originality/value The study specifies where the additive resource-to-performance pipeline is not observed: Digital endowment reaches innovation performance through an orchestrated cluster, with no direct pathway detectable in this sample. The contribution is the architecture and the conditions under which it should fail.

all.title: AI in Science Collaboration
all.abstract: On November 16, about 40 researchers, students, and builders, from Stanford and beyond, gathered at Stanford’s Computing and Data Science building to work alongside each other and alongside their AI agents. The question behind the AI in Science Collaboration hackathon was simple: what changes when everyone on a research team brings their own context and their own agent? By design, the day started with 16 two-person teams that merged into eight larger ones, so people had to bring their work, their context and their agents into new groups as they progressed through the day. By the demo, the most interesting answers were less about what agents could build for the people they work for than about how people and agents share what they know to further collaboration.

all.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
all.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore [Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022]. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not reflect the views of the Social Science Research Council (Singapore) and the Ministry of Education (Singapore). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08443 .

all.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
all.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

all.title: Getting Teachers Back to Study: Input-Based Teacher Incentives and Student Achievement
all.abstract: Rewarding teachers on the basis of student performance is a growing trend in educational policy. This paper estimates the effects of a policy that ties payments with teachers’ pedagogical skills instead. We study a large-scale reform in Chile that introduced financial incentives tied to a teacher evaluation system. Using a unique administrative data set of over 500, 000 student-teacher-year matches, we estimate the effect of the policy on student performance exploiting the program’s gradual roll-out through a differences-in-differences analysis. We document precise, null effects of the policy on student math and language standardized test scores. Estimating a structural model of teacher skills and student performance, we show that by making incentives more homogeneous across the distribution of teacher characteristics policymakers can improve the policy’s effects on student performance and overall welfare.

all.title: Cognitive Ambidexterity: Balancing Algorithmic Efficiency and Contextual Judgement in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
all.abstract: AI-enabled decision systems make algorithmic recommendations appear objective and ready for action before contextual, ethical, and stakeholder concerns are fully considered. This study examines how leaders preserve judgment under these conditions. We develop cognitive ambidexterity as a leader-level meta-cognitive capability through which managers balance algorithmic exploitation with contextual exploration in AI-mediated decisions. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first examine five U.K. procurement and infrastructure organizations and identify four mechanisms of cognitive ambidexterity. We then examine these mechanisms through vignette experiments with managers. The findings show that leaders preserve contextual judgment by treating AI outputs as interpretive cues, calibrating trust under ambiguity, slowing decisions when reflection is needed, and building supports that make algorithmic recommendations contestable. The study extends ambidexterity theory by showing how exploration–exploitation tensions are cognitively regulated when exploitation is embedded in algorithmic decision processes. It also uses leadership cognition and Upper Echelons Theory to explain why leaders differ in their capacity to enact this regulation. Together, these insights position cognitive ambidexterity as a critical leader-level capability for using AI’s efficiency gains while preserving the contextual judgment.

all.title: Institutional ambiguity and its dimensions in anti-enslavement arena
all.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how institutional ambiguity enables the persistence of contemporary enslavement. The authors analyze organizations engaged in eradicating slave labor as well as those resisting such efforts. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on interviews, shadowing and documentary analysis, the authors applied Constructivist Grounded Theory to develop a framework linking ambiguity and conflict, and their manifestations within, through, over and against organizations. Findings The findings show that institutional ambiguity not only legitimizes exploitative labor practices but also undermines efforts to combat them. Social implications By addressing the Decent Work and Economic Growth Sustainable Development Goal, this study contributes to organizational theory by demonstrating how ambiguity operates as power that shapes organizational responses to contested social issues and restructures institutional fields. Originality/value This paper derives its originality from being based on previously unexplored data regarding the “Dirty List” and from within an organization that managed the National Pact.

all.title: A call for rebellion: demanding justice in operations and supply chain management
institutions: Escola de Administração de Empresas de São Paulo
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to reflect on the operations and supply chain management (OSCM)-dominant focus on traditional stakeholders (e.g. buying firms, top managers) and its instrumental view of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) to discuss how to position excluded, marginalized and historically underrepresented stakeholders into the OSCM research stream. Design/methodology/approach Through provocative theorizing, the authors problematize how OSCM research can integrate people, especially workers and underrepresented groups, to embrace justice, reduce inequalities and promote social impact. Findings This essay offers insights into structural challenges beyond the empirical context to (re)think research choices and outcomes, recognize what needs to change in OSCM scholarship and practice and embrace novel and impactful research. Social implications This essay highlights different ways to connect OSCM with real-world problems and needs toward societal well-being. Originality/value Aiming to address existing supply chain structural injustices, the authors propose five reorientation shifts: reframing DEI, shifting the unit of analysis, rethinking the source of knowledge, changing the rules of the field and redefining impact. These shifts can transform OSCM into a more diverse, equal and inclusive field.

all.title: Partnerships for development: collaborative governance in blended finance strategies in Brazil
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how antecedent and initial conditions of collaborative governance combine to shape the approval of consortium proposals in blended finance. Using the first BNDES Blended Finance Fund in Brazil, it asks which combinations of organizational resources, expertise, prior relationships and sectoral diversity make consortia more credible to a development finance institution. The study addresses a gap in research on the organizational and relational conditions that precede partnership formation and influence access to development finance. Design/methodology/approach The study applies fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to 27 consortia competing in the BNDES call, eight of which were approved. Six conditions were analyzed: social entrepreneurship expertise, financial expertise, diversity of capital sources, prior relationship with BNDES, sustainability expertise and sectoral diversity. Organizational data were coded from websites and activity reports, aggregated at consortium level and calibrated into set memberships. Necessity and sufficiency analyses were complemented by robustness tests across alternative calibrations and analytical thresholds. Findings Approval is associated with a stable configurational backbone combining social entrepreneurship expertise, capital diversity, prior ties with BNDES, sustainability expertise and sectoral diversity. Sectoral diversity is the condition closest to necessity and becomes necessary under alternative calibrations. Rejection is more equifinal and follows multiple pathways, but the absence of sectoral diversity recurs across all specifications. Financial expertise is not a stable component of approval: its role changes with analytical thresholds, while financially sophisticated but thematically weak or sectorally closed coalitions are consistently associated with non-approval. Research limitations/implications The analysis concerns the selection stage of a single BNDES call and relies on observable organizational attributes, potentially understating informal capabilities and internal governance practices. With 27 cases and six conditions, the study also has limited generalizability despite covering the analyzed proposal universe and conducting robustness tests. Approval may partly reflect BNDES-specific policy preferences, while factors such as project quality, territorial fit and leadership remain unmodeled. Future research should compare programs and countries and track how initial configurations translate into implementation performance and impact. Practical implications Public development banks can treat sectoral diversity as a design criterion rather than merely a scoring bonus, require governance charters defining decision rules and accountability and monitor whether formal diversity produces effective participation. Matchmaking and capacity-building can reduce advantages enjoyed by organizations with prior funder relationships. Applicants should document verifiable socio-environmental experience, while financial intermediaries should partner with mission-driven organizations and adopt governance arrangements that genuinely share authority. Technical assistance and blended-structuring support can help manage the coordination costs created by diverse partnerships. Social implications The findings show that blended finance allocation is also a governance and equity issue. Requiring broader sectoral participation can reduce closed, technocratic coalitions, limit concentration of influence and improve representation of organizations connected to beneficiary communities. Measures that lower entry barriers for actors without prior relationships with development banks can broaden access to public-backed finance. By linking composition, participation and accountability requirements to financing decisions, development institutions can better align blended finance with the public-purpose ambitions of SDG 17 and the equity objectives of SDG 10. Originality/value The study connects collaborative governance theory with the selection stage of blended finance, an area in which antecedent conditions remain underexplored. It shows empirically that actor composition functions as an implicit governance mechanism: funders select not only projects but configurations expected to sustain legitimacy, trust and joint action. The configurational approach reveals an important asymmetry – approval requires a relatively narrow bundle of strengths, whereas rejection can arise through several pathways – and clarifies that financial expertise has conditional rather than independent value when not accompanied by sectoral openness and thematic legitimacy.

all.title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
all.abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

all.title: Redefining smart citizen engagement: an integrative framework for citizen-centric urban governance
institutions: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul
Universidade do Vale do Rio dos Sinos
Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul
all.abstract: Purpose While smart city research has expanded rapidly, citizen engagement remains conceptually fragmented across technological, sociopolitical and critical silos. Addressing this theoretical gap, this study aims to develop an integrative framework for citizen-centric urban governance. It proposes reframing the smart citizen from a passive data provider or service end-user to an active, politically situated cocreator of sustainable urban futures. By synthesizing instrumental efficiency models and critical sociopolitical perspectives, the study articulates the macroscopic drivers, theoretical approaches, systemic risks and normative safeguards conceptualized to foster meaningful civic empowerment in smart cities. Design/methodology/approach Guided by PRISMA protocols, the authors conducted a software-supported systematic literature review of 62 peer-reviewed English articles from Web of Science and Scopus in early 2023. The corpus organically spanned 2015–2022. The authors applied an abductive research design integrating quantitative lexicographical software outputs with qualitative semantic synthesis across five phases: (1) PRISMA search; (2) VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence analysis identifying macroscopic drivers; (3) Iramuteq Descending Hierarchical Classification extracting four theoretical approaches; (4) full-text qualitative cross-analysis generating driver-approach matrices; and (5) abductive theoretical consolidation proposing a 12-risk typology and conceptualizing five foundational governance pillars. Findings The synthesis maps three macroscopic drivers (technological, social and political) and four core theoretical approaches (Community Sense, Critical Perspective, Network Relationship and Solution Development). The cross-analysis indicates two overarching dynamics: positive civic mechanisms and 12 systemic risks (e.g. dataveillance, technocratic determinism and digital exclusion). To address these governance distortions, the study conceptualizes five foundational pillars (trust, inclusiveness, sustainability, transparency and accessibility) as potential structural safeguards. The resulting Integrative Framework offers a conceptual reframing of smart citizenship from passive user compliance toward a political capability to codesign urban futures through two-way open data models and embedded data activism. Research limitations/implications This study relies on a software-assisted systematic review of 62 peer-reviewed secondary sources without direct empirical field validation. Furthermore, the corpus organically spans 2015–2022, reflecting a pre-generative artificial intelligence (AI) theoretical baseline. Future research should empirically test the framework’s five foundational pillars across non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic) urban contexts in the Global South, develop quantitative measurement scales for the 12 systemic risks, investigate emerging generative AI in municipal governance and examine gray literature alongside municipal policy frameworks. Practical implications The framework offers urban managers, municipal leaders and civic technology developers a strategic diagnostic tool for conceptualizing transitions from top-down technocratic efficiency to citizen-centric governance. By proposing the five foundational pillars as potential structural safeguards against systemic risks, the framework offers public agencies pathways to design inclusive digital workflows, promote auditable administrative algorithms and establish transparent public–private–civic partnerships. Ultimately, these pathways are intended to help municipal administrators mitigate corporate data capture, reduce conflicts of interest and preserve civic data as a public common while supporting public service delivery and digital literacy. Social implications By reframing residents from passive data providers to active, politically situated cocreators, the framework supports social equity, digital inclusion and democratic accountability. Operationalizing inclusiveness and accessibility is suggested to help protect non-digitally fluent, elderly and marginalized populations from technological alienation and digital divides. Furthermore, embedding trust and transparency is posited to help buffer civil society against pervasive dataveillance and market-led commodification. Ultimately, these citizen-centric pathways are proposed to align municipal strategies with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 10, 11, 16 and 17). Originality/value This study addresses theoretical fragmentation in smart city research by integrating instrumental technology streams with critical sociopolitical perspectives into a unified sociotechnical ecosystem. Using an abductive research design that combines quantitative bibliometric and qualitative content analyses, it articulates three macroscopic drivers and four theoretical approaches. Its primary originality lies in proposing a novel 12-risk typology of governance distortions alongside a typological architecture of five foundational pillars, conceptualizing normative values as potential structural safeguards and reframing smart citizenship as a political capability to codesign urban futures.

all.title: Professor Brad Bell Named Fellow of the National Academy of Human Resources
all.watch_source: Center for Advanced Human Resource Studies (CAHRS)
all.abstract: ILR professor has received one of the highest distinctions in the human resources profession.

all.title: Two big points from this new Anthropic paper: 1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization &…
all.abstract: Two big points from this new Anthropic paper: 1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization & roles 2) There is wide worker resistance to AI adoption (partially due to point 1) Changes that expand what workers do & share AI gains with them could help. https://www.anthropic.com/research/working-with-ai

all.title: “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
institutions: University of Science and Technology of China
all.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

all.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
all.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

all.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
all.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

all.title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
all.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.17926 .

all.title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
all.abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .

all.title: From patient to purpose: How a cancer diagnosis creates existential liminality to motivate crafting for work-related generativity.
institutions: The University of Texas at Arlington
The University of Texas at Dallas
all.abstract: The life-threatening nature of cancer makes it a unique work-life shock event with distinctive implications for one's work and life. Drawing on inductive analysis of 50 employees with cancer, we theorize how this life-threatening, dynamic work-life shock event forces a reckoning with mortality that existing theory has not captured. This occurs through a process we label existential liminality, where people grapple with tensions of time and meaning, reflecting on what is meaningful in paid and unpaid work within an unknowable mortal timeline. When people have the cognitive space to engage in this process (i.e., when demands are manageable and resources are sufficient), existential liminality can catalyze crafting for generativity across paid and unpaid work. This work extends work-life shock events theory by revealing existential liminality as a unique sensemaking process that differs meaningfully from the identity-focused processes this theory describes. We also challenge the dominant death anxiety-based paradigm in the death awareness research by centering death reflection, a positive but undertheorized pathway with significant consequences for how people invest in work activities. Confronting death, we find, can prompt people to pursue a positive, lasting impact on others through work-related crafting for generativity. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

all.title: When CSR signals fail: perceived quality as a credibility condition for consumer–brand identification
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how corporate social responsibility (CSR) translates into consumer–based brand equity (CBBE) by identifying the mechanisms and conditions underlying this process. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on signaling theory, data from 172 Mexican consumers exposed to a CSR initiative were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings CSR does not generate consumer value through direct effects. Instead, consumer–brand identification acts as the central mechanism linking CSR to CBBE. Empathic concern positively influences identification, but only when perceived quality is high. Under these conditions, effects extend to trust, purchase intention, recommendation intention and engagement. When perceived quality is low, the mechanism collapses. Socially responsible consumption exhibits weak and unstable effects. Social implications Social initiatives are more likely to mobilize consumer trust, engagement and support when social purpose is accompanied by credible organizational performance. Originality/value This study advances CSR research by proposing a conditionally bounded signaling model in which perceived quality serves as the credibility condition that enables or suppresses CSR value creation.

all.title: Experiences of female police officers from the psychodynamic of work perspective
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze pleasure, suffering and defensive strategies among civil police officers at specialized police stations for women, based on the psychodynamics of work. Design/methodology/approach This is a qualitative study with 30 civil police officers in Ceará, Brazil. Data were collected through interviews and analyzed using sense nuclei analysis. Findings Pleasure relates to identity, recognition, practical intelligence and collaboration; suffering relates to workload, violence, institutional constraints and gender discrimination. Subjective conditions predominate. Individual defenses address suffering; collective strategies mobilize and strengthen officers but have limited capacity to prevent illness. Sisterhood emerges as resistance and collective empowerment. Practical implications Mental health monitoring, dialogue and gender equity are recommended. Social implications Findings reinforce public policies on mental health and equity. Originality/value This study extends the psychodynamics of work by highlighting the ambivalence of compensation and repression and proposing sisterhood as collective action beyond adaptation, fostering resistance and transformation.

all.title: From self-awareness to social change: a model of social entrepreneurial intention
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the formation of social entrepreneurial intention (SEI) by extending intention-based models through the integration of mindfulness, social entrepreneurship networks (SENs) and generative consciousness for social innovation (GCSI). Design/methodology/approach Covariance-based structural equation modelling is applied to a sample of 523 university students in Mexico. Findings SENs and GCSI exert significant positive effects on SEI, while mindfulness operates indirectly through GCSI. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design and student sample limit temporal inference and generalizability beyond the Mexican university context. Practical implications Universities and support organizations should strengthen collaborative ecosystems and cultivate critical thinking, ethical sensitivity, empathy and reflective capacities. Social implications The findings support entrepreneurship education aligned with socially responsible action and the sustainable development goals. Originality/value The study validates an integrative framework connecting psychological, ethical and relational dimensions in the emergence of socially oriented entrepreneurial action.

all.title: Cultivating Team Psychological Safety: A Model Rooted in Conservation of Resources Theory
all.abstract: We examine team psychological safety (TPS), the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk‐taking, in its function as a resource caravan passageway. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, we develop a multilevel process model explaining how individual initiative, team interaction, and organizational conditions cultivate and sustain this shared climate, and how it shapes resource protection, investment, and acquisition. Our theoretical model comprises three stages: Cultivation, in which TPS is established, maintained, and nourished; Bloom, in which TPS supports participation, engagement, and sustained performance; and Harvest, in which these processes generate opportunities for resource acquisition across levels. We advance psychological safety research by specifying mechanisms connecting its development and consequences across levels and extend COR theory by explaining how resource caravan passageways are cultivated and renewed.

all.title: Toward an Integrative Model of Layoff Effects: A Strategic Human Capital Resources Framework
institutions: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey
all.abstract: Despite decades of research yielding rich theoretical insights and empirical evidence, the layoff literature remains fragmented. It lacks an overarching framework integrating findings across levels of analysis (e.g., organizational, group, and individual), stakeholder groups (e.g., layoff decision‐makers, executioners, survivors, and displaced employees), and outcomes from proximal processes to distal performance consequences. This fragmentation impedes understanding of how layoff effects unfold and why they vary across individuals and organizations. We review and synthesize layoff research and integrate insights from recent advancements in the strategic human capital resources literature. Our framework explains how layoffs first trigger an outflow of human capital and then reshape the quality, complementarity, and deployment of remaining human capital resources, while shaping the social‐psychological reactions of stakeholder groups. We further identify layoff characteristics as contingencies that determine whether layoffs produce negative or positive shifts in strategic human capital resources states, shape stakeholder reactions, and condition whether individual outcomes aggregate to the organizational level. In doing so, we delineate the organizational‐, individual‐, and cross‐level pathways through which layoffs influence individual performance and, ultimately, organizational outcomes. We offer implications for firms seeking to plan layoffs strategically, manage social and psychological processes, and leverage human capital resources before, during, and after layoffs.

all.title: How do agribusiness start-ups apply the circular economy? Evidence based on the resolve framework
institutions: Universidade do Oeste de Santa Catarina
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how agribusiness start-ups, known as agtechs, adopt circular economy strategies, using the ReSOLVE framework as its theoretical foundation, to understand patterns of circularity implementation within these organisations. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a quantitative approach combining partial least squares structural equation modelling and multidimensional scaling. Data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 155 Brazilian agtechs. Findings The findings reveal a predominance of circular practices focused on the internal efficiency of agtechs, particularly those associated with the actions of optimise, loop and exchange. More collaborative actions, such as regenerate, virtualise and share, were found to be less developed. This pattern suggests a lower level of collaborative maturity, indicating that circularity remains concentrated in internally driven organisational initiatives. Practical implications The findings provide valuable insights for stakeholders, outlining strategies capable of strengthening circularity within the agribusiness sector. Social implications By identifying pathways for implementing circularity within the agribusiness sector, this study contributes to achieving targets related to Sustainable Development Goal 12 of the 2030 Agenda, which promotes responsible consumption and production patterns. Originality/value This study advances the circular economy literature by investigating adoption patterns of the strategies encompassed within the ReSOLVE framework, moving beyond the predominantly descriptive approach to identifying circular practices found in previous studies. Consequently, it extends the application of the ReSOLVE framework as an analytical tool for understanding the circular transition.

all.title: Why Time Management Leads to Well-Being (and Performance)
all.abstract: Time management is usually seen as a way to get more done. Yet research suggests that it is more strongly associated with well-being than with performance. Why time management improves well-being and why the benefits vary remain unclear. This article proposes three pathways linking time management to well-being and productivity. First, structure brings order to daily life by giving people a sense of control and predictability. Second, synchrony aligns activities with social and biological rhythms, reducing conflict and strengthening social ties. And third, concordance aligns activities with personal values and long-term goals, giving daily life meaning and strengthening the connection between present and future selves. These benefits depend on both individual practices and organizational conditions. Fragmented work, excessive demands on people’s time, and a focus on short-term results can obstruct the pathways. An imbalance among the pathways can also turn otherwise useful time management practices into sources of strain. By distinguishing these mechanisms and their limits, the framework helps explain why time management can improve well-being and productivity in some circumstances, have little effect in others, and sometimes make things worse.

all.title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
all.abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Wang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72322017]. Y. Li acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72132007]. Q. Zhang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 724B2024]. all.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
all.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .

all.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
all.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

all.title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability
all.abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. When research indicates that differences in overconfidence are associated with other behaviors, beliefs, or evaluations, researchers should account for the possibility that differences in ability could provide a sufficient explanation. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by the UCLA Anderson Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05184 and https://researchbox.org/1597 .

all.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
all.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .

all.title: Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification
all.abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods and the University of Michigan School of Information for financial support. They also gratefully acknowledge support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy (EXC 2126/2 – 390838866), and from the Center for Social and Economic Behavior at the University of Cologne. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08000 .

all.title: Pengaruh Work-Life Balance Dan Beban Kerja Mental Terhadap Turnover Intention Karyawan Pada PT Alloy Mandiri Food
all.venue: Journal of Business Economics and Management
all.abstract: This study is entitled "The Effect of Work-Life Balance and Mental Workload on Employee Turnover Intention at PT Alloy Mandiri Food". This study aims to examine and analyze the effect of Work-Life Balance ( ) and Mental Workload ( ), both partially and simultaneously, on Employee Turnover Intention ( ) at PT Alloy Mandiri Food. The research method used is quantitative associative with a saturated sampling (census) technique involving 65 operational employees. Primary data collection was conducted through closed questionnaires using a 1-5 Likert scale, adapting NASA-TLX indicators for the Mental Workload variable. Data were processed using multiple linear regression analysis, t-test, F-test, and the coefficient of determination ( ). The results showed the regression equation . Partially, Work-Life Balance has a significant effect on Turnover Intention ( ; Sig. ) with a partial contribution of 27.4%. Mental Workload was proven to be the most dominant positive predictor with a significant effect ( ; Sig. ), contributing 59.7% partially. Simultaneously, Work-Life Balance and Mental Workload significantly affect Turnover Intention ( ; Sig. ) with a simultaneous contribution ( ) of 60.1%, while the remaining 39.9% is influenced by other variables outside the research model.

all.title: Implementasi Peran Pemilik Umkm Dalam Menunjang Strategi Mempertahankan Karyawan Di Tengah Persaingan Tenaga Kerja
all.venue: Journal of Business Economics and Management
all.abstract: This study aims to identify and understand the role of SME owners in implementing employee retention strategies amid labor market competition at Rumah Makan Barokah. This research employs a descriptive qualitative method, using purposive sampling to select three informants, consisting of one business owner and two employees. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and literature reviews. The findings indicate that the business owner plays a direct role in employee management through task allocation, guidance, supervision, and the development of positive working relationships. Employee retention strategies include providing compensation according to the business's financial capacity, offering appreciation, maintaining open communication, addressing employee needs, and creating a comfortable working environment. The challenges encountered include financial limitations in meeting employee expectations and the availability of alternative employment opportunities. This study concludes that attention, support, effective communication, and harmonious working relationships are important elements in supporting employee retention in SMEs.

all.title: Can Voluntary Corporate Transparency Curb Corruption? Community-Level Evidence from Oil and Gas Fields in Africa
all.abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substantive reporting and local opportunities to scrutinize and use the information.

all.title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
all.abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06801 .

all.title: Workforce Analytics for Talent Retention and Organizational Growth
all.abstract: Workforce analytics has become an important strategic tool for improving talent retention and organizational growth. Analytical techniques examine the influence of workforce analytics on employee engagement, workforce stability, and organizational sustainability. Employees from various sectors were surveyed using a structured questionnaire for data collection. The analysis employs regression, SEM, ANN, bibliometric analysis, text mining concepts and a longitudinal view of workforce trends. The results showed that workforce analytics significantly improves employee retention, communication, transparency and workforce planning. The model, that uses ANNs, has achieved 91.2 percent prediction accuracy. The study has identified that the AI-enabled HR systems are becoming increasingly relevant for organizational managerial decision-making and long-term organizational performance.

all.title: ROLE OF HR ANALYTICS IN IMPROVING EMPLOYEE RETENTION AND WORKFORCE PLANNING IN ORGANISATIONS
all.abstract: Human Resource (HR) Analytics, also known as people analytics or workforce analytics, involves the systematic use of employee-related data and analytical methods to support human resource decisions. This paper examines how HR Analytics can contribute to employee retention and workforce planning. Employee turnover creates direct and indirect costs, while ineffective workforce planning can lead to skill shortages, overstaffing, workload imbalance and disruption to organisational performance. Drawing on published research and established human resource management theories, the paper discusses how descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics can help organisations understand workforce patterns, identify retention risks, forecast staffing requirements and evaluate HR interventions. The literature indicates that analytics can strengthen evidence-based decision-making when reliable data, appropriate analytical skills, managerial support and employee trust are present. However, predictive models cannot fully explain an employee’s decision to stay or leave, and careless use of employee data may create privacy, fairness and surveillance concerns. The paper recommends a gradual, transparent and human-centred approach in which analytics informs, rather than replaces, professional judgement. The study is based entirely on secondary sources and does not claim to have collected original survey or interview data. Keywords: HR Analytics, people analytics, employee retention, employee turnover, workforce planning, predictive analytics, human resource management.

all.title: HR Analytics for The Employee Productivity Enhancement: A Theoretical Perspective
all.abstract: Human resource is recognized as the major asset of the organization. In global business environment it is accepted that an effective human resource management can be a competitive advantage for the organization. Investment on manpower of the organization, its utilization contributes for the overall organizational success. Cost of manpower is to be managed effectively. Otherwise, it may be a bottleneck problem for the organization. During Covid19 it is proven that various cost of the organization can be avoided but not cost of manpower, at the same time HR is the asset will contribute more for performance of the organization. Strategic human resource planning can strengthen the organizational activity. Proper management of effective and efficient manpower increase level of the organization. HR analytic can be the source used for the purpose. Technological development in all the areas created the need of collecting and analysing data frequently for the future decisions. In the same way data related to manpower availability, performance, turnover is essential for managing the constant, effective and efficient human capital. The purpose of this study is to analyse the need and importance of HR analytics in different HR functions. This study focusses on analysing how HR analytics contribute in employee productivity enhancement in the organization.

all.title: The Strategic Impact of HR Analytics on Talent Management: A Bibliometric Review
all.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the evolution and structure of scientific production on HR Analytics and its relationship with strategic human talent management. A quantitative, descriptive, and retrospective study was conducted using a bibliometric approach applied to 60 scientific publications from 2019 to 2026. The results identified 190 unique authors, 860 accumulated citations, and an h-index of 18. Scientific production was mainly concentrated in 2024 and 2025, while collaboration networks revealed relatively fragmented research clusters. Keyword co-occurrence analysis highlighted human resource management, decision-making, and artificial intelligence as the predominant thematic areas. The findings indicate that HR Analytics is an expanding research field characterized by the convergence of analytical capabilities, organizational management, and emerging technologies.

all.title: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Data-Driven Employee Performance Management through HR Analytics
all.abstract: Human resource management is changing as organisations increasingly use digital systems and workforce data, and employee performance management is one area where this change is most relevant. Traditional appraisal systems often rely on a manager's memory, personal judgement, and feedback given only once or twice a year. Such practices may overlook employees' daily contributions and raise concerns about fairness. HR analytics can help organisations use workforce data in a more structured way. However, collecting data alone does not improve performance. For data to be useful, it must be accurate, relevant, and used carefully by managers who understand both the work and the people involved. This paper develops a conceptual framework to explain how HR analytics may support performance management. It adopts a qualitative approach based on secondary sources, drawing on research related to HR analytics, appraisal, organisational justice, evidence-based management, and human resource development.The framework explains two connected pathways. The first is an employee-focused pathway, in which useful performance information reduces avoidable subjectivity, improves perceptions of accuracy and fairness, and encourages employees to accept feedback and improve their work. The second is a management-focused pathway, in which HR analytics supports better decisions on goal setting, performance gaps, learning and development, and workforce planning. The framework also highlights data quality, appropriate technology, HR analytical skills, leadership support, and ethical safeguards. It argues that analytics should support, not replace, human judgement.

all.title: Impact of HR Analytics on Organizational Performance: A Study of Central Coalfields Limited (CCL), Ranchi
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: In today's dynamic business environment, HR Analytics has become a key element in any organization and they are increasingly adopting it to improve their organization's effectiveness as well as performance. HRA helps organizations to make better decisions based on data related to employees in areas like recruitment, selection, training, performance appraisal, etc. This study, "Impact of HRA on Organizational Performance – A Study on CCL Ranchi," focuses on understanding the impact of HRA and how it influences the performance of CCL as an organization. The main focus revolves around the role of HRA in improving employee productivity, efficiency, training needs and effectiveness, decision-making process, and workforce planning in the organization. It also attempts to identify various challenges faced by CCL while adopting HRA effectively. The research relies on an extensive review of literature that aims to provide evidence for the impact of HRA on OP. Through a quantitative approach, primary data has been collected through a structured questionnaire and interactions with various employees and HR officials of CCL, Ranchi. The findings are expected to demonstrate how HRA enhances OP by assisting management in making more precise, data-driven HR decisions, and may also help CCL, Ranchi in better adopting and improving its HR practices. Overall, this study emphasizes the growing importance of HRA in modern organizations and how it contributes to their performance, organizational growth, and effectiveness.

all.title: Employee Attrition Predictive Modeling Using CRISP-DM: A Supervised Learning and Workforce Analytics Framework
all.venue: Transactions on Engineering and Computing Sciences
all.abstract: Employee turnover represents a critical operational, financial, and strategic bottleneck across contemporary enterprise environments, frequently incurring replacement expenditures ranging between 50% and 200% of an annual salary while eroding institutional human capital. This study presents a rigorous end-to-end predictive modeling framework adhering strictly to the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) methodology to identify empirical risk factors and reliably forecast voluntary employee turnover prior to formal resignation. Leveraging a curated enterprise human resources dataset encompassing 1,270 personnel records across 35 multi-modal attributes, rigorous data sanitation, automated zero-variance filtration, and factor encoding were performed alongside Exploratory Data Analysis, Recursive Partitioning (Decision Trees), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Unsupervised K-Means clustering ( ). Supervised predictive models—specifically Binomial Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes Classification—were trained and benchmarked against an independent 30% test holdout ( ) and further validated against a 200-record unseen verification holdout. The primary institutional research goal was to determine whether voluntary attrition could be classified with an accuracy exceeding 70.0%. Experimental results demonstrate that Logistic Regression substantially outperformed Naïve Bayes, achieving a test accuracy of 88.71% (95% CI: 85.10%–91.71%), an Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.8282, a sensitivity of 98.11%, and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.4906. When evaluated against the unseen verification cohort, the model demonstrated outstanding generalization capability with an accuracy of 91.00%, a sensitivity of 98.80%, an improved specificity of 51.52%, and a Kappa of 0.6064. Key empirical predictors of attrition identified include overtime commitments, business travel frequency, tenure without promotion, distance from home, and reported environmental satisfaction. A modular production turnover pipeline and ethical governance framework are formalized to operationalize real-time individual risk stratification while safeguarding against algorithmic bias.

all.title: Digital maturity, green HR analytics, and sustainable logistics performance in agri-food supply chains
