institutions: Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital

all.title: Writing with AI, Speaking with Confidence: Exploring the Role of Artificial Intelligence in English Language Development
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools, including Grammarly, ChatGPT, and QuillBot, have increasingly become integrated into students' academic practices, particularly in English as a Second Language (ESL) contexts. Despite their growing use, empirical evidence concerning students' patterns of engagement with these tools and their perceived contribution to English-language development in Pakistani higher education remains limited. This study investigated undergraduate students' frequency of AI-tool use, perceptions of their contribution to English writing and speaking skills, and challenges associated with their use. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 300 BS students from the University of Sargodha, Pakistan, recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected using a 16-item questionnaire comprising closed-ended questions, five-point Likert-scale statements, and two open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, one-sample t-tests against the scale midpoint, Cohen's d effect sizes, 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and chi-square goodness-of-fit tests. The findings indicated that ChatGPT (43.3%) and Grammarly (33.3%) were the most frequently used AI tools, while 73.3% of participants reported using AI tools at least three to four times per week. Students expressed favourable perceptions of AI-assisted writing support, with mean scores ranging from 3.80 to 4.17; all reported differences were statistically significant (p < .001), with moderate-to-large effect sizes (d = 0.79–1.16). Perceptions of speaking-related benefits were comparatively less pronounced, with mean scores ranging from 3.30 to 3.83. In particular, the perceived contribution of AI tools to pronunciation development was relatively limited, although statistically significant (M = 3.30, p < .001, d = 0.27). Furthermore, 46.7% of participants acknowledged that they sometimes copied AI-generated output rather than using it as an opportunity for independent learning. Overall, the findings suggest that students primarily perceive AI-based tools as supplementary resources for improving written accuracy and developing linguistic confidence, whereas their perceived contribution to speaking development is comparatively constrained. The findings can be interpreted in relation to Krashen's Input Hypothesis and Affective Filter Hypothesis, Swain's Output Hypothesis, and Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development. Nevertheless, given the study's reliance on self-reported data and a convenience sample drawn from a single institution, the findings should be interpreted cautiously and cannot be generalised beyond the study context without further investigation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; AI-assisted language learning; English as a Second Language (ESL); English-language writing; speaking proficiency; second language acquisition; ChatGPT; Grammarly; Pakistani higher education.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and green human resource management integration for sustainable organizational performance: a systematic review
all.venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
all.abstract: The latest research on the integration of Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for sustainable organizational performance is compiled in this systematic literature review (SLR). Digital transformation has emerged as a key factor in both environmental sustainability and organizational resilience in the context of Industry 5.0. The analysis looks at how AI can strategically support employee-level organizational performance, green training and development, and green recruitment and selection. Using the PRISMA methodology, 118 records were first found by searching Scopus and Web of Science between 2021 and 2026. Following a five-step screening procedure, 18 publications satisfied the inclusion requirements. Three additional peer-reviewed research articles published in 2025–2026 were later identified through supplemental citation chasing to increase the currency and depth of the evidence base, bringing the final synthesis to 21 rigorously vetted, Web of Science- and/or Scopus-indexed studies. Results show that AI significantly enhances sustainable organizational performance and environmental decision-making, although algorithm aversion and ethical governance issues limit its effectiveness. The Integrated AI-Enabled Green HRM Sustainability (AI-GHRM-S) framework, which unifies micro-level (AMO Theory, Social Cognitive Theory), meso-level (Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory), and macro-level (Stakeholder Theory, ethical AI governance) explanations of how AI-enabled Green HRM translates into sustainable organizational performance, fills a theoretical gap found throughout the reviewed literature. For practitioners, researchers, and policymakers seeking sustainable performance through appropriate integration of AI and Green HRM, the review provides useful information.

all.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Online Learning: A Dual-Path Model of Learner Autonomy and Cognitive Dependence
all.venue: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science
institutions: Faculty of Economics and Management of Sfax
all.abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education ranges from seeking formative hints to delegating the reasoning required by an assignment. These practices cannot be adequately distinguished by consultation frequency alone. This study examines how constructive and substitutive GenAI use relate to self-regulated learning, perceived cognitive dependence, learner autonomy, and perceived learning in Tunisian online higher education. A cross-sectional online survey, reported as conducted between October 2025 and March 2026, comprised an analytic sample of 300 students. Eight proposed constructs were represented by 24 five-point self-report items, combined into three-item scores. Twelve direct hypotheses were examined using six ordinary least squares regressions of standardized composites, with HC3-robust confidence intervals. Evaluative AI literacy and perceived pedagogical scaffolding were positively associated with constructive use (β = 0.423 and 0.323), and this equation explained 33.5% of its in-sample variance; the corresponding substitutive-use equation explained 3.6%. Constructive use was positively associated with self-regulation (β = 0.459), autonomy (β = 0.255), and perceived learning (β = 0.257). Substitutive use was positively associated with perceived dependence (β = 0.377), but its adjusted relationship with self-regulation was not significant (H9: β = −0.018; 95% CI [−0.120, 0.085]; p = 0.738). These findings suggest that perceived difficulty working without AI and general study regulation should be examined separately. However, the recruitment denominator and response-screening procedures are not documented in the reported materials, and the abbreviated measures lack item-level factorial and discriminant-validity evidence. All variables are self-reported; the design cannot establish causal effects or objectively demonstrated learning. These limitations delimit the contribution and establish priorities for reproducible measurement analysis and independent assessments of reasoning retained after AI use.

all.title: Electricity infrastructure and artificial intelligence innovation: Evidence from China's ultra-high-voltage grid expansion
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on continuous, reliable, and affordable electricity supply, yet empirical evidence on how large-scale energy networks affect frontier AI technologies remains limited. Using a balanced panel of 282 Chinese cities from 2006 to 2024, this study exploits the staggered commissioning of ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission projects as a quasi-natural experiment and applies a staggered difference-in-differences design to examine the effect of UHV infrastructure on AI innovation. The results show that connection to an operational UHV network significantly increases city-level AI innovation. This finding remains robust after accounting for treatment-effect heterogeneity, pre-trends, placebo tests, potential endogeneity, sample selection, overlapping policies, and nonlinear economic relationships. Further analyses show that UHV infrastructure lowers industrial electricity prices and mitigates the adverse effect of extreme climate risks on electricity-supply stability, thereby providing lower-cost and more resilient energy conditions for AI-related R&D. The positive innovation effect is concentrated in cities with stronger initial digital infrastructure, indicating that energy and digital networks are complementary inputs into AI innovation. Firm-level evidence further shows that UHV infrastructure expands firms’ opportunities to engage in AI-related activities, whereas stronger local AI innovation is associated with greater AI-related capital investment and recruitment, less AI disclosure, and lower AI talk-action inconsistency.

all.title: Association between artificial intelligence literacy and clinical reasoning competency among nurses: a cross-sectional study
institutions: State Key Laboratory of Oncology in South China
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence in healthcare has increased the need for nurses to understand, evaluate, and apply artificial intelligence-related information. From the perspective of Cognitive Load Theory, AI-generated information may increase the cognitive demands of clinical decision-making, while strong clinical reasoning competency may help nurses organize and process this additional information more effectively. Clinical reasoning competency may therefore be associated with artificial intelligence literacy in AI-assisted clinical contexts. This study examined the association between clinical reasoning competency and artificial intelligence literacy among nurses in China. A convenience sample of 306 registered nurses was recruited from healthcare institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Data were collected using the professional online survey platform SO JUMP.28, including participants’ sociodemographic information, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, and the Nurse Clinical Reasoning Scale. The statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, the Mann-Whitney U test, the Kruskal-Wallis H test, Spearman’s correlation, and multiple linear regression. Nurses’ AIL had a median total score of 90.00 (IQR = 79.00–97.00). Each dimension of artificial intelligence literacy was significantly positively correlated with clinical reasoning competency ( r = 0.289–0.551, P < 0.001). After adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, multiple linear regression analysis showed that clinical reasoning competency ( β = 0.509, P < 0.001) and highest educational degree ( β = 0.111, P = 0.047) were independently associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Clinical reasoning competency is an important cognitive capability associated with artificial intelligence literacy. The close relationship between these two competencies highlights the importance of considering both clinical reasoning competency and artificial intelligence literacy in nurses’ professional development and artificial intelligence-related education. Not applicable.

all.title: Attitudes towards risks and benefits of using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for African American family members of a person with dementia
all.abstract: Adopting generative AI (GenAI) technologies in health care is imminent, making it urgent to address systemic barriers to equitable technology. GenAI has the potential to alleviate the burden on healthcare professionals and care coordination by crafting personalized messages for family members of a person with Alzheimer's Disease and Related dementia (ADRD) who are at high risk. We conducted a cross-sectional online survey from April 8 to May 3, 2024, among 527 family members of a person with ADRD or memory issues, recruited via social media and flyer postings at an urban medical center. We applied machine learning techniques to characterize demographic and caregiving factors that predict attitudes toward the risks and benefits of using GenAI for caregiving. We examined these factors across three representative scenarios at the individual level of the socioecological model. Notably, Black or African American participants were more than twice as likely as White participants to express an overall positive view of the AI tools (OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.43-3.48; p<0.001). While the benefits of using GenAI for family members were recognized well among all age groups, those aged 25-34 expressed more caution. Engaging these younger family members as community partners is critical to identifying anticipated risks and to ensuring that GenAI implementation promotes health equity rather than reinforcing existing disparities for high-risk populations.

all.title: Machine learning-based prediction of initial gonadotropin dosage in antagonist protocols
all.abstract: This study aimed to construct a machine learning-based predictive model to determine the initial gonadotropin (Gn) dose in antagonist protocols. The GnRH antagonist protocol has become increasingly prevalent in IVF treatment due to its shorter duration, reduced risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and improved patient convenience compared to the long agonist protocol. However, determining the optimal initial Gn dose in antagonist protocols presents unique challenges due to the shorter suppression period and more rapid follicular recruitment. Inappropriate initial dosing can lead to severe clinical consequences, including ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) with excessive dosing, or poor ovarian response and cycle cancellation with insufficient dosing. Current formula-based approaches and nomograms relying on simple linear regression show limited predictive accuracy, particularly for complex cases requiring dose modifications. A retrospective analysis was conducted using data from 1,970 women undergoing antagonist protocols at Peking University People’s Hospital between October 2016 and December 2021. Two advanced machine learning models were selected after preliminary evaluation of multiple algorithms: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), a powerful ensemble learning method using gradient boosting on decision trees, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), a neural network with multiple layers. These models were chosen for their superior performance in handling nonlinear relationships and high-dimensional medical data compared to traditional linear regression, random forest, and support vector regression approaches. LGBM demonstrated superior overall performance with test set MAE of 53.25 IU and R² of 0.527, significantly outperforming the baseline formula (MAE 61.03 IU, R² 0.298). MLP achieved the lowest mean relative error (0.212) compared to baseline (0.271). In complex cases requiring dose modifications, LGBM achieved MAE of 67.53 IU, substantially lower than the clinical adjustment error of 87.07 IU, demonstrating the model’s ability to provide more accurate dosing recommendations than clinician estimates in challenging scenarios. Machine learning models, particularly LGBM, offer substantially greater predictive accuracy than conventional formula-based approaches for determining initial Gn dose in antagonist protocols. These findings support the integration of machine learning-based decision support systems into clinical practice to enhance dose optimization, potentially improving IVF outcomes, reducing complications, and decreasing treatment costs. Future research should focus on prospective multicenter validation, development of user-friendly clinical interfaces, and exploration of advanced deep learning architectures to further enhance predictive performance. Not applicable.

all.title: Data Marauders and Organised Data Warriors for Hire in the Liquid Order: From Historical Private Force to Algorithmic Neo-Contractors and the Rise of Contestable Security Constructors
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper examines the emerging possibility of organised data marauders and data warriors for hire as a structural feature of the liquid order. Drawing on the analysis of trans-sovereign force, algorithmic neo-contractors, cyber-mercenaries and private sector offensive actors, it traces historical precedents of private violence and information operations through to contemporary zero-day markets, commercial spyware, narrative laundering and LLM data poisoning. These actors operate across strategic, infrastructural, algorithmic and cognitive domains, exploiting the inverse law of sovereign accountability. The paper connects this development to the rise of independent security constructors who offer Dual-Core compatible, contestable services rather than pure extraction. Within the Flow Sovereignty and Reserve of Humanity framework, such constructors can be integrated as peripheral agents whose morphisms remain auditable, while unconstrained data marauders constitute a cohomology threat. The analysis closes with architectural propositions for containing the former and constraining the latter under Permanent Systemic Instability. KSCCN article (3 pages).

all.title: Perceptions and ethical-legal challenges of artificial intelligence among Spanish healthcare professionals: a cross-sectional survey study
all.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the healthcare sector is generating growing debate about its ethical and legal implications. Empirical data on the perceptions of Spanish healthcare professionals in this field remain scarce. An observational cross-sectional study was conducted using an anonymous, voluntary, ad hoc opinion questionnaire directed at Spanish healthcare professionals. Non-probability convenience and snowball sampling was used, with a recruitment target of 385 participants; responses were received between 18 May and 4 July 2023. Descriptive and bivariate analyses were performed using chi-square tests (exact tests when expected counts were small). A total of 398 questionnaires were analysed. The majority (75.1%) reported being unfamiliar with AI in the healthcare sector. While 50.8% were uncertain whether AI is currently improving healthcare, 58% considered it beneficial for their work and 70.4% believed it would improve healthcare in the future. The main ethical concerns were dehumanisation of medicine (70.1% of participants), technological failure (62.1%), access barriers (54.5%), and lack of clarity regarding responsibility for medical acts (54.0%). The vast majority (94.5%) considered specific regulation necessary. In exploratory bivariate analyses (40 comparisons, no correction for multiple testing), eight associations reached p ≤ 0.05, involving sex, age group, years of experience, and professional category. Spanish healthcare professionals show an ambivalent perception of AI, recognising its future potential while expressing uncertainty about its current impact. These findings highlight the need for targeted training programmes and a comprehensive regulatory framework for AI in Spanish healthcare. Given the exploratory nature of the study, findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

all.title: Generative artificial intelligence-related concerns among medical students in the West Bank, Palestine: a cross-sectional study
all.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical education. However, concerns about its professional, ethical, and psychological implications for future physicians remain insufficiently studied, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study assessed GenAI-related concerns among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, using the Fear, Anxiety, Mistrust, and Ethics (FAME) scale. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling via online recruitment was conducted among medical students at Palestinian universities between March and April 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic and academic characteristics, prior GenAI tool use, self-reported level of AI concern, and FAME scores. Non-parametric tests and multiple linear regression were used for analysis. Results Of 399 participants included in the analysis, 96.0% reported using ChatGPT. The median total FAME score was 40 (IQR, 35–45). Median domain scores were highest for Mistrust and Ethics, both with a median score of 11, compared with Fear and Anxiety, both with a median score of 9. Male students had higher Fear and Anxiety scores than female students, but total FAME scores did not differ significantly by gender. In the exploratory adjusted regression model, no sociodemographic, academic, or AI-use variable was independently associated with the total FAME score, and the overall model explained only a small proportion of score variability. Conclusions GenAI use was widespread among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, with higher median scores observed in the mistrust and ethics domains than in fear of professional displacement. None of the variables included in the exploratory multivariable model was independently associated with total FAME score. Structured AI-literacy education addressing ethical reasoning and critical appraisal of AI-generated information may represent a potential educational implication of these findings.

all.title: Associations of Moral Sensitivity and Metacognition with Artificial Intelligence Ethics Awareness Among Clinical Nurses: The Potential Mediating Role of Technostress
all.abstract: Background/Objectives: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare, understanding nurses’ awareness of AI-related ethical issues is essential. Although previous studies have examined ethical and cognitive factors associated with AI ethics awareness, the potential role of technology-related stress among practicing nurses remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the associations of moral sensitivity and metacognition with AI ethics awareness and explored indirect associations through technostress. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 120 clinical nurses recruited from four tertiary hospitals in the Republic of Korea. Moral sensitivity, metacognition, general information and communication technology-related technostress, and AI ethics awareness were assessed using self-report questionnaires. Exploratory indirect associations were estimated using regression-based path analysis with 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI ethics awareness was positively correlated with moral sensitivity (r = 0.36), metacognition (r = 0.33), and technostress (r = 0.22) (all p < 0.05). A positive indirect association between moral sensitivity and AI ethics awareness through technostress was observed (indirect estimate = 0.058, 95% bootstrap CI [0.008, 0.135]). The corresponding indirect association for metacognition was not statistically significant (−0.037, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.104, 0.006]). Metacognition showed a significant direct association with AI ethics awareness despite a non-significant total association. Conclusions: The findings provide preliminary evidence of associations among ethical sensitivity, metacognitive characteristics, general technostress, and AI ethics awareness in clinical nurses. Although a positive indirect association involving moral sensitivity was observed, its statistical significance was sensitive to individual observations, warranting cautious interpretation. Longitudinal studies with larger samples and AI-specific measures are needed to clarify these relationships.

all.title: Artificial intelligence and human-centred OSCE preparation: A national mixed-methods study of UK pharmacy students' comparative perceptions
all.venue: Currents in Pharmacy Teaching and Learning
institutions: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust

all.title: Predicting late-pregnancy depression using machine learning: A longitudinal study with external validation
institutions: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Depressive symptoms in late pregnancy is a serious public health issue with profound effects on maternal well-being and infant development. Developing a data-driven predictive model for depressive symptoms in late pregnancy can facilitate early identification and provide a basis for timely intervention. METHODS: Six machine learning (ML) models were compared by nested cross-validation (5 × 3 repeats), including Lasso Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Multilayer Perceptrons, Naive Bayes, Random Forests, and Extreme Gradient Boosting. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) was used for the assessment of depressive symptoms during pregnancy. The models were evaluated on accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Matthews correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were utilized to improve model interpretability and highlight important predictive features. The development cohort comprised 713 pregnant women at 28-36 weeks of gestation recruited during prenatal visits at the obstetrics clinic of a major hospital in Wuhan, China. For temporal external validation, a separate cohort of 515 pregnant women at 37-40 weeks of gestation was recruited at the same clinic during a later period. RESULTS: The Lasso Logistic Regression model outperformed the other models in terms of predictive accuracy and generalizability in the temporal external validation. Key predictors of depressive symptoms in late pregnancy included early-pregnancy insomnia symptoms, EPDS score, and fear of pregnancy. The model demonstrated robust performance in temporal external validation, offering an effective tool for predicting depressive symptoms in late pregnancy. CONCLUSION: This study developed a reliable and interpretable ML model for the early identification of women at high risk of depressive symptoms in late pregnancy. The findings suggest that ML, particularly Lasso Logistic Regression, can be integrated into prenatal care to enhance early screening and facilitate timely intervention for high-risk women, improving maternal mental health outcomes. We further developed a web-based tool to facilitate the clinical application of the model.

all.title: Explainable AI: Making Machine Learning Decisions Transparent And Interpretable — A Review Of Methods, Evaluation And Human-Centred Explanation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Machine learning models increasingly influence decisions in healthcare, finance, hiring and public services, yet many of the most accurate models are complex black boxes whose reasoning cannot be inspected. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make these decisions transparent and interpretable so that users can understand, trust, debug and contest them. This paper reviews XAI as a general discipline rather than for a single domain. It clarifies concepts of interpretability, explainability, transparency and faithfulness, and organizes methods into inherently interpretable models, global explanations such as partial dependence and accumulated local effects, local feature attribution with LIME, SHAP and integrated gradients, visual explanations for deep networks, concept-based explanations and counterfactuals. Evaluation of explanations, including sanity checks that reveal misleading saliency maps, and insights from social science on what makes a good explanation are discussed. A five-layer explainable ML pipeline comprising data, model, explanation engine, evaluation and audience-specific presentation is proposed, with research gaps, objectives, a comparison of methods and challenges such as the accuracy–interpretability trade-off, unstable explanations and regulation. The review concludes that explanations should be faithful, evaluated and designed for the people who use them.

all.title: Measuring Technostress Among Tunisian Remote and Hybrid Engineers: A Descriptive Study and Preliminary Psychometric Assessment in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
all.venue: Cureus Journal of Business and Economics.
all.abstract: Remote and hybrid work are now common in software engineering, although their prevalence varies across countries and firms. They expose engineers to a form of psychological strain known as technostress, which the spread of generative AI tools in development practices has renewed. To our knowledge, no study to date has measured technostress among Tunisian engineers. This study offers a first descriptive mapping of technostress in this population, along with a preliminary psychometric assessment of the scales used to measure it. A cross-sectional quantitative survey was conducted among 85 Tunisian engineers working fully remote or hybrid, recruited through Facebook groups and pages for Tunisian IT professionals between March and May 2026. The questionnaire, administered via Google Forms, measured techno-overload, techno-complexity, AI-related techno-insecurity, techno-isolation, well-being, and work-couple conflict among respondents in a relationship (n = 53). The structure of the instrument was examined through an exploratory factor analysis of the 17 technostress items, and its relationship to well-being was explored through linear and logistic regression and an interaction analysis. Techno-complexity (M = 3.70) and techno-overload (M = 3.12) were the highest-scoring dimensions, ahead of AI-related techno-insecurity (M = 2.79) and techno-isolation (M = 2.37). The scales showed satisfactory to good internal consistency (alpha between 0.74 and 0.91). The factor analysis supported four factors, with every item loading on its intended scale. The four scores were almost uncorrelated with one another, a pattern that is unusual in this literature and needs testing on a larger sample. AI-related techno-insecurity was negatively associated with well-being in every analysis, but the significance of this association depended on how well-being was measured. The relationship between techno-isolation and well-being appeared to differ by telework arrangement. It was negative among hybrid respondents and reversed, without reaching significance, among the 12 fully remote respondents. This study offers a first measurement of technostress among Tunisian remote and hybrid engineers, with preliminary evidence of scale reliability and structure, for future larger-scale research. It also points to two exploratory leads, AI-related techno-insecurity, and telework arrangement. Limitations include the small sample size (n = 85), non-probability sampling limited to a single recruitment channel, newly written scales without external validation, and the cross-sectional design.

all.title: AASHA Net AI: An Offline-First, Voice-Based Health Record Assistant for ASHA Workers Using a Large Language Model
all.venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology
all.abstract: Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) record health information during household visits in rural India, often without reliable internet access and usually in a regional language. Typed, connectivity-dependent mobile forms make this documentation slow and error-prone. This paper presents AASHANet AI, an offline-first, voice-based health record assistant. A Flutter application stores every record on the device first and synchronises it with a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend through an idempotent, versioned three-step protocol that guarantees exactly-once server records under retries and detects conflicting confirmations instead of overwriting them. Voice notes in Kannada, Hindi or English are processed by the Google Gemini large language model, which returns a transcript, an English translation and schema-validated fields (patient name, age, symptoms and duration) that the health worker reviews before confirmation. The system was verified with 44 backend tests (5 against PostgreSQL), 41 mobile unit and widget tests, including 17 synchronisation fault-injection scenarios, and a live end-to-end run against the real services. Measurements showed that model selection dominates latency: on the same recording, processing took 3.0–3.4 s with one model and 96–302 s with another, which motivated configurable model fallback with time limit.

all.title: Interventions Regulating Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI and Subsequent Independent Performance: A Systematic Review Protocol
all.abstract: This systematic review examines interventions designed to regulate cognitive offloading to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and their effects on subsequent independent performance in educational and employee development contexts. The review aims to identify how interventions structure the distribution of cognitive work between individuals and GenAI, evaluate their effects on learning and task performance after AI assistance has been withdrawn, and examine the conditions under which these effects may differ. Eligible evidence will include comparative experimental and quasi-experimental studies assessing independent knowledge, skills or task performance following GenAI-supported activities. Electronic searches were conducted in six bibliographic databases and preprint repositories, followed by deduplication and pilot screening. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data. The review will use structured descriptive synthesis, supplemented by meta-analysis where the evidence permits. Risk of bias will be assessed using JBI tools, and certainty of evidence for key outcomes will be evaluated using GRADE. The expected contribution is an evidence-based understanding of which approaches to regulating cognitive offloading have been evaluated, what effects they produce on independent performance, and how confidently these effects can be interpreted. Findings may inform the design of GenAI-supported education and employee development activities.

all.title: Using the Tool That Replaces You: Generative AI and the Adoption Bind among Bangladeshi Platform Freelancers
all.abstract: Platform studies show that generative AI has reduced demand for freelance writing and image work, and experiments show that it makes individual workers faster. This letter asks how these two findings look to workers who are both users of the technology and exposed to it. I analyze 30 interviews with Bangladeshi online freelancers, conducted in Bangla between May and August 2025. Twenty-one participants used generative AI in their own work, sixteen said that it was replacing freelance work, and thirteen said both. Eleven of the sixteen placed replacement on others: on beginners and workers who do not update their skills, on "basic" tasks, or on other sectors. Participants also described how prices fell as tasks became faster, and how clients cited AI to offer less. I propose the term adoption bind for this pattern: each worker adopts generative AI to stay on the safe side of the line, while the same tools, in the hands of competitors and clients, lower what the market pays for the work. The bind suggests that productivity gains measured for individuals can become price losses for workers as a group, and that these losses fall first on entry-level work.

all.title: Short-Term Efficiency, Long-Term Cognitive Cost? A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Use in Professional Work
all.abstract: Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasks faster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledge they would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences of LLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studies remained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work. Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experienced workers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than ten studies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work, impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lowerself-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track performance. Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiency gain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose a framework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

all.title: Polysexuality-Informed Value Alignment for General-Purpose Generative AI: A First Exploratory Framework and Blind Comparative Evaluation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The alignment of general-purpose generative artificial intelligence (AI) with diverse human values remains a central challenge in responsible AI development. Existing approaches have extensively examined helpfulness, harmlessness, fairness, human preferences, and broad value pluralism. However, the explicit operationalization of principles inspired by polysexuality as a value-alignment condition for general-purpose generative AI has received little direct empirical attention. This study introduces Polysexuality-Informed Value Alignment (PVA), an exploratory framework that translates selected principles associated with recognition of diversity, individual autonomy, non-discrimination, contextual understanding, value pluralism, equitable representation, and mutual respect into a configurable system-level alignment condition. To the best of the author's knowledge, this study is the first explicitly designed and experimentally evaluated investigation of polysexuality-informed value alignment for general-purpose generative AI using a baseline-controlled, blind comparative design. The experiment employed a general-purpose language model, tpgic-gemma3-4b, to generate responses under two conditions: an unmodified baseline and a PVA-informed condition. Eight scenarios covering education, workplace inclusion, technology, social conflict, public policy, health and wellbeing, communication, and sustainable community wellbeing produced 16 responses. A second model, tpgic-qwen3-4b, evaluated the responses through randomized X/Y blind comparisons using six dimensions: value adherence, task competence, resistance to harmful compliance, resistance to sycophancy, communication without excessive preachiness, and avoidance of unnecessary refusal. All 16 generations and eight evaluations were completed successfully. The baseline achieved higher mean scores across all six dimensions. The mean paired differences (PVA minus baseline) were −0.375 for value adherence, −0.750 for task competence, −0.375 for resistance to harmful compliance, −0.375 for resistance to sycophancy, −0.375 for communication without excessive preachiness, and −0.250 for avoidance of over-refusal. In the blind preference assessment, the baseline was preferred in six scenarios, the PVA condition in one, and one comparison was tied. These exploratory findings do not demonstrate an improvement from the current PVA implementation. Instead, they identify a potential trade-off between introducing an explicit identity-informed value framework and maintaining general-purpose response quality. The study establishes an initial experimental foundation for investigating identity-informed value alignment and motivates context-adaptive approaches that preserve task competence while applying relevant values proportionately.

all.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations
all.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

all.title: Cognitive Offloading and Automation Bias in Generative AI-Assisted Learning Systems: A Systematic Review and Secondary Evidence Synthesis
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in learning systems is growing rapidly and is changing the way people learn, solve problems and make decisions. Cognitive offloading refers to the transfer of mental tasks such as remembering, reasoning and evaluating to external systems, while automation bias describes the tendency to rely on the output of automated systems in place of independent judgement. Both phenomena are more visible in generative AI settings, because these systems produce fluent, human-like responses that imitate the process of reasoning itself. Over-reliance on generative AI can therefore threaten intellectual independence and accountability for decisions: it tends to reduce verification behaviour, weaken skill development and increase the risk of reasoning errors, particularly in educational and workplace learning. This paper examines the role of cognitive offloading and automation bias in generative AI-supported learning systems through a systematic review and secondary evidence synthesis of recent empirical studies from educational, technical and professional fields. The results show that unstructured use of generative AI is frequently associated with lower cognitive engagement and greater reliance on automation, and that these effects are reduced by structured and guided interaction models. The paper argues for a human-centred strategy for integrating AI into learning and outlines directions for future research on long-term cognitive outcomes and responsible AI-based learning design.

all.title: Hindu Value-Aligned General-Purpose Generative AI: A Dharmic Framework for Cross-Domain Behavioral Alignment and Preliminary Experimental Evaluation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The development of general-purpose generative artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified the need for alignment approaches that can guide system behavior across heterogeneous tasks, including programming, scientific reasoning, education, business, interpersonal communication, and everyday decision-making. Although existing AI ethics research increasingly recognizes the importance of cultural and philosophical diversity, translating specific philosophical traditions into operational behavioral guidance for general-purpose generative systems remains an important research challenge. This paper introduces Hindu Value-Aligned General-Purpose Generative AI (HVAGAI), a framework that integrates Hindu philosophical and ethical principles into the behavioral guidance of a general-purpose generative AI assistant without restricting its functionality to religious subject matter. Unlike religion-specific conversational systems, HVAGAI treats Hindu-inspired values as cross-domain behavioral principles that influence how an AI system responds to ordinary and ethically sensitive requests alike. The proposed framework operationalizes nine interconnected dimensions: Dharma (responsible conduct and contextual duty), Ahimsa (non-harm), Satya (truthfulness), Karma (consequence-aware reasoning), Seva (constructive contribution), Daya (compassion), Aparigraha (moderation), Atma-Vichara (reflective examination), and contextual interpretation informed by Hindu philosophical plurality. A preliminary local feasibility experiment was conducted using Gemma 3 4B as the response generator and Qwen3 4B as the blind evaluator. Eight scenarios covering ordinary programming, educational explanation, data analysis, manipulative advertising, unsupported interpersonal suspicion, résumé dishonesty, scientific overclaiming, and unsustainable work practices were evaluated under baseline and HVAGAI-guided conditions. All 16 requested generations were completed successfully, and all eight paired evaluations produced valid outputs. The evaluator identified meaningful behavioral distinctions in several ethically sensitive scenarios, including concerns about manipulative assistance, unsupported agreement, excessive moralization, and harmful productivity recommendations. However, the available experimental log does not preserve the randomized evaluator-label mapping required to attribute X/Y scores to the two experimental conditions. Consequently, this study reports qualitative feasibility observations rather than claiming a statistically established performance advantage. The findings provide preliminary evidence that a Hindu-inspired ethical constitution can be operationalized as a general-purpose behavioral guidance mechanism and motivate more extensive evaluation across models, domains, cultural contexts, and human judgments.

all.title: Human expert-generated flexibility program versus single-attempt AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro)-generated flexibility program for office workers: a quasi-randomized controlled trial
all.abstract: Sedentary office environments contribute to flexibility loss and musculoskeletal disorders. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers scalable rehabilitation, its clinical reasoning and biomechanical safety remain scrutinized in academic literature. This study compared the efficacy of 15-minute home-based flexibility exercises designed by human experts versus those generated by AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro) on flexibility, lower back health, and muscle stiffness. In this quasi-randomized controlled trial, 30 male participants were allocated to a Human Expert Group ( n = 15) or an AI Group ( n = 15) using a random start (single coin toss) followed by alternating allocation, which differed from the wording of the ethics-approved application (simple random method, coin toss) and carries a risk of selection bias. Interventions lasted 4 weeks (3 days/week). Assessments included Sit-and-Reach tests, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and MyotonPRO stiffness measurements. Initially, the groups exhibited similar characteristics ( p > .05). In the Sit-and-Reach test, a measure of flexibility, the average score for the human expert group increased from 14.93 ± 10.67 cm to 22.60 ± 11.49 cm, while in the artificial intelligence group, this value reached only from 16.23 ± 7.91 to 17.53 ± 7.60 cm; a statistically significant Time × Group interaction with a large effect size was detected between the groups (F(1,28) = 28.26, p < .001, ηp² = 0.502). A significant Time × Group interaction was also found for the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) (F(1,28) = 7.49, p = .011, ηp² = 0.211). Following Benjamini–Hochberg False Discovery Rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity adjustment across the eight interaction tests, statistically significant Time × Group interactions robustly survived for Sit-and-Reach flexibility ( p < .001), Oswestry Disability Index ( p = .011), dominant biceps femoris stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.01, p = .003, ηp² = 0.282), and non-dominant gastrocnemius stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.16, p = .002, ηp² = 0.285) in favor of the human expert group. In contrast, the Time × Group interaction for dominant erector spinae stiffness was nominally significant prior to adjustment only (F(1,28) = 4.41, raw p = .045, ηp² = 0.136) and did not survive FDR correction. No significant interactions were observed for the remaining muscle groups ( p > .05). Based on the observed Time × Group interaction effects, human expert-generated programs containing dynamic and static flexibility exercises yielded significantly greater improvement over time in flexibility and lower-back health than the single-shot static stretching program generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro. These findings highlight the short-term efficacy of the specific expert-designed dynamic protocol rather than demonstrating a generalized limitation of generative AI in exercise prescription. Trial registration : The study was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov under the number NCT07242287. (Date of Registration 11/17/2025)

all.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
all.abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

all.title: Scholarly Editing and AI Co-Working as Practice
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) can productively act as a co-worker in scholarly editing, not by replacing editorial judgement but by accelerating complex, repetitive tasks that depend on established forms of critical reasoning. Drawing on historical examples of digital scholarly editing, it situates generative AI within a longer trajectory of machine-assisted approaches and distinguishes computational systems that reveal patterns in textual data from those that propose interpretative decisions. Its principal case study is the C21 Editions Project, which experimented with generative AI and retrieval-augmented generation to produce a teaching edition of Chaucer’s The Pardoner’s Prologue and Tale. The experiments found that approximately 64% of AI-generated translation was satisfactory, while only 13% of AI-generated annotation and topic-summary text required editorial intervention when prompts were supported by curated knowledge resources. These findings demonstrate both the potential for reducing editorial labour and the limitations of generative AI, whose outputs remain dependent on expert prompting, source selection and critical evaluation. The article proposes a model of human–AI co-working in which editorial expertise shifts from the repetitive execution of established procedures towards methodological design, supervision and evaluation. It concludes that realising the potential of machine-assisted scholarly editing will require transparent, trustworthy and intuitive human–AI interaction tools and editorial workbenches.

all.title: Fully automated safety monitoring via sensor-based agentic LLM with Model Context Protocol
Artificial Intelligence–Empowered Knowledge Management and Technological Innovation: A Systematic Review, Bibliometric Analysis and Research Agenda
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of knowledge work in organisations. However, research on how AI affects technological innovation through knowledge management (KM) remains fragmented. This study combines a bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review. Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR, it analyses 232 Web of Science articles and reviews published up to 27 October 2026. The analysis uses performance analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, co-word analysis, and thematic mapping. A core sample of 65 studies is then synthesised. The field has grown rapidly since generative AI tools were released, and 70.7% of the documents appeared in 2025–2026. Output is concentrated in the Journal of Knowledge Management and in China. The intellectual base of the field combines the knowledge-based view, organisational learning, absorptive capacity and dynamic capabilities with recent work on AI capability and human–AI augmentation. Five research fronts are identified: AI and organisational learning in innovation; AI capability, green KM and sustainable innovation; AI in KM processes and knowledge sharing; knowledge transfer and ecosystems; and knowledge graphs for technological innovation. The synthesis shows that AI affects innovation indirectly, through knowledge creation, storage and retrieval, sharing and application. This effect depends on absorptive capacity, learning orientation, complementary resources and employees’ responses to AI. Knowledge risks, such as leakage and the loss of human exploration, can offset the benefits. The study proposes an integrative framework with five propositions and a research agenda based on the theory–context–characteristics–methodology framework.

all.title: Anticipated-Response Shaping of Conduct: Silent Engagement, Withheld Disclosure, and the Evidence Others Receive
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper introduces Anticipated-Response Shaping of Conduct, a mechanism in the Relational Conditions and Dynamics series of On Human Modeling. Drawing on published empirical studies, it examines how an expected reaction changes conduct before anyone responds. That expectation becomes part of the history of the action or omission that other people or systems later interpret. In a 2012 diary study, a Facebook user held back a link to an article about cohabitation and divorce. She wanted to avoid a drawn-out exchange with friends who objected to couples living together. The study documents her reported expectation and her decision to withhold the link. What her friends made of the omission remains open. The case raises a question about how to interpret conduct whose visible form leaves its reasons undisclosed. Research on AI use at work examines a related expectation. Participants imagining generative AI use expected to appear lazier and less competent and reported lower willingness to disclose their use than participants imagining a dashboard tool. A separate study measured evaluators’ judgments of employee profiles describing AI assistance. These findings concern expectations, stated intentions, and evaluations within hypothetical scenarios. The paper also considers withholding personal information in simulated hiring tasks and a 2014 experiment in which participants told that a virtual interviewer was automated were rated as more willing to disclose. An expected evaluation can therefore bear on both withholding and expression. The analysis asks what response was expected, what evidence shows that the expectation influenced conduct, and what another person inferred from the result.

all.title: Desire Path: Follow the Clicks Volume Two
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Desire Path: Follow the Clicks Volume Two is an illustrated technology and business mangazine by Maphi Bayolo. The publication brings together the second set of ten essays in the Desire Path series, examining the unofficial routes people create through work, technology, artificial intelligence, governance and institutional systems when the official path no longer reflects reality. Combining editorial essays, manga-inspired visual storytelling and reflective commentary, Volume Two explores themes including attention and long-form value, labour market transition and who carries its cost, the timing of AI adoption, judgement and taste as emerging skills, workplace presence and security clearance, accessibility and reasonable adjustments in hiring, enterprise software and the changing cost of building, corporate public benefit funds and who shapes the safety net, reusable candidate identity and AI assessment in recruitment, and the penalties attached to honest AI disclosure. Volume Two also marks the expansion of Desire Path beyond written posts into video, with short-form work on TikTok and long-form storytelling on YouTube, including the series The Hiring Circus. As in Volume One, the publication documents its own AI-assisted creative process, distinguishing the author’s ideas, lived experience, editorial judgement and final decisions from the roles played by generative AI tools during research, discussion, drafting and development. Volume Two contains: The Attention Value Problem Who Pays for the Transition? Experiment Early. Commit Late. Got Any Taste? What Exactly Is in the Building? Why Do I Need to Be Here? The Reasonable Adjustment Inquisition Nobody Is Rebuilding SAP. So Why Does the Renewal Feel Different? If Charity Begins at Home, Who Decides Who Lives There? Workday Graded You a D Once. Does Its AI Still Know? The Disclosure Trap Published by Desire Path Mangazine.Official website: https://desirepathmangazine.com

all.title: LLM-Assisted Co-Optimization of RTL and Synthesis Algorithms via Bottleneck Analysis
all.abstract: Post-synthesis power, performance, and area (PPA) depend jointly on the register-transfer-level (RTL) code and the synthesis algorithms. However, the benefits of RTL optimization may be limited by bottlenecks in synthesis algorithms, and vice versa, leaving opportunities for better PPA unexplored by methods that optimize either level alone. In this work, we present a large language model (LLM)-assisted framework for regional co-optimization of RTL and synthesis algorithms via bottleneck analysis. A key insight behind our approach is that RTL structures and the Boolean networks used in synthesis expose complementary opportunities for addressing bottlenecks that lead to suboptimal PPA in different regions of the circuit. Our bottleneck analysis uses a Gaussian process (GP) to assess whether optimizing RTL or synthesis algorithms is more promising for each region. The GP learns from regional graph representations and PPA feedback. Using the GP's predictions and predictive uncertainty, Bayesian optimization (BO) provides guidance that an LLM Router combines with circuit analysis to choose how to address each region's bottlenecks. Self-improving LLM workers then optimize the RTL or synthesis algorithms in their assigned regions, and their regional changes are greedily integrated into the current design configuration. Experiments on 16 RTL designs show average improvements of 103.27% in worst negative slack (WNS), 1.23% in area, and 13.26% in power relative to the initial designs. These improvements exceed those of the strongest baseline for each metric by 47.80, 2.75, and 13.17 percentage points, respectively.

all.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
all.abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

all.title: Large language models in education: How have research hotspots evolved? A longitudinal scientometric analysis
all.venue: Iberoamerican Journal of Science Measurement and Communication
all.abstract: Objective. This study examined the evolution of China-affiliated scholarship on large language models (LLMs) in education following the ChatGPT debate. It analyzed the transformation of this scholarship into diverse research domains, including pedagogical, technical, and evaluative aspects. Design/Methodology/Approach. To this end, a comprehensive set of records was retrieved for the period spanning from 2018 to 2026, employing a meticulous approach that entailed the utilization of criteria such as LLM, education, Chinese institutional affiliation, and date. The screening cascade, as reported, reduced a total of 2,212 records to 539 articles, conference papers, and reviews that exhibited explicit LLM/model signals and education-centered titles. The analysis incorporated a multifaceted array of methods, including descriptive scientometrics, citation indicators, institutional productivity and affiliation summaries, controlled thematic coding, and seven-topic term frequency–inverse document frequency/non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) modeling. Results/Discussion. The final corpus, which was scheduled to commence in 2023, encompassed a total of 20 publications in 2023, 90 publications in 2024, 244 publications in 2025, and 185 publications in the partial-year 2026. Research attention shifted from broad discussions of opportunity, ethics, and adoption to more specialized topics such as teaching design, agentic/retrieval-augmented generation learning systems, empirical feedback and cognitive outcomes, and model-performance evaluation. Tsinghua University and East China Normal University were identified as the most prolific affiliations, with a total of 519 Chinese institutions represented in the corpus. The field exhibited rapid thematic differentiation, rather than merely volume growth. Conclusions. The publication record shows a broader range of research topics after 2023, particularly in instructional design, learning systems, feedback, and model evaluation. These findings reflect shifts in scholarly attention, not changes in classroom practice. Originality/Value. This study employs a multifaceted approach that integrates longitudinal NMF topic modeling with controlled thematic coding, aiming to elucidate the dynamics of scholarly attention. Sensitivity tests were conducted to assess the membership of the five leading controlled themes. The set's integrity remained uncompromised, irrespective of the exclusion of records from the partial-year 2026 period or the implementation of a more rigorous education-title criterion. The restriction to articles and reviews yielded four of the five themes. These tests did not assess the stability of NMF topics or institutional findings. The 2026 results describe a partial year through September 16.

all.title: AI-Assisted Regulatory Intelligence and Adaptive Compliance Verification System for Banking Supervision
all.abstract: Regulatory requirements issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) fall into categories including numerical thresholds, deterministic conditions, temporal obligations, and qualitative standards such as ''adequate due diligence,'' each of which requires a different mode of verification. Bank employees and officers must first locate and interpret the appropriate requirement among an ever-growing corpus of Master Directions, circulars, and notifications, while the regulator must independently verify (at scale) whether submitted bank evidence satisfies the requirement. We present a two-module regulatory intelligence system that addresses both sides of this problem in a single pipeline. The Regulation Comprehension module ingests an RBI circular or Master Direction and segments and categorizes its clauses, extracts a typed and machine-readable rule representation, simplifies regulatory language for reading by humans, and enables natural-language question answering with clause-level sourcing. The main technical contribution is an adaptive reasoning-modality router that determines, for a given regulatory requirement and evidence set, whether a deterministic rule engine, a retrieval-based large language model (LLM), or human escalation should be used, governed by an explicit cost--accuracy--latency objective and a hard architectural override that directs fully specified deterministic rules and complete evidence to the rule engine unconditionally. This differs from the well-studied task of routing between LLMs of differing capability, since our router chooses among fundamentally different reasoning mechanisms rather than among models. We also contribute a rule-grounded synthetic RBI compliance benchmark across nine difficulty categories and a dedicated regulation-comprehension benchmark design (with extraction, question-answering, and simplification variants), such that the two modules can be evaluated with equal rigor rather than treating comprehension as a subordinate preprocessing step, yielding two distinct sets of metrics, baselines, and ablation points, each for one of the modules, across extraction accuracy, retrieval and answer-faithfulness, simplification quality, compliance accuracy, and routing efficiency. We also contribute an evidence-grounded explanation architecture that traces every such decision and comprehension answer to a specific rule, clause, and evidentiary or source field. Since operational bank data cannot be accessed for confidentiality and regulatory reasons, evaluation is performed on a synthetic, rule-grounded benchmark of 1,393 cases drawn from 215 rules. On the 294 held-out test cases, whose rules were never seen in training or tuning, the adaptive router reaches 92.2\% automated accuracy and 96.9\% end-to-end accuracy, compared with 85.4\% for a fixed hybrid router, 72.5\% for retrieval-augmented LLM-only reasoning, and 56.8\% for LLM-only reasoning, and ablations show that removing adaptive routing, the rule engine, or evidence grounding lowers accuracy. Adversarial and ambiguous cases remain the hardest. All results are on synthetic rather than operational bank data, the decisions of the LLM reasoning paths in these runs were produced by a deterministic surrogate of the LLM judge, and results of the regulation-comprehension benchmark are not reported in this paper.

all.title: Cognitive Science of Co-Intelligence 1.0 / 協働知性認知科学 1.0
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Abstract This study proposes Cognitive Resource Reallocation Theory as a foundational framework for understanding how sustained collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence transforms human cognitive activity. Rather than treating AI primarily as a tool for automation, productivity enhancement, or knowledge retrieval, the study examines how human–AI collaboration can reorganize the allocation of finite human cognitive resources and enable new forms of intellectual development. Human cognitive capacity is constrained by biological limitations in working memory, attention, processing speed, and information management. Traditionally, substantial cognitive resources have been devoted to foundational operations such as memorization, information retrieval, calculation, document composition, and data organization. The emergence of advanced AI systems makes it possible to externalize significant portions of these operations, thereby creating opportunities to redirect human cognitive resources toward higher-order intellectual activities. The central proposition of Cognitive Resource Reallocation Theory is that AI-assisted cognitive offloading enables human cognitive resources to be reallocated toward abstract reasoning, structural recognition, discrepancy detection, creativity, conceptual architecture, and long-term strategic thinking. This transformation is interpreted not merely as an increase in task efficiency, but as a structural reorganization of human intellectual activity. The study further examines the relationship between cognitive maturity and co-intelligence. While certain cognitive functions, including processing speed and working-memory performance, may decline with biological aging, accumulated experience, contextual judgment, and structural understanding can provide complementary intellectual strengths. Human–AI collaboration is therefore proposed as a mechanism through which operational limitations may be compensated for while mature cognitive capabilities are more effectively utilized. Within this framework, the Concept Architect is introduced as a model of human intellectual activity centered on conceptual design, structural synthesis, and strategic judgment. Furthermore, the study proposes a co-evolutionary model of co-intelligence in which human intellectual development, improvements in AI capabilities, and the accumulation of structured knowledge interact through mutually reinforcing processes. This dynamic may produce cumulative and potentially compounding intellectual growth, extending the significance of co-intelligence beyond individual tasks toward the development of an evolving cognitive ecosystem. The framework is also examined in relation to scientific research, education, enterprise management, public policy, and creative production. An accompanying historical perspective considers writing, printing, computing, and digital information technologies as earlier stages of cognitive externalization, positioning generative AI within a broader history of transformations in human cognitive resource allocation. This study establishes the conceptual foundations of the Cognitive Science of Co-Intelligence, defining sustained human–AI collaboration as an integrated cognitive system and a distinct subject of scientific investigation. Future research will require empirical measurement of cognitive resource reallocation, comparative studies across age groups and professional domains, and longitudinal investigations into how continued AI collaboration influences human cognitive development. The resulting perspective suggests that the fundamental significance of AI lies not only in expanding what humans can accomplish, but also in transforming how human intelligence allocates its resources, develops its capabilities, and participates in the creation of knowledge. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-1530-4234 Matsuoka × GPT Thought-Experiment Lab Japanese Abstract 本研究は、人間と人工知能の継続的な協働が人間の認知活動をどのように変化させるのかという問題に対し、「認知資源再配分理論(Cognitive Resource Reallocation Theory)」を提案するものである。従来のAI利用論が業務効率化、作業の自動化、知識検索能力の向上を中心としてきたのに対し、本研究は、人間とAIの協働によって有限な認知資源の配分構造そのものが変化し、新たな知的発展が可能になるという視点を提示する。 人間の認知能力は、作業記憶、注意、情報処理速度、情報管理能力などの生物学的制約を受けている。従来の知的活動では、記憶、情報検索、計算、文章構築、情報整理などの基礎的認知処理に多くの認知資源が配分されてきた。しかし、高度な人工知能との協働によって、これらの処理の相当部分を外部化することが可能となり、人間の認知資源をより高次の知的活動へ再配分する条件が形成される。 本研究が提示する認知資源再配分理論の中心命題は、AIによる認知負荷の外部化によって、人間の認知資源が抽象思考、構造認識、違和感検知、創造性、概念設計、長期戦略思考などへ再配分され得るというものである。この変化は単なる作業効率の向上ではなく、人間の知的活動における認知資源配分の構造的再編として理解される。 さらに本研究は、認知成熟と協働知性の関係を考察する。加齢に伴って情報処理速度や作業記憶などの能力が低下する場合がある一方、長年の経験によって培われる判断力、文脈理解、構造認識能力などは、異なる発達特性を持つ。AIとの協働は、基礎的認知処理の負担を補完しながら、成熟した人間知性の強みをより効果的に発揮させる可能性を持つ。この枠組みの中で、概念設計、構造統合、戦略的判断を中心的役割とする「コンセプトアーキテクト」の認知モデルを提示する。 また、人間知性の発展、AI性能の向上、知識基盤の蓄積が相互に作用する「協働知性の共進化モデル」を提案する。このモデルでは、人間とAIの反復的な協働によって知的成果が蓄積され、それが次の知的活動の基盤となることで、累積的かつ複利的な知的成長が生じる可能性を考察する。協働知性は、個別の作業を支援する技術にとどまらず、継続的に発展する知的環境として位置づけられる。 本研究では、この理論を学術研究、教育、企業経営、政策立案、創造活動などの領域へ適用する可能性についても検討する。さらに付録では、文字、印刷技術、計算機、インターネットなどの発展を認知機能の外部化という観点から整理し、生成AIによる認知資源再配分を人類史における知的技術の発展過程の中に位置づける。 以上を通じて本研究は、人間とAIが継続的に協働する統合的知的システムを研究対象とする、「協働知性認知科学(Cognitive Science of Co-Intelligence)」の概念的基盤を提示する。今後は、認知資源再配分の定量的測定、年齢や専門分野による比較研究、長期的なAI協働が認知活動へ及ぼす影響の実証的検証などが課題となる。 本研究が提示するのは、AIによって人間が何を実行できるようになるかという従来の問いを超え、AIとの協働によって人間知性そのものがどのように再編され、発展し、知識創造へ参加するのかという、新たな認知科学的研究視点である。

all.title: SCAFFOLD-CF: Causally Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Employee Turnover and Attrition
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Counterfactual explanations identify feature changes that can flip a classifier’s prediction, but most methods treat features as independently mutable, producing recourse that conflicts with specified causal relations. This study proposes a formalized causal structure using two conditions: changes are either deliberate interventions or rule-entailed consequences, and entailed consequences are realized. Thus, SCAFFOLD-CF is proposed, which enforces both requirements as hard filters that a candidate counterfactual must respect. The main advantages of this method are the actionability and real-world alignment that a causal-aware counterfactual produces, alongside its ability to handle trade-offs with cost and manifold considerations. The method initially builds a library of candidate interventions, applies clipping, causal propagation, and snapping. It then filters candidates for predictive validity, causal admissibility, local density, and a query-scaled confidence margin before selecting diverse counterfactuals from a four-objective Pareto front. The method is evaluated against ten causally-agnostic baselines, the causally-aware ProCE, and a soft-constraint variant that penalizes causal violations as an objective, assessing cost, manifold conformity, and causal consistency. A stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA) aggregates three metric families and is extended with a penalty that prices abstentions. Conformity with the rule set is a property of the filter’s design. The alternatives differ: ProCE departs from the declared rules on 14.4% and 13.9% of returned counterfactuals, and the soft-constraint variant on 54.3% and 28.0%. The guarantee costs coverage, with SCAFFOLD-CF abstaining on 10.5% and 6.6% of queries. Before pricing abstentions, it is preferred under 51.5% of sampled weightings on the first dataset, 35.0 percentage points above the next method, and ranks second on attrition. Pricing abstentions reverses the attrition result, with SCAFFOLD-CF leading from a 2% penalty, and bounds the turnover result, where it leads until the penalty reaches 80% before the full-coverage causal baseline overtakes it. It is envisaged that SCAFFOLD-CF’s hard causal filter and Pareto front improve causal consistency while remaining competitive on trade-offs with other metrics, measured against an assumed rule set on employee-turnover data.
