Beyond Quit Intention: Implicit–Explicit Attitude Profiles, Uncertainty Stress, and Stage-Based Smoking Cessation Status Among Chinese Young Adult Smokers
all.abstract: Background: Smoking behaviour change is commonly conceptualized as a stage-based process, yet stage-based cessation status, quit intention, and cessation action may be associated with psychological factors beyond self-reported motivation. Dual-attitude theory suggests that implicit and explicit attitudes may jointly relate to smoking behaviour, while uncertainty stress may further influence these associations. This study examined the associations of implicit–explicit attitude profiles with smoking behaviour change and the moderating role of uncertainty stress among young adult smokers. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of 292 Chinese smokers aged 18–35 years from a source sample of 659 adult smokers. Participants were classified into four implicit–explicit attitude profiles based on SC-IAT and self-reported attitudes. Ordered and binary logistic regression models examined associations of attitude profiles with stage-based cessation status, quit intention, and cessation action, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Uncertainty stress was examined as a moderator. Results: Compared with the consistent positive profile, the consistent negative profile was associated with higher odds of being at a later stage of behaviour change (OR = 6.02, 95% CI 2.78–13.03), having quit intention (OR = 5.27, 95% CI 2.08–13.31), and reporting cessation action (OR = 6.75, 95% CI 2.37–19.47). The implicit positive-explicit negative profile showed similar associations with stage of behaviour change (OR = 4.78, 95% CI 2.13–10.70), quit intention (OR = 5.81, 95% CI 2.09–16.12), and cessation action (OR = 3.96, 95% CI 1.31–11.94). Higher uncertainty stress was associated with greater odds of behaviour change, while interactions between uncertainty stress and attitude profiles indicated smaller differences between profiles at higher stress levels. Conclusions: Implicit–explicit attitude profiles were differentially associated with stage-based cessation status, quit intention, and cessation action, and these associations varied by uncertainty stress. Assessing both implicit and explicit attitudes alongside psychological stress may provide a broader basis for understanding individual differences in smoking behaviour change among young adult smokers.

all.title: When turnover intention translates into action: the influence of having a boundaryless mindset and time
Analisis Continuous Improvement pada PT Tera Data Indonusa Tbk. Periode 2023-2025
all.abstract: The computing device manufacturing industry faces dynamic challenges that require the implementation of continuous improvement as an organizational capability. This study aims to analyze the implementation of continuous improvement at PT Tera Data Indonusa Tbk (AXIO) during the 2023-2025 period and evaluate its progress across five key dimensions: quality, employee turnover, revenue and sales, innovation, and customer loyalty. This study employs a descriptive qualitative approach with a case study design based on secondary data obtained from the company’s annual reports. The findings indicate that quality improvement and innovation have been systematically implemented through ISO standards and product updates, although quantitative data, such as product defect rates, remain unavailable. Human resource performance improved, as reflected in a decrease in employee turnover from 37% to 14%. Net revenue grew by 31% in 2025, driven by a strategic shift toward the retail segment. However, the net profit margin declined due to a surge in operating expenses that remained insufficiently controlled. Furthermore, the high level of customer satisfaction does not necessarily demonstrate long-term loyalty due to the lack of repeat purchase data. This study recommends that AXIO balance sales growth with cost efficiency, diversify its commercial segment, and report more measurable performance indicators to ensure the sustainability of continuous improvement.

all.title: Family First: CEOs' Private Incentives in Corporate Relocations
all.abstract: Using novel data on executives’ families, we identify CEOs’ private motives in moving corporate headquarters (HQ). CEOs systematically relocate HQs closer to their families over plausible location alternatives. Over 35% of relocations place the new HQ within 50 miles of the CEO’s children and away from production sites and industry clusters. Such relocations entail negative announcement returns, higher employee turnover, and weaker insider reviews. Using an out-of-state marriage of a CEO’s child as an instrument for the CEO’s location preferences, we show that executives’ private incentives affect corporate migration.

all.title: Effectiveness of Performance Management System: A Study on Selected Cement Manufacturing Units in the Kalyan-Karnataka Region
all.abstract: The study focuses on examining the various components of performance management and how they are implemented in selected cement manufacturing units located in the K.K region. It adopts systematic approaches to assess and improve the effectiveness of the PMS. A convenience sampling technique was employed, with a sample size of 300 respondents drawn from top-level and middle-level management. Primary data were gathered through a structured questionnaire. The PMS plays a crucial role within organizations by evaluating, encouraging, and enhancing overall performance. It also aligns individual and organizational efforts with clearly defined goals, there by supporting the development of goal oriented organizational culture. To ensure long term stability and productivity, organizations need to recognize and implement distinctive employee retention strategies.

Mental Health Initiatives of Employers in Fostering Employee Well-Being: Challenges & Strategies
all.venue: The International Review of Multidisciplinary Research
all.abstract: This study examined the mental health initiatives, operational challenges, and strategic responses adopted by employers to support worker well-being in General Santos City. Adopting a qualitative phenomenological design, the investigation gathered direct insights into the lived experiences and institutional viewpoints of organizational leaders. Data were collected through detailed face-to-face interviews with fifteen (15) employers selected via purposive sampling across five major sectors: hospitality, healthcare, retail, education, and fishing. Through thematic analysis, the findings revealed several core wellness initiatives, including medical and healthcare provisions, awareness sessions, flexible scheduling, recreational outlets, and faith-based support systems. However, despite implementing these measures, leaders faced persistent hurdles. These stemmed from deep-rooted cultural stigma, resource limitations, scarce access to specialized mental health care, and hesitation among staff to openly discuss psychological health. To address these obstacles, employers relied on practical leadership strategies rooted in empathy, open communication, structured feedback, formal policy changes, and persistent training collaborations. Such efforts highlight a growing commitment to cultivate healthier, more supportive work environments despite clear resource constraints. Overall, the research highlights that advancing workplace mental health requires coordinated action between enterprise leaders, staff members, and public policy developers. Embedding mental health considerations into formal corporate policies does more than just improve job satisfaction and day-to-day output; it helps secure long-term organizational stability across diverse industries.

all.title: The Evolution and Intellectual Structure of Employee Well-Being Research: A Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Analysis
all.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
all.abstract: Background and Purpose: Employee well-being research encompasses diverse themes, including work engagement, burnout, job satisfaction, and changing work arrangements. This study aims to describe the development of publication activity and identify the author-keyword themes visible in a retained Scopus corpus, without claiming to provide an exhaustive representation of the entire field. Methodology: The study employs a descriptive bibliometric approach using 2,011 Scopus records exported on May 19, 2026. The analysis examines annual publication counts, selected author-keyword frequencies across defined periods, and an exploratory interpretation of the available three-cluster keyword co-occurrence output. Because the original pre-screening export and complete screening log were unavailable, the intermediate selection counts could not be independently verified. Accordingly, the analysis is restricted to the retained corpus and the results supported by the available metadata. Findings: Publication activity in the retained corpus increased markedly in recent years, particularly between 2020 and 2025. Employee well-being, well-being, work engagement, burnout, and job satisfaction were recurring author-keyword themes. Later-period keywords also included remote work, technostress, work-life balance, psychological safety, and digital transformation. The available keyword co-occurrence output indicated three exploratory thematic groupings. These findings describe patterns within the retained dataset and do not establish causal relationships or represent a validated mapping of the entire research field. Contribution: This study provides a bounded descriptive account of publication trends and thematic patterns in the retained employee well-being corpus. It highlights the value of examining temporal publication activity alongside author-keyword patterns while emphasizing the need for reproducible search and screening records, transparent keyword normalization, and fully documented bibliometric procedures in future research.

all.title: Memahami Employee Well-Being Integrasi Dinamika Kerja–Keluarga dan Meaning of Work
The Role of Employee Well-Being, Digital Leadership, and Workplace Flexibility in Enhancing Organizational Performance

all.title: Algorithmic Management and Employee Well-Being: A Text Mining and Behavioral Science Review (2020–2026)
all.abstract: Algorithmic management (AM)—the use of algorithms and data-driven systems to allocate, monitor, evaluate and discipline work—has expanded from platform labor into conventional organizations and is increasingly linked to employee well-being. This review maps 255 publications from the reference corpus supplied for this study (nominal window 2020–2026) by combining a transparent title-level text-mining workflow, a behavioral-science coding frame and a reference-by-reference narrative synthesis in which every record is discussed. Methods: titles were parsed, tokenized and screened with stop-word removal; term and bigram frequencies, six theme codes and theme co-occurrence were computed, and the records were then synthesized in seventeen thematic sections covering conceptual foundations, platform-worker evidence, double-edged effects, autonomy, technostress, surveillance, fairness, trust, behavioral outcomes, AI adoption, AI-based well-being tools, careers, Industry 5.0 and sectoral contexts. Results: output is strongly recent (175 of 255 records, 69%, fall in 2025–2026), and the literature concentrates on well-being, burnout and stress (152 titles), AI-enabled HRM and analytics (107) and gig/platform work (68), whereas fairness, transparency and ethics are comparatively less studied (22). The synthesis shows that effects are conditional: algorithmic control can exhaust or energize depending on appraisal, autonomy, fairness, support and the specific control dimension, and that dignity-related pathways complement stress pathways. Conclusions: AM research is dominated by outcome-focused studies of stress and well-being, with ethical and design-oriented work lagging behind; future studies should test moderators such as autonomy and explainability with full-text corpora, longitudinal designs and harmonized measurement.

all.title: Perfectionism and its associations with stress, burnout, job satisfaction, and performance among nurses and nursing students: A scoping review
Agotamiento emocional, conflicto de rol y satisfacción laboral en docentes universitarios
institutions: Amazon National University of Madre de Dios
all.abstract: En este estudio se utilizó una muestra de153 profesores universitarios de Lima Metropolitana para explicar la influencia mediadora del agotamiento emocional en el vínculo entre el conflicto de rol y la satisfacción laboral. Para medir las dimensiones mencionadas, se utilizaron tres medidas autoadministradas con suficientes cualidades psicométricas en un diseño no experimental, transversal, correlacional y mediacional. Los resultados mostraron que el conflicto de rol tenía un impacto global negativo sustancial en la satisfacción laboral (β = -0,576, p < 0,001), que explicaba el 33,2% de la varianza. Además, el agotamiento laboral se vio afectado positivamente por el conflicto de rol (β = 0,728, p < 0,001), que explicaba el 53,1% de la varianza. Por último, se encontró una mediación parcial, con un efecto directo negativo significativo (β = -0,326, p <,001) y un efecto indirecto negativo sustancial (β = -0,25, p <,001) del conflicto de rol sobre la satisfacción laboral a través del agotamiento emocional. Estos hallazgos subrayan la necesidad de abordar estas variables en el abordaje de las diferentes exigencias laborales de los profesores universitarios y, en consecuencia, optimizar su salud y productividad general.

all.title: Satisfacción, expectativas y motivación laboral en empleados del sector energético colombiano
institutions: Corporación Universitaria Empresarial Alexander von Humboldt
all.abstract: El estudio tuvo como objetivo examinar la asociación entre las expectativas e intereses laborales y los niveles de satisfacción, motivación y bienestar en 116 trabajadores de una empresa del sector de servicios de energía en Colombia. La investigación fue de enfoque cuantitativo, transversal y descriptivo-correlacional. Asimismo, se realizó una prueba piloto del Cuestionario de Satisfacción y Expectativas en el Trabajo (CSET) para evaluar su claridad, pertinencia contextual y consistencia interna. Los resultados evidenciaron que los intereses y expectativas laborales se relacionan significativamente con la satisfacción, el bienestar y las condiciones organizacionales, respaldando la relevancia de la congruencia persona-organización en la experiencia laboral. Además, la percepción de apoyo organizacional y las oportunidades de desarrollo mostraron una relación positiva, aunque débil, con el nivel educativo. En contraste, el estrato socioeconómico presentó una relación inversa con el reconocimiento y el bienestar. Se recomienda desarrollar estudios longitudinales y profundizar la validación psicométrica del CSET.

all.title: Digital Work Stressors and Employee Well-Being: A Systematic Review of Evidence Types, Boundary Conditions, and Organisational Responses
all.abstract: Background Digital technologies have changed how work is paced, monitored and bounded. Studies of technostress and related digital demands differ in what they treat as the exposure and the outcome, and in their evidence on processes, boundary conditions and organisational responses. Methods We searched Scopus, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library and Springer Nature on 3 September 2026 for English-language empirical studies published from 2010 to 2026 that linked a work-related digital stressor to employee well-being. Study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings were synthesised by vote counting based on direction of effect, without meta-analysis. The review was not registered. Results Of 2,742 records, 353 full-text reports were assessed and 80 were included (78 quantitative non-randomised studies, one mixed-methods study, one experiment), with about 95,900 participants. Seventy reports pointed to poorer well-being (87.5%; 95% confidence interval 78.5% to 93.1%), eight pointed in conflicting directions and two to better well-being. Among reports of a demand, the share ranged from 72.2% for positive well-being to 95.7% for recovery and sleep, and was 76.3% in larger and 97.4% in smaller studies. Three studies that separated the demand from technology use found the adverse association for the demand only. Process and moderation tests (57 and 45 reports) gave selective support, and lagged tests gave mixed results. No report evaluated an implemented organisational response; 62 offered recommendations only. Certainty of the evidence was rated very low. Conclusions Digital demands experienced at work are associated with poorer employee well-being in most studies, though less uniformly in larger and better-controlled ones; the association appears to belong to the demand, not to technology use as such. Evidence for processes is largely cross-sectional, and evidence for organisational responses is absent.

all.title: Navigating the Ethical Landscape of AI in HRM: An Umbrella Review and Integrated Framework of Trust, Fairness, and Employee Well-being
all.abstract: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

all.title: Job Satisfaction and Instructional Excellence of Teacher Education Faculty
all.venue: World Journal of Sustainable Advances in Multidisciplinarity
all.abstract: This study determined the job satisfaction and instructional excellence of teacher education faculty members in the seven (7) campuses of the University of Rizal System offering Teacher Education programs during the School Year 2025–2026. Specifically, it examined the respondents’ demographic and professional profiles, assessed their level of job satisfaction, determined their instructional excellence based on performance ratings, and investigated significant differences and relationships among the variables. The study employed the descriptive method of research, involving the entire population of 151 core faculty members. A researcher-made questionnaire checklist served as the primary data-gathering instrument. Findings revealed that most respondents were 40–49 years old, female, married, holders of a Master of Arts in Teaching or Master of Arts in Education degree, and held the academic rank of Instructor III. Most had served for 11–15 years and attended in-service training activities at the national and campus levels. The respondents perceived themselves as extremely satisfied with their jobs, with workload equity and manageability emerging as the most identified dimension. Significant differences in job satisfaction were observed across selected profile variables and dimensions, particularly in terms of sex, educational attainment, length of service, academic rank, and in-service training. Regarding instructional excellence, 81 percent of the respondents obtained performance ratings ranging from 4.50 to 5.00, verbally interpreted as Outstanding, while 19 percent received ratings ranging from 3.50 to 4.49, interpreted as Very Satisfactory. However, no significant relationship was established between the respondents’ perceived job satisfaction and instructional excellence. The study concluded that selected professional characteristics, particularly participation in in-service training, were associated with variations in job satisfaction, while instructional excellence was not significantly related to job satisfaction. It is recommended that the Individual Performance Commitment and Review (IPCR) be continuously utilized to support faculty performance improvement, institutional support and professional development opportunities be sustained, and the proposed action plan be considered in reviewing faculty development programs. Further studies may explore other factors influencing instructional excellence.

all.title: Moderating Role of Organizational Resources in PSM— Employee Engagement Relationship
Teachers’ Job Satisfaction and Work Performance in Matag-ob District
all.venue: The International Review of Multidisciplinary Research
all.abstract: This study examined teachers’ job satisfaction and work performance in Matag-ob District, Matag-ob, Leyte, during School Year 2022–2023. Specifically, it described teachers’ job satisfaction, assessed their work performance based on their Individual Performance Commitment and Review Form (IPCRF) ratings, and sought to determine the relationship between the two variables. The study employed a descriptive-correlational research design and utilized total enumeration involving 100 public elementary school teachers. Job satisfaction was measured using a questionnaire adapted from Troeger (2021), reviewed by two district principals, and pilot-tested with 30 elementary teachers from Palompon North District, Leyte. Work performance was assessed using the teachers’ IPCRF ratings. The respondents consisted of 49 males (49%) and 51 females (51%). Results revealed that 80 teachers (80%) obtained a Very Satisfactory rating, while 20 teachers (20%) received an Outstanding rating. No respondents were classified under the Satisfactory, Unsatisfactory, or Poor categories. The mean IPCRF point score was computed using the weighted mean method by multiplying the representative rating assigned to each performance category by its corresponding frequency, summing the weighted scores, and dividing the result by the total number of respondents. Based on the reported mean of 4.00, equivalent to 80% of the maximum rating of 5.00, the teachers' overall work performance was interpreted as Very Satisfactory. However, the computed mean and standard deviation of job satisfaction and the Pearson correlation coefficient and corresponding p-value were not available; thus, the level of job satisfaction and the statistical significance of its relationship with work performance could not be conclusively established. The findings highlight the importance of examining teacher satisfaction alongside performance outcomes and may provide a basis for strengthening supervision, recognition, professional development, and collegial support.

all.title: Perceived Organizational Membership and Extensive Work-from-Home: Qualitative Insights from Germany
all.abstract: There is a global trend towards increasingly flexible work arrangements, including extensive work-from-home. Two concerns are associated with it: First, there is the fear that employees’ sense of organizational belonging (perceived organizational membership, POM) might be eroded which, secondly, causes a drop in performance. To investigate the POM-effects of extensive work-from-home, we draw from 27 qualitative interviews with white collar employees in the German industrial sector. These were conducted during the only period in time in which extensive work-from-home was made mandatory in Germany, namely the first half of 2020, due to COVID-19 induced social distancing requirements. COVID-19 induced crisis mirrors the present BANI-environment in relevant ways and unifies sensemaking; it serves a burning glass for patterning New Work POM. Contrary to common belief, POM under extensive work-from-home conditions is relocated rather than diminished. We find that POM moves from organizational to team-levels and furthermore becomes individualized, e.g., as related to care-work obligations and individual perceptions of workplace conditions. Team-managers need to assume the role of POM-leaders; they need to engage in individualized interactions for shaping employee experiences and membership perceptions. POM-leaders’ diverse own POM-needs must then be acknowledged and integrated on overall organizational levels. We thus pattern a novel phenomenon – New Work POM – and derive implications for a better ‘gluing’ of the employee to the organization. Our study furthermore underscores the need to view belonging as an organizational ‘must-have’ factor in the present BANI-environment and to take up the challenges of facilitating such belonging.

all.title: Home office no serviço público: impactos na saúde de servidores e servidoras em uma instituição federal de ensino
institutions: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul
all.abstract: This article investigates the impacts of remote work on the health of staff at a federal educational institution, in the context of the transition to remote work driven by the covid-19 pandemic. Focusing on administrative-educational staff, the study identifies the impacts of this work modality and investigates the factors affecting workers’ health. A qualitative, exploratory approach was adopted, with data collected through a sociodemographic questionnaire (76 respondents) and semi-structured interviews (18 participants), analyzed through content analysis. Results indicate that most participants experienced greater flexibility and autonomy, contrasting with increased stress and anxiety. The discussion is situated within the regulatory framework of telework in the federal public service and the specificities of administrative work in universities, linking the accounts to the psychodynamics of work and the sociology of work.

all.title: Pengaruh Work From Home dan Work Motivation terhadap Employee Performance Generasi z di DKI Jakarta
all.venue: Journal of Business Economics and Management
all.abstract: This research examines the influence of Work From Home and Work Motivation on Generation Z employees’ performance in DKI Jakarta. A quantitative approach and associative design were adopted. Primary data were gathered through questionnaires and analyzed using SPSS. The procedures involved multiple linear regression, t-tests, an F-test, and determination coefficient analysis. The findings show that Work From Home has no statistically significant partial effect on Employee Performance, with a significance value of 0.057. Conversely, Work Motivation has a positive and significant effect, recording a significance value of 0.000. Considered simultaneously, Work From Home and Work Motivation significantly affect Employee Performance, as reflected by an F-statistic of 38.547 and a significance level below 0.001. Moreover, the R-squared value of 0.602 indicates that these two independent variables explain 60.2% of the variation in Employee Performance, whereas the remaining 39.8% is associated with factors outside the scope of this research among the respondents.

all.title: Effectiveness of Work-From-Home Scheme and Productivity Performance Among Non-Teaching DepEd Personnel in the Midst of a Pandemic
all.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
all.abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of the work from home (WFH) arrangement and productivity performance among non-teaching personnel in the Division of Valencia City, DepEd Region X, during the Covid-19 pandemic. The research utilized a descriptive method, employing a questionnaire to gather data from ninety (90) respondents. The study focused on assessing the respondents' profile, work arrangement, accessibility, productivity, and innovations implemented by the Division Office to track employee performance. The findings revealed that the WFH arrangement, in compliance with basic health protocols, yielded positive results, indicating the successful adaptation of the office to the new normal. Additionally, the study identified the demographic factors of gender and civil status as having a significant influence on the effectiveness and productivity of the WFH arrangement. Based on these findings, the study recommends continued WFH arrangements, enhancing remote work support, implementing targeted training, monitoring and evaluating the arrangement, considering hybrid work models, providing family support, and fostering a positive work culture. These recommendations aim to optimize productivity, employee well-being, and organizational performance in the context of remote work.

all.title: Hybrid work models: transforming team dynamics and collaborative practices
ASN DIGITAL PLATFORM CAPABILITY AND EMPLOYEE DIGITAL COMPETENCE AS DETERMINANTS OF WORK PRODUCTIVITY: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF WORK FROM HOME
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: I Gusti Ayu Agung Dewi Sucitawathi Pinatih

all.title: Personality Was Robust to the Transition to Remote Work Under the COVID‐19 Pandemic
all.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The current study examines whether the transition between work contexts (in-person work to remote work) during the COVID-19 pandemic influenced an individual's personality in a sample of 1475 working adults. Previous work on personality change during the COVID-19 pandemic suggests that people experienced a significant change in personality. METHOD: Drawing from the personality dynamics literature and frame-of-reference effects, we extend this work by conducting IRT-based invariance analyses and by fitting linear mixed-effects models on longitudinal, archival data. RESULTS: Results indicate that transitioning to remote work did not affect either interpretations of personality items nor mean-level personality trait scores during the COVID-19 pandemic. CONCLUSIONS: Findings from the current study suggest that while many aspects of work and non-work life changed in 2020 and 2021, we did not find evidence that the pandemic and the sudden shift to remote work influenced personality assessment. Findings also provide support for the established theory that personality is robust to situational changes, highlighting the robustness of personality to predict future behaviors and attitudes regardless of changing work contexts.

all.title: SINTONIA: APLICATIVO COM VISÃO COMPUTACIONAL E AUTORRELATO PARA O ACOMPANHAMENTO DE ADULTOS COM TDAH EM TRABALHO REMOTO
all.venue: Anais do Congresso Brasileiro de Iniciação Científica
all.abstract: This paper presents SINTONIA, a desktop application that supports the follow-up of the professional routine of adults with ADHD in remote or hybrid work. Requirements were defined through a literature review and meetings with a psychology specialist. The system integrates a configurable self-report checklist, session records, periodic reports, and webcam-based visual indicators, such as gaze direction and face framing, implemented with JavaScript, MediaPipe and OpenCV. The interface was positively assessed by the specialist and the monitoring was tested in controlled scenarios. SINTONIA combines self-reported data and behavioral indicators in a longitudinal view that supports professionals, with no diagnostic purpose.

all.title: Longing for community: Academics’ dystopian and utopian imaginaries of remote work in the future university
institutions: Norwegian University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Purpose In this paper, we explore how academics envision the future university and the role of remote work within it by exploring utopian and dystopian imaginaries, based on 12 in-depth individual interviews with senior academics at a large Norwegian university. We approach imaginaries as a “history of the present”, and draw on Lauren Berlant’s theorization of affect, hope and “cruel optimism” in our interpretation. Major findings Participants’ responses were overwhelmingly dystopian, focused on potential threats to their sense of community and professional identity. Four dystopian scenarios emerged: the Factory, Desert, Anarchy, and Micronation, each highlighting different dimensions of fear, including bureaucratization, dehumanization, atomization, and insulation. The dystopias were often portrayed as already partly unfolding in the present. Alternative hopeful imaginaries were mostly framed as partial and pragmatic acts of resistance, aimed at limiting negative outcomes. Across imaginaries, the longing for community remained a central theme. Community was understood in different ways: as human “contact” (not necessarily in person), collaboration across institutions, redistribution of power within each institution, dependability among colleagues, or the ability to preserve a sense of professional (academic) identity. Conclusions These findings suggest that the university’s future depends on collective efforts to re-think and re-imagine meaningful academic communities amid technological and organizational change, and to transform the pursuit of a good academic life from a private, individual struggle into a shared project.

all.title: Automatic Time-Tracking Software and Productivity in Remote and Hybrid Work: A Case Study of DeskTime
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper synthesizes literature on remote-work productivity and electronic performance monitoring, then examines DeskTime as a case study of automatic time-tracking software. It covers features, pricing, user feedback signals, and comparative positioning relative to other tools, while discussing benefits, limitations, and implications for organizations. Based on publicly available information as of late 2026.

all.title: Digital Eye Strain in Online Learning and Remote Work: A Systematic Review of Prevalence, Risk Factors and Management Strategies
all.venue: Journal of Ophthalmology and Advance Research
authors: Mohamed Abd Elmoamen Mohamed Saad Eldeen
all.abstract: Background: Digital Eye Strain (DES) is a common ocular and visual complaint associated with prolonged use of digital devices. The widespread move to online learning and remote work has markedly increased screen exposure, which may place students and remote workers at greater risk. This systematic review assessed the prevalence, risk factors and management of DES in these populations. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from January 2020 onward, with Google Scholar used as a supplementary source. Primary observational and interventional studies of individuals engaged in online learning, distance education, remote work or work from home were eligible if they reported the prevalence or severity of DES, associated factors or the effects of preventive or therapeutic interventions. Methodological quality was appraised descriptively against the domains of the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies. Because of marked heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 302 records screened, 28 full-text articles were assessed and five cross-sectional studies were included, all of students engaged in online learning (3,955 participants in total). No eligible study of remote workers and no interventional study was identified. In the three studies that defined computer vision syndrome using the CVS-Q (score ≥6), prevalence among online learners ranged from 69.1% to 81.0%. The proportion reporting at least one symptom, a broader outcome, was 92.0% and 97.9% in two studies. Longer screen or online-learning time was associated with symptoms or their severity in all five studies. Other reported correlates included inadequate breaks, glare, short viewing distance, low screen brightness, refractive error, pre-existing dry eye, use of multiple devices and sex (in inconsistent directions). These associations came almost entirely from unadjusted analyses. Conclusion: DES appears common among students engaged in online learning and longer screen exposure is its most consistent correlate. However, the evidence comes from five cross-sectional studies with largely unadjusted analyses and no eligible study of remote workers was found. Recommendations on regular breaks, ergonomics, refractive correction and ocular surface care currently rest on evidence obtained outside these populations. Prospective studies using standardized definitions and intervention trials in online learners and remote workers, are needed.

all.title: Rhythm and blues in hybrid work: Distinct working from home configurations and related HR policy demands
all.venue: German Journal of Human Resource Management Zeitschrift für Personalforschung
all.abstract: Working from home (WFH) research typically presents employees’ preferences and companies’ policies for offsite work in an aggregate manner but neglects differences between employees’ rationales in the light of how digital technology has formed their performative interaction in teams. In this paper we argue that the shortcoming results from underestimating the digital artifact as merely a passive job resource. Thus, we explore WFH preferences as contextualized construct reflecting individual, team, and technological characteristics of digital work also in their interrelatedness. Our theoretical framework adopts a sociomaterial perspective that integrates human-centric and team-centric approaches and guides the identification of distinct WFH configurations. The empirical basis consists of two cross-sectional surveys conducted in 2023 (n = 296) and 2025 (n = 290) among German-speaking respondents with WFH options. Using exploratory and confirmatory latent profile analyses to substantiate our configurational approach, we identify three different and robust profiles: (1) a Life Balance Profile emphasizing individual interests for offsite work while expecting HR policies supporting individual detachment, (2) a Chronos Profile emphasizing onsite synchrony with colleagues while expecting mandated same office days for all, and (3) a Kairos Profile emphasizing (hybrid) performative interaction and availability in critical moments independently from the work location. Differences between configurations can be explained by employees’ centrality of work, their digital collaboration preferences, their perceived operational team readiness, and digital competences. Notably, similar aggregate preferences for more offsite work go along with different HR policy expectations.

all.title: Functional portfolio and work-demand configuration in digital marketing jobs under remote-work signaling: a network analysis of job advertisements
institutions: Huanggang College of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Introduction Remote-work labels describe an advertised work arrangement, but whether they accompany different advertised requirements remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory and work design research, we examine two layers of advertised demand: platform-native functional categories and O*NET-anchored work-style language. Methods The primary analysis uses 550 digital-marketing advertisements from one public LinkedIn dataset, including 220 with an explicit remote-work flag and 330 without a recorded flag. An expanded sample of 1,394 advertisements includes the primary sample and assesses sensitivity to the occupational boundary. Overlap-weighted regression adjusts for role family, seniority, employment type, and description length, with standard errors clustered by employer identifier. The seven-element Work-Style Demand Index (WSDI) measures the breadth of matched work-style signals, rather than their intensity or employees' traits. Results The adjusted WSDI remote-flag contrast was –0.018 (95% CI –0.047 to 0.012); the five-element adaptive/growth subindex (AWDI) contrast was -0.008 (95% CI –0.043 to 0.026). Functional breadth differed by +0.058 categories (95% CI –0.091 to 0.206). These estimates provide no clear evidence of an association and do not establish equivalence. The descriptive networks each retained 10 work-style edges, with six shared edges. A rule-based context check found most matches outside identified benefits/equal-opportunity text, but did not establish construct validity. Discussion The study offers a transparent way to examine how work-arrangement information co-occurs with advertised demands. It distinguishes employer-side text signals from applicants' interpretations and employees' experiences.

all.title: Adaptive digital communication management and its influence on employee interpersonal connectivity and collaborative performance in hybrid work environments
all.venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
all.abstract: As hybrid work arrangements have become the norm, how employees share information, connect with one another, and organize group work has changed, but are organizations keeping up with digital communication? This study tackles the issue of communication fragmentation in hybrid organizations, defined by the use of a variety of digital platforms, norms of responsiveness that vary by platform, and lower face-to-face meeting rates, which are linked to lower interpersonal bonds and less collaborative production. The study is quantitatively designed and uses a cross-sectional survey design that is based on a conceptual model linking adaptive digital communication management (ADCM) with employee interpersonal connectivity (EIC) and collaborative performance (CP). This paper introduces an empirical testing protocol for knowledge workers in hybrid workplace settings. To demonstrate the analytical pipeline, a simulated dataset (n = 412) was analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability testing, Pearson correlations, and mediation regression (PROCESS Model 4). The illustrative results demonstrate construct validity (Cronbach's alpha range .84–.91), a positive ADCM–EIC link (r = .61, p < .01), and partial mediation of the ADCM–CP relationship through EIC (indirect effect = .28, 95% CI [.21, .35]; direct effect = .24, p < .01). Leadership support and platform quality moderated the ADCM-EIC path. These results indicate that adaptive, flexible, and responsive digital communication practices foster interpersonal relationships and, consequently, collaborative outcomes. The paper argues that communication adaptability is a capability, not a mere side-effect of adopting technology for sustainable hybrid work, and identifies a research agenda to empirically test the framework presented.

all.title: The Paradox of Remote Work: How Flexibility, Autonomy, Monitoring, Self-Regulation and Distractions Shape Productivity and Task Avoidance in the UK Professional Services
all.abstract: Remote work has become an important feature of contemporary employment, yet evidence remains unclear on how specific remote-work conditions relate to employee productivity and task avoidance. This study examined how work flexibility, work autonomy, remote-work monitoring, self-regulation and digital/non-digital distractions relate to employee productivity and task avoidance in UK professional service organisations. Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) Theory and Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory provided the theoretical foundation. The study adopted a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Data were digitally collected from 206 remote and hybrid employees in selected UK professional service organisations. The measurement and structural models were assessed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Work autonomy and remote-work monitoring were positively related to employee productivity, while distractions were negatively related to productivity. Flexibility and self-regulation were not significantly related to productivityFor task avoidance, self-regulation had a significant negative relationship, while distractions had a strong positive relationship. Flexibility, autonomy and monitoring were not significant. The five dimensions explained 14.0% of employee productivity and 27.6% of task avoidance. These findings show that remote-work conditions relate differently to productivity and task avoidance.The study unbundles remote work into five distinct conditions and examines productivity and task avoidance as separate outcomes within UK professional services. It contextually validates adapted measures and contributes to the measurement of the operationalised remote-work constructs. By integrating JD-R and COR theories, the study develops and empirically tests a conceptual model of remote work arrangements, employee productivity and task avoidance, providing a framework for understanding which remote-work conditions relate to productivity, task avoidance or both.

all.title: Screen Burnout in the Digital Workplace: Examining the Impact of Digital Fatigue on Work Performance among Generation Z Employees in Remote Work Settings
all.abstract: Technology has been an integral part of human lives in the 21st century, but the overdependence has constantly triggered both psychological and physical well-being. Generation Z is the first generation to be considered digital natives, and significantly constitutes today's growing workforce. The present study seeks to understand the impact of exhausting screen exposure on the overall performance at work of those employees who are working remotely from home, particularly in the information technology (IT) sector in Eastern India. The sample consisted of 106 Generation Z employees comprising 55 females and 51 males working remotely in the IT sectors of Eastern India through the purposive sampling technique. The data collection was conducted using digital fatigue and work performance questionnaires, along with a general information schedule. One-way analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Pearson product-moment correlation were employed to test the hypotheses. Concerning digital fatigue, males and females were found to have a statistically significant difference, with female employees reporting a higher level of screen burnout than males. Furthermore, the relation between digital fatigue and work performance revealed a significant negative correlation (r = -0.227, p < .05), showing that higher digital fatigue corresponded to lower work performance among employees working in a remote work setting. The findings accentuate how prolonged digital engagement affects not only the physical but also the psychological health of individuals working remotely from their homes. It underscores the importance of organizational strategies such as mandated micro-breaks, short meeting durations, and targeted well-being support that will benefit Generation Z employees by mitigating fatigue, preserving cognitive health, and improving overall work efficiency.

all.title: Virtual Human Resource Management Practices and Employee Performance in Hybrid Work Environments: A Systematic Review of the Mediating Roles of Digital Communication and Work Engagement
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The rapid diffusion of digital technologies and the institutionalization of hybrid work arrangements have prompted widespread organizational investment in Virtual Human Resource Management (VHRM) – e-recruitment, virtual onboarding, e-learning, digital performance management, and virtual employee support systems. Practitioner discourse routinely asserts that these practices enhance employee performance, often through improved digital communication and stronger work engagement. This article systematically reviews the peer-reviewed evidence underlying that assertion. Following a PRISMA-informed protocol, the review synthesises findings from studies published between 1989 and 2025, interpreted through the Technology Acceptance Model and Social Exchange Theory. The synthesis finds that the evidentiary picture is considerably more qualified than practitioner discourse suggests. Marler and Fisher's (2013) evidence-based review of forty e-HRM studies found no empirical evidence that e-HRM predicts strategic HRM outcomes, characterising the field as theoretically and empirically immature; more recent studies report mixed, context-dependent associations between digital HR practices and engagement, with at least one study finding only a weak correlation between digital innovation adoption and employee engagement. Evidence on hybrid work itself is more rigorous but similarly qualified: a large randomized controlled trial at a multinational technology firm found that hybrid work-from-home arrangements improved retention and job satisfaction without damaging performance – a more modest finding than the performance-enhancement claims common in practitioner literature. The review concludes that digital communication and work engagement plausibly function as mechanisms linking VHRM to performance, consistent with theory, but that rigorous, sector-specific empirical confirmation of this mediated pathway remains limited. Implications for HR practice, theory, and a future empirical research agenda are discussed. Keywords: Virtual Human Resource Management; Electronic HRM; Hybrid Work; Employee Performance; Digital Communication; Work Engagement; Technology Acceptance Model; Systematic Review.

all.title: When Flexibility Follows Employees Home: Remote-Work Latitude, Work-to-Life Spillover and the Paradoxical Role of Organisational Support in India's IT-Enabled Services Sector
all.abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether the latitude to work remotely is associated with the spillover of work into personal life among employees of IT-enabled services (ITES) firms, whether techno-stress and boundary concerns explain this association, and whether organisational support weakens or strengthens it.Design/methodology/approach: Survey data were collected from 104 ITES employees in Karnataka, India.Hierarchical regression, bootstrapped parallel mediation and moderated regression with simple-slope and Johnson-Neyman analyses were used.Findings: Remote-work latitude was positively related to work interference with personal life (β = .283,p = .004),while the number of days worked from home was not.Techno-stress and boundary, isolation and career concerns did not mediate this relationship.Contrary to the buffering hypothesis, organisational support strengthened the relationship: latitude was associated with spillover only when support was moderate to high. Practical implications:Flexibility and a caring climate do not by themselves protect employees' personal time.ITES firms need explicit norms on after-hours availability, and supervisors should actively encourage supported employees to disconnect. Originality/value:The study separates the discretion to work remotely from the amount of remote work and provides evidence, consistent with social exchange theory, that organisational support can amplify rather than buffer the spillover of work into personal life.

all.title: WinWin4WorkLife D8.2 General EC Policy Briefs - version 2.4
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This policy brief examines how employers across Europe adopt and perceive remote work, drawing on one of the largest employer surveys conducted on this topic. Based on responses from more than 6,000 organisations in Germany, Finland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Slovakia, it provides new insights into the organisational factors that shape access to remote work. A key finding is that job compatibility alone does not determine whether employees can work remotely. Even where employees perform remote-work-compatible tasks, many organisations do not authorise remote work. This highlights the importance of organisational decision-making alongside the nature of employees’ job tasks. The findings further show that employers already offering remote work generally perceive remote work more positively than organisations that do not authorise remote work, while employers expect hybrid work to remain a lasting feature of work organisation rather than a temporary response to the COVID-19 pandemic. These results have important implications for European and national policy. Rather than promoting remote work as an objective in itself, policies should support organisations in making informed decisions about whether and how remote work can be implemented successfully within their organisational context. Practical guidance, organisational learning and the exchange of good practices can help organisations where remote-work-compatible jobs exist but remote work has not yet been adopted. At the same time, policy frameworks should remain sufficiently flexible to recognise the diversity of organisational contexts, sectors and occupations across Europe.

all.title: (Un)Fairness in the digital labour market: a socio-legal and comparative perspective
all.abstract: Modern instances of discrimination in the digital labour market exhibit a sophisticated and elusive form, and they can be highly impactful in terms of the scale, scope and volume. Such discrimination impinges on equality paradigms, undermine users’ trust in technology and results in legal uncertainty for workers, providers and adopters alike. In this chapter, we use two case studies to illustrate our argument. The first involves using AI to manage work. This entails a set of practices whereby decisions are partly or fully delegated to automated systems, which is known as ‘algorithmic management’ (AM). A common example of this is an AI program being used to screen, assess and select job candidates and prospective employees. The second case study involves work that is performed via information communication technology (ICT), mainly in the case of remote work or work from home. In this case, ICT allows the worker to distance herself from the workplace and situates her in private surroundings. In this chapter, we examine the solutions that exist to overcome these difficulties in the United States and Europe, combining legislation meant to enshrine equality, unleash opportunities and regulate the use of AI and remote work arrangements. Thereafter, we sketch a paradigm for dealing with discriminatory outcomes in the digitalised workplace, geared towards proposals to promote fairness by using data protection and involving workers’ representatives.

all.title: Remote Delegation Skills: Why Managers Revert to Micromanaging
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Autonomy disappears the moment managers return to the office. David Ohnstad reveals why 63% of managers increased day-to-day involvement post-RTO, and how leaders can break this habit to preserve the high-performing teams they built remotely. Full article: https://davidohnstad.info/remote-delegation-micromanaging-return-to-office/

all.title: What Makes a Place Livable? Residential Location Priorities and Scenario-Based Area Preferences Across Preferred Work Arrangements in a Mid-Sized U.S. Metropolitan Area
all.abstract: The expansion of remote work has raised new questions about how residents evaluate housing locations, particularly as daily workplace proximity may become less central for some workers and space, amenities, and lifestyle considerations may become more salient. This study examines residential location priorities and scenario-based area-type preferences across preferred future work arrangements in the Roanoke Metropolitan Statistical Area, Virginia, a mid-sized U.S. metropolitan region. Data were drawn from a 2023 cross-sectional online survey of verified adult residents, producing an eligible analytical base of 636 respondents. Thirteen residential-priority items were analyzed using complete cases (n = 620). Exploratory factor analysis, supported by parallel analysis and interpreted using polychoric correlations with oblique rotation, identified two related exploratory priority orientations: a broad space/stability/community-related orientation and an accessibility/amenity-related orientation. Kruskal–Wallis tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction showed statistically significant but generally modest differences across preferred work-arrangement groups, with the largest differences observed for proximity to the central business district and rural/suburban lifestyle preference. Scenario-based area rankings were analyzed among respondents with valid paired rankings under both in-person and remote-work conditions (n = 579). Under the remote-work scenario, suburban areas were ranked significantly more favorably, while city center/CBD locations were ranked significantly less favorably; changes in urban and rural rankings were not statistically significant after correction. These findings indicate that preferred future work arrangements and hypothetical remote-work scenarios are associated with differentiated stated residential preferences in this mid-sized metropolitan sample. The results should be interpreted as stated preference patterns and scenario-based ranking differences, not as evidence of actual relocation behavior, realized housing-market demand, verified access to remote-capable employment, or causal effects of remote work on urban spatial change.

all.title: Research trends on virtual teams: A bibliometric study
all.abstract: The growing reliance on digitally mediated work has expanded the importance of virtual teams (VTs) for organizations operating across distance, time zones, and technological infrastructures. Although virtual collaboration enables flexibility and global connectivity, it introduces persistent challenges related to communication, trust development, coordination, and performance management. The current article uses the Scopus and Web of Science databases to examine research on VTs from 1995 to 2025. Employing bibliometric techniques, including citation analysis, co-citation networks, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence analysis, and intellectual structure mapping, the most influential contributors, sources, themes, and evolving research priorities in the VT literature are identified. The findings demonstrate a strong upward trend in publication output after 2011, with peak activity observed in the most recent period (2021–2025), reflecting the normalization of remote and hybrid work arrangements. Key publication outlets include Team Performance Management , IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication , and Small Group Research , indicating the interdisciplinary positioning of VT scholarship across management and information-systems domains. The United States emerges as the most productive and collaborative country that maintains extensive international ties with major research hubs in Europe and the Asia-Pacific region. Keyword and thematic analyses reveal that topics such as VT in general, trust, computer-mediated communication, teamwork, leadership, and team performance remain dominant, while recent terms such as COVID-19, remote work, virtual work, virtual reality, and digital leadership signal an expanding agenda shaped by digital transformation. Overall, the results show that VT research continues to mature through stable foundational streams and the integration of emerging technology-enabled collaboration themes.

all.title: Machine learning decision system for analyzing digital eye strain factors Among Filipino remote workers
all.abstract: Background The global shift to remote work necessitates a better understanding of the system-level factors that influence digital eye strain (DES) and functional impairment in screen-based professions. In the Philippines, where remote work is increasingly common, there has been little empirical research on the behavioral and ergonomic predictors of DES severity. Objectives The global shift to remote work or telework necessitates a better understanding of the system-level factors that influence digital eye strain (DES) or also known as asthenopia and functional impairment in screen-based professions. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 408 remote workers looked at nine latent constructs: task, exposure and behavior, psychophysical, equipment, environment, musculoskeletal strain, digital eye strain, emotional strain, and functional limitations. Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering was used on standardized construct-level scores, with Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-seeded initialization and a grid search of cluster parameters. Results A highly structured two-cluster solution emerged (c = 2, m = 1.5, F P C = 0.8552) partitioning respondents into High-Strain (46.6 %) and Low-Strain (53.4 %) risk profiles. Exposure & Behavior served as the single most discriminating construct (Δ = 1.274), showing the largest between-cluster separation between antecedent work conditions and strain outcomes. Task demand was universally high across both clusters (M = 4.352), demonstrating minimal power to differentiate high-risk from low-risk personnel. Equipment (Δ = 0.780) and environment (Δ = 0.851) also exhibited between-profile differences on DES outcomes. Conclusions Behavioral self-regulation emerged as a prominent distinguishing characteristic of the lower-strain profile, which is supported by ergonomic setup. To improve remote workforce health and productivity, management should prioritize software-enforced micro-breaks, localized ergonomic training, and hardware stipends.

all.title: Regulation, Demand Shocks, and Renter Cost Burdens: Did Land-Use Restrictiveness Shape Who Bore the 2013–2024 Housing Squeeze?
all.abstract: About half of U.S. renter households spend more than 30 percent of their income on housing. Against this backdrop, the study asks whether restrictive land-use regulations make local housing demand shocks more burdensome for renters. The analysis covers 156–163 U.S. metropolitan areas from 2013 to 2024, using the 2018 Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index to examine two sources of demand variation: shift-share predicted employment growth and pre-pandemic exposure to remote work. Employment shocks were associated with lower renter cost burdens, whereas greater remote-work exposure was linked to rising rents and burdens, especially for middle- and higher-income renters. Neither response, however, was significantly larger in metropolitan areas with more restrictive regulations, and permitting was no less responsive to demand shocks in those areas. The findings were consistent across alternative samples and a zoning measure derived from municipal code text. Measured regulatory restrictiveness therefore appears to be a weak predictor of short- and medium-term changes in renter affordability, underscoring the importance of combining land-use reform with targeted rental assistance.

all.title: THE IMPACT OF FLEXIBLE WORK ARRANGEMENTS ON EMPLOYEE PRODUCTIVITY IN PRIVATE ORGANIZATIONS: A SURVEY OF KANO STATE, NIGERIA
all.venue: Journal of Management Science and Career Development
all.abstract: The increasing adoption of flexible work arrangements (FWAs) in Nigerian private organizations—accelerated by the 2024 fuel subsidy removal and its attendant commuting cost burdens—has raised critical questions about whether workplace flexibility genuinely enhances employee productivity or merely redistributes work effort across time and space. This study examined the effect of flexible work arrangements on employee productivity in private organizations in Kano State, Nigeria, focusing on three dimensions: flexible scheduling, remote work, and compressed workweeks. Anchored in Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, the study adopted a mixed-methods explanatory sequential design combining a cross-sectional survey of 286 employees drawn from ten purposively selected manufacturing, technology, and professional services firms with key informant interviews. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson Product Moment Correlation, and multiple regression analysis, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings revealed that flexible scheduling exerted the strongest significant positive effect on employee productivity (β = 0.642, t = 13.658, p < 0.001; R² = 0.412), followed by remote work (β = 0.530, t = 8.650, p < 0.001; R² = 0.281), whereas compressed workweeks had no significant effect (β = 0.062, t = 1.014, p = 0.312). Qualitative evidence attributed the superiority of flexible scheduling to its independence from infrastructural constraints, and the null effect of compressed workweeks to the offsetting strain of extended daily hours. The study concludes that not all flexibility arrangements function as equally effective job resources. It recommends that private organizations in Kano State prioritize core-hours flexible scheduling as the most cost-effective productivity intervention, invest in reliable digital infrastructure and collaboration tools to unlock the full benefits of remote work, and exercise caution with compressed workweeks by ensuring genuine workload reduction rather than mere compression, while providing consistent managerial training and clear boundary-setting protocols for all FWA policies.

all.title: Pengaruh Kesiapan Menggunakan AI (AI readiness) dan Kerja Hybrid Terhadap capability Learning Mahasiswa Pekerja Universitas Pamulang
all.abstract: This study is motivated by the challenges faced by working students in balancing their work responsibilities and academic activities, as well as the increasing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology in learning activities. This study aims to examine the effects of AI Readiness and Hybrid Work on the Learning Capability of working students at Universitas Pamulang, both partially and simultaneously. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method through the distribution of Likert-scale questionnaires to 25 respondents selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed using multiple linear regression, t-test, F-test, and the coefficient of determination. The results indicate that AI Readiness has a positive and significant effect on Learning Capability, with a significance value of 0.000. Hybrid Work also has a positive and significant effect, with a significance value of 0.010. Simultaneously, both variables have a significant effect, with an R-squared value of 0.833. Therefore, AI readiness and work flexibility are factors associated with the learning capability of working students.

all.title: The Role of Gamification in Enhancing Employee Engagement and Productivity in Globally Distributed Remote Workforces
all.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN MANAGEMENT
all.abstract: The increasing adoption of remote and hybrid working arrangements has significantly transformed organizational practices, employee relationships, and performance management systems. Although remote work provides flexibility and access to global talent, it also creates challenges related to employee engagement, motivation, communication, teamwork, and productivity. Gamification has emerged as a promising managerial approach for addressing some of these challenges through the integration of game-based elements into ordinary workplace activities. This review examines the potential role of gamification in improving employee engagement and productivity among globally distributed remote workforces. It discusses important gamification features, including points, badges, leaderboards, performance feedback, achievement recognition, and collaborative challenges. The study adopts a narrative literature review approach, drawing upon relevant academic publications on workplace gamification, employee motivation, human resource management, and remote working. The reviewed literature suggests that well-designed gamification systems can strengthen employees' sense of achievement, participation, recognition, and organizational connection. However, their effectiveness depends on individual preferences, organizational culture, technological accessibility, and the fairness of performance evaluation. The review also highlights potential concerns, such as excessive competition, employee stress, privacy, and the risk of prioritizing measurable activities over work quality. It concludes that gamification can serve as a useful supplementary management strategy when implemented through transparent, inclusive, and employee-centred practices. Keywords: Gamification, Employee Engagement, Remote Work, Employee Productivity, Workplace Motivation, Digital Workforce, Organizational Performance.

all.title: Rural and remote social work practice
all.abstract: This chapter focuses on the vexing issue of social work practice in rural and remote areas. Noting the vast areas and sometimes sparse populations across rural Australia, this chapter outlines the way these factors compound health inequalities and poor service delivery. Yet rural people are vulnerable to policy changes and to the lack of attention paid to rural issues. Addressing the significance of the hub and spoke model, this chapter notes the commitment of rural practitioners to innovative service delivery – a practice made easier with new technological advances. Future developments of social work practice and delivery in rural areas will be shaped by these advances and the opportunity they offer for workers to work from home, delivering social work, and clients to access social workers online.

all.title: Being(s) there(s)—geographies of tacit knowledge through avatars, telepresence robots, and holograms
all.abstract: We aim to understand emerging geographies of tacit knowledge through advanced remote-work technologies: telepresence robots, holograms and virtual avatars. These technologies enable ‘being there’ in more than one location (and space) at once and using communication that resembles a face-to-face experience. We examine, if tacit knowledge can be shared through these technologies. Based on interviews and autoethnography, we find that each technology confers the ability to exert specific spatial agency elsewhere. From the intellectualist perspective, all studied technologies allow the sharing of some tacit knowledge, whereas virtual avatars enable the sharing of some tacit knowledge also from the phenomenological perspective.

all.title: WinWin4WorkLife D3.1 National data collection reports
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This deliverable reports on the implementation of the WinWin4WorkLife WP3 data collection campaigns across five European case study countries: Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, Portugal and Slovakia. Building on Deliverable D3.2, it documents how the planned employer study, employee study, time-use diary, interviews and digital nomad survey were implemented in practice, including recruitment strategies, achieved samples, data protection and ethics procedures, data processing, weighting, pseudonymisation and the main methodological implications for later analysis. The employer study collected organisation-level evidence on remote work arrangements, including employer practices, perceived effects on productivity and well-being, skills retention, and possible implications for office location and space needs. The employer survey targeted organisations with at least five employees and used stratified sampling designs based on organisation size and economic sector. Recruitment strategies differed across countries, reflecting the availability of sampling frames, contact information, institutional support and survey-company involvement. The resulting datasets were cleaned, augmented with spatial information where possible, weighted against available population benchmarks, and pseudonymised before being shared for analysis. The employee study was implemented as a linked, multi-stage process. The employee survey collected information on individual and household circumstances, working conditions, remote work practices, mobility, well-being, work-life balance, preferences, and possible residential or job relocation. Respondents could then opt in to the time-use diary (TUD), which collected detailed information on daily activities, work location, mobility behaviour and geolocation positioning. A subset of participants was subsequently invited to take part in qualitative interviews, allowing to explore lived experiences, opportunities, tensions and trade-offs related to remote work in depth. This design created a rich empirical basis for mixed-method analysis, while also requiring careful management of participant burden, recontact consent, data linkage, pseudonymisation and data quality. The Portuguese digital nomad survey was implemented as a standalone and exploratory data collection focused on digital nomads in Lisbon. The survey used adaptive recruitment strategies. An initial approach based on social media, online groups and QR-code promotion generated only a limited number of responses, after which the recruitment strategy adopted street-based recruitment in locations frequented by digital nomads. As no reliable population benchmarks are available, the digital nomad survey cannot be weighted in the same way as the employer and employee surveys and should be interpreted as exploratory evidence on a hard-to-reach group. Across all data collection activities, the consortium implemented a harmonised project-level framework for ethics and data protection while adapting procedures to national and institutional contexts. A single central ethics approval was explored but was not feasible because local partners acted as Data Controllers and institutional interpretations of GDPR and ethics requirements differed. Shared templates for Data Protection Notes, informed consent and ethics applications supported consistency, while local review remained necessary. Particular attention was required for geolocation data, interview recording, transcription, translation, anonymisation, AI-assisted tools, secure ID matching and the conditions for possible future archiving or reuse. Overall, WP3 successfully implemented a complex, multi-country, multi-method and multi-stage data collection strategy under demanding practical, ethical and data protection conditions. The implementation experience provides important context for interpreting data: country comparisons, linked analyses, time-use and geolocation outputs, interviews and digital nomad results can be assessed in light of recruitment strategies, sample sizes, cleaning and weighing procedures, and methodological limitations documented in this deliverable. The resulting datasets provide the empirical foundation for the project’s analysis of the economic, social, spatial, environmental and policy implications of remote work arrangements.

all.title: Digital supervision of remote workers: balancing productivity requirements with the protection of constitutional rights
all.venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
all.abstract: With rapid technological development across various fields of life and the increasing reliance of national systems on modern communication networks, the pattern of remote work has gradually emerged as an advanced digital means by which contemporary legal systems address emergencies and disasters affecting their national systems. Accordingly, the state has to intervene by updating traditional work systems to accommodate these exceptional crises and gradually mitigate their serious effects on its national community and citizens. So that the state agencies keep on performing their supervisory functions in maintaining public order, and for private sector institutions to achieve productive efficiency in their activities despite the inappropriate circumstances, the legislator in many legal systems has been keen to regulate remote work in all public and private sector institutions, being an indispensable necessity for maintaining the public order of the state and to prevent the collapse of this order, especially in times of crisis. In light of this transformation, digital monitoring of remote workers has emerged as a tool employers use to verify the extent of a worker’s commitment to performing their professional duties efficiently. While this type of monitoring is effective in achieving its intended purpose, its use in digital environments has been accompanied by numerous constitutional challenges, including concerns that it may shift from legitimate to excessive monitoring, thereby negatively affecting the constitutional rights of remote workers. The topic of this research, therefore, has emerged to shed light on the controls aimed at preventing such types of monitoring from shifting from legitimacy to illegitimacy.

all.title: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT AND PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL PRACTICES IN THE PRIVATE SECTOR: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT AND PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL PRACTICES IN THE PRIVATE SECTOR
all.abstract: Performance appraisal and performance management systems are part of the core functions of HRM practices which support organizational goals. This study analyzes the conceptual and practical differences between performance appraisal and performance management systems within organizations in the private sector. This study uses a qualitative, descriptive-comparative research design using secondary data sources. Data were sourced from peer-reviewed journals, industry reports, case studies and textbooks published within the last 10 – 15 years. The findings reveal that various organizations fail to incorporate performance appraisal and performance management systems effectively leading to inconsistencies in their applications and limited developmental outcomes. The sectoral analysis shows that service-oriented and IT corporates adopt more progressive, feedback-driven performance management systems, whereas sectors such as manufacturing and banking organizations rely on rigid assessment approaches. The common challenges include subjectivity, insufficient employee involvement and weak alignment of the individual efforts with organizational strategic goals. The study underscores the need for a holistic, inclusive and a context-specific approach to performance assessment. It concludes with some actionable recommendations to enhance the conception, implementation and the effectiveness of performance appraisal and performance management systems in the private sector.

all.title: Emotional Intelligence for Performance Appraisal in the Organization Behaviour
all.abstract: This paper examines how Emotional Intelligence is related to Performance Appraisal in public and private project-based organizations operating in Pakistan.
