Overall, the findings suggest that ESG disclosure provides a buffering mechanism that partially mitigates the adverse financial implications of capital intensity without eliminating its negative association with financial health.

all.title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Labor Laws in Safeguarding Female Workers: A Comparative Study
all.venue: The International Journal of Law Review and State Administration
all.abstract: This study evaluates the efficacy of existing labor laws in safeguarding the rights and well-being of female workers through a comparative legal analysis across selected jurisdictions. Despite international conventions and national statutory frameworks aimed at eliminating gender discrimination, women in the workforce continue to face structural barriers, gender pay gaps, workplace harassment, and inadequate maternity protections. Utilizing a qualitative comparative methodology, this research examines statutory provisions, enforcement mechanisms, and judicial interpretations across distinct legal systems. The findings indicate that while comprehensive legal frameworks exist on paper, significant implementation gaps persist primarily driven by weak regulatory enforcement, socio-cultural constraints, and the expansion of unregulated informal employment. Furthermore, jurisdictions featuring proactive institutional monitoring, transparent corporate reporting, and stringent statutory remedies demonstrate substantially higher rates of compliance and worker protection. This paper concludes by proposing targeted legislative reforms, emphasizing the need for strengthened enforcement mechanisms, cross-jurisdictional alignment of labor standards, and robust policy interventions to ensure substantive equality for female employees.

all.title: Managerial Ability and Employee Workplace Health and Safety
all.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between managerial ability to efficiently convert capital into revenue (which we refer to as “managerial ability”) and employee workplace health and safety violations. We document a positive association between managerial ability and employee workplace health and safety violations. This relation is more pronounced in firm environments with weaker labor unionization, and becomes weaker in more innovative firm environments, when executive compensation includes stronger employee workplace health and safety incentives and when CEOs have longer horizons. Collectively, these findings suggest that while higher managerial ability is associated with greater employee workplace health and safety violations, firm environments that emphasize stakeholder protections and longer‐term managerial horizons attenuate this relation. Finally, while employee workplace health and safety violations do not significantly affect short‐ to medium‐term financial performance, they appear to harm long‐term financial performance in firms led by high‐ability managers.

all.title: The employment effects of data asset disclosure: from the perspective of scale expansion and structural optimization
all.venue: Journal of Chinese Economic and Business Studies
all.abstract: Data assets are increasingly important production inputs and firm-specific strategic resources that improve operational quality and create transactional value. Using text analysis and the Word2Vec neural network model, this study constructs a data asset disclosure index to examine its impact on firm employment in China. The results show that data asset disclosure significantly expands employment scale and improves employment structure. Channel analysis shows that these effects operate through the alleviation of liquidity constraints, the enhancement of intrinsic firm value, and the improvement of market entities’ expectations. Further analysis shows that data asset disclosure increases employee compensation and benefits, thereby attracting labor inflows. In addition, it significantly raises the labor income share while reducing the capital–labor ratio. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for data asset disclosure as an effective means of stabilizing firm employment.

all.title: Urban Agglomeration Development Policies and Firms’ Labor Outsourcing: Evidence from China
all.abstract: Using panel data on Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, this study examines how national urban agglomeration development policies affect labor outsourcing through a staggered difference-in-differences design. Policy implementation significantly increases labor outsourcing intensity, and the finding is robust to alternative estimators and specifications. The mechanism analysis shows that policy implementation is associated with greater firm specialization, increased labor dispute litigation, and lower regional labor market segmentation. The outsourcing response is concentrated in core cities. Further analysis finds lower internal employment and internal labor costs relative to revenue, alongside higher average employee compensation. These findings extend the evaluation of regional integration policies to firms’ organization of labor inputs and highlight the need to distinguish changes in internal employment from changes in firms’ reliance on external labor services.

all.title: Análisis de los programas de bienestar integral de los colaboradores del sector bancario hondureño, en Tegucigalpa 202626
all.abstract: Introduction. Holistic well-being has established itself as a strategic factor in Honduras’s financial sector, serving as a pillar for the sustainability of both individuals and organizations. The purpose of this study was to assess financial sector employees’ perceptions of the components of corporate wellness programs and how these programs influence their quality of life at work. Methods. The research was based on the theories of Herzberg, Maslow, and Gartner’s model, employing a quantitative design using a structured survey validated with the content validity coefficient (CVC) and Cronbach’s alpha, which demonstrated the instrument’s reliability. Results. The findings show that intrinsic motivation, a sense of belonging, and job security are the strongest aspects, while stress management and pay equity are critical areas for improvement. Conclusions. Holistic well-being extends beyond the individual sphere, becoming an essential element for competitiveness, stability, and organizational culture in the Honduran financial sector, which not only contributes to the strengthening of human talent but also to the country’s economic and social sustainability.

all.title: When Climate Incentives Matter: CEO Compensation Design and Stock Market Responses to Climate Transition Risk in Europe
all.abstract: As climate transition risk becomes increasingly priced in capital markets, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate their preparedness for the low‐carbon transition. Climate‐linked CEO incentives have emerged as a prominent governance mechanism, yet their market relevance remains unclear. Using a sample of listed European firms from 2018 to 2022, we examine when climate‐linked CEO incentives are associated with stock market responses to climate transition shocks. We find that a greater economic weight of climate‐linked compensation is associated with more favorable market responses. This association varies with incentive design and context. Transition‐oriented KPIs exhibit the largest association, whereas process‐oriented KPIs also show a positive association. Broader environmental KPIs, by contrast, show no significant association, although this result may partly reflect their low prevalence in the sample. Moreover, the association is stronger when transition risk is more economically material, emerges under stronger internal climate governance, and is further strengthened by greater responsible capital ownership. These findings contribute to the literature by showing that the market relevance of climate‐linked executive compensation varies with incentive design, transition risk materiality, and the broader governance environment.

all.title: The current status and strategies of intergenerational workforce management in China
all.abstract: In the context of China’s declining birth rate, ageing population, and increasingly generationally diverse workforce, where five generations from the 1960s to the 2000s now coexist, this study systematically examines the current state and effectiveness of intergenerational workforce management. An analysis of 290 questionnaires completed by corporate managers shows that while employees across generations express strong agreement on non-material aspects such as teamwork, clear cognitive differences emerge regarding pay equity, reflecting deeper divergences in values. The findings further indicate that basic measures, including teamwork and technological adaptation, have proven effective by fostering intergenerational collaboration and producing tangible outcomes. In contrast, long-term and humanistic measures, such as retirement transition plans and adaptive leadership, remain underdeveloped, facing significant challenges in aligning diverse expectations and immediate results. To better bridge generational divides, this study suggests that Chinese organisations redesign compensation systems to balance competence and seniority, modularise benefits, and adopt flexible leadership styles. These recommendations provide a theoretical and practical foundation for building sustainable intergenerational management systems within enterprises.

all.title: Gender Wage Inequality in Bangladesh: A Historical and Comparative Microeconomic Analysis of Private Companies and NGOs in Dhaka
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Although significant strides have been made in the country's overall educational attainment at the micro level in the last five decades (1976-2026) and more girls are entering the workforce, significant gender disparities in wages persist in Dhaka. Often, non-public employment in urban areas has been regarded as a uniform sector in the literature, with the institutional heterogeneity between privatised and maximising profit firms and mission oriented Non-Govemmental Organisation (NGOs) not being reflected on. This study makes a contribution by harboring the fifty years of Bangladesh Labor Force Survey with the stratified primary enterprise data and by providing a historical and comparative micro-economic analysis of wage gender gap in the pan Dhaka metropolitan area in private enterprises and NGOs. The empirical strategy was to combine the Heckman sample selection model for non-random labor market entry with Blinder–Oaxaca means decompositions and unconditional quantile regressions that are based on Recentred Influence Function (RIF). It finds that the mean gap between men's and women's wages is 0.264 log points, and that 63.6% can be attributed to unexplained structural discrimination in the private companies, whereas in the NGOs it is substantially smaller at 0.112 log points (31.2% unexplained) because of standardized bureaucratic wage grades and donor-mandated equity frameworks. Moreover, RIF quantile decompositions reveal strong evidence of a "sticky floor" and a "glass ceiling" in the distribution of the earnings of private firms, with selection to this group further compounded by the urban commuting friction. In order to reduce the gender pay gap in Dhaka, pay-scale transparency in the private sector needs to be legislated, minimum wage needs to be enforced, and urban transport infrastructure must be gender responsive Keywords: Wage Discrimination; Female Labor Supply; Institutional Wage Segmentation (Private vs. NGOs); Human Capital Endowments

all.title: Mapping Gender (In)Justice in the European Green Transition: a Comparative Analysis of Eco-Social Indicators
all.abstract: The green transition is frequently evaluated through narrow technocratic or economic lenses, overlooking the gendered distribution of power and resources. The study aims to map the gendered domains of the European green transition, revealing how gender-blind policy design may reproduce existing social inequalities. Integrating eco-feminist and intersectional perspectives, the research identifies critical intersections between environmental and social goals, and investigates the selected domains of the green transition: mobility, housing and green labor market. Utilizing secondary data from Eurostat and the European Institute for Gender Equality, we select and evaluate eleven gender-sensitive indicators across the EU-27. Descriptive analysis is used to map gender gaps and hierarchical cluster analysis is applied to classify national performance profiles. The findings reveal systemic gender inequality across the EU. While men dominate the green labor market, women remain more dependent on public transport and bear a disproportionate housing-related burden. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the achievement of gender justice is deeply contingent upon prevailing welfare state models. The analysis identifies four profiles: North-Western group demonstrating horizontal professional segregation despite egalitarian pragmatism; Continental group reflecting a conservative compromise with moderate gender gaps across all analyzed domains; Central-Eastern group marked by high horizontal labor segregation and significant internal variation in both sustainable mobility and housing; South-Eastern group exhibiting the highest gender pay gaps and a significant risk of transport poverty for women. We argue that achieving just sustainability requires shifting towards policies that explicitly address structural gender imbalances, both though policy design and indicators used for evaluation.

all.title: Geographic distance and corporate innovation: empirical evidence from the separation of registered and actual operational office
all.abstract: Addressing the prevalent spatial mismatch between registered and operational offices in transition economies, this paper explores how administrative geographic separation affects micro-firm technological innovation. Utilizing panel data of Chinese A-share non-financial listed companies from 2009 to 2025, we employ high-dimensional fixed-effects models, difference-in-differences policy shock designs, and panel trajectory permutation placebo tests to evaluate causal identification. The empirical results indicate that the physical distance between registered and operational offices exerts a negative effect on both utility model and invention patent innovations. Mechanism analyses show that spatial distance affects innovation outputs primarily by increasing administrative expense friction and impairing internal control quality. Moderation tests further reveal that high-tech listing board positioning, high market valuation expectations, and enhanced executive compensation incentives effectively buffer this negative impact through compliance-forcing pressures, financial redundancy, and agency cost counteractions, respectively. Considering this, corporate executives should comprehensively evaluate cross-regional site selections, and local governments should reverse the investment promotion orientation of empty shell registrations, thereby substantially lowering daily administrative coordination and institutional transaction costs for cross-regionally operating enterprises.

all.title: Compensation Structures and Staff Retention in Rwanda’s Construction Sector: Evidence from Access International Construction
all.venue: Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education
all.abstract: Voluntary staff attrition constrains project continuity in Rwanda's construction industry.This study examined the role of employee compensation on staff retention at Access International Construction Rwanda, focusing on four reward dimensions: performance-based bonuses and incentives, competitive base pay and overtime, employee benefits packages, and career skill-based pay.Anchored in Expectancy Theory, Equity Theory and the Total Rewards Model, the study adopted a correlational, cross-sectional design.From a target population of 377 employees, a sample of 128 was drawn through simple random sampling, supplemented by interviews with three key informants.Data were collected using a structured Likert questionnaire and analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression in SPSS.Instrument reliability exceeded the 0.70 Cronbach alpha threshold for all constructs, and content validity was 0.80.The regression model was statistically significant and the four dimensions jointly explained a substantial share of the variance in retention, with employee benefits packages and performance-based bonuses exerting the strongest effects.The study recommends that construction firms prioritise comprehensive benefits and transparent, milestone-linked incentive schemes over base-pay adjustments, and that policymakers incorporate welfare-mechanism guidelines into construction-sector labour policy.

all.title: Alta identificación institucional, baja justicia retributiva percibida: valoración de puestos y satisfacción laboral en una empresa pública municipal de agua de Ecuador
all.abstract: Job evaluation is the technical foundation of internal pay equity, yet its relationship with work attitudes has received little attention in Latin American public enterprises that run their own human resource regimes. This study describes how employees of the Municipal Public Water and Sewerage Enterprise of Guayaquil (EMAPAG EP, Ecuador) perceive the distributive and procedural components of their job evaluation and pay system, and how these perceptions compare with institutional identification, role clarity and working conditions. A quantitative, descriptive, cross-sectional design was used: a 30-item Likert questionnaire was answered by 103 of the organization’s 174 employees (59.2%). Means, favourable proportions with Wilson intervals and Holm-corrected sign tests were estimated, and items were grouped into eight theory-driven dimensions. Identification with the mission and the meaningfulness of work were nearly unanimous (91.3% favourable responses), whereas pay justice was the lowest-rated dimension: only 33.0% perceived that pay increases follow a structured and transparent process, 29.1% considered pay policies clear and 19.4% reported additional compensation, even though 82.5% perceived their job as risky. The results reveal a gap between vocationally grounded commitment and a pay system perceived as opaque. The main shortfall is procedural and informational, and an explicit, transparent, factor-based internal job evaluation standard is the priority intervention.

all.title: Professional workforce composition and compensation in accounting firms: evidence from Taiwan
all.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether professional workforce composition is conditionally associated with firm-level aggregate compensation and benefits (CB) in Taiwanese certified public accounting (CPA) firms and whether the associations differ between partnership firms and sole proprietorships. Design/methodology/approach The study uses de-identified firm-level data from the 2019 Survey Report on the Service Industry of CPA Firms. The final sample comprises 1,134 firms. Ordinary least squares models are estimated separately by organizational form. Additional count-based, separate-ratio and incremental workforce-share analyses are used to assess sensitivity to alternative workforce specifications. Findings The joint ratio models show positive associations between several professional-service ratios and firm-level aggregate CB. However, the supplemental analyses show that these associations are sensitive to the measurement and joint inclusion of interdependent workforce-share variables. The evidence is therefore interpreted as composition-based firm-level associations rather than as robust independent headcount effects or individual wage premiums. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design cannot resolve reverse causality between staffing composition and compensation budgets, and the firm-level compensation measure does not estimate individual employee pay. The results should be read as conditional associations that identify how workforce configuration, organizational form and aggregate compensation governance are related. Practical implications The implications are differentiated across large partnership firms, small sole proprietorships, regulators and industry associations. They emphasize cautious use of staffing-ratio evidence, clearer separation of employee compensation from owner distributions and more detailed industry data on functional staff counts, ranks, full-time equivalents and compensation components. Originality/value The study treats firm-level aggregate CB as a strategic outcome related to workforce configuration, while explicitly showing that the interpretation depends on whether workforce allocation is measured as proportions, absolute headcounts or incrementally introduced staffing shares.

all.title: If You Fire Your Employee Tomorrow, You Will Lose Your Customer: AI Agents, Sudden Displacement, and the Collapse of Consumer Demand
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper argues that displacement by AI agents will be sudden, not gradual, and that its primary casualty is not employment but demand. Firms adopt agents only when they are certain the technology cuts cost and headcount; because the proof of that certainty is broadcast to every firm at once, and because whole functions — call centres, customer service, bookkeeping — are standardised across firms, adoption crosses its threshold everywhere in the same short window: function by function, all companies together. The displaced employee, however, is the same person as the customer. In the United States, household consumption accounts for roughly 68 percent of GDP, and labour income is its largest single funder: wages and salaries alone supply about half of all personal income, and employee compensation roughly three-fifths of it. Each firm captures the full saving from its own automation while the demand destruction falls on the market as a whole, so individually rational adoption aggregates into collapsing purchasing power. The market cannot correct this: falling prices are powerless against zero income, falling wages chase a competitor whose cost tends toward zero, and the new tasks that might reabsorb labour are contested by the same technology. Business owners, individually, have no available remedy — a firm that refuses to adopt is undercut by one that does. The paper therefore addresses governments. Governments will not solve this by mandating employment: the owners of automated production hold the stronger hand in that contest and will win it. The remedy actually available is the complete transition to a rentier economy — an allocation state in which taxes and fees on the technology companies that own automated production, and will hold the market, are redesigned as rent on machine output and on access to the population itself, collected centrally and distributed as the population's primary income. State support thereby changes its nature completely: from temporary insurance against job loss into the distribution mechanism of the economy — and the tax base, and the nature of money itself, change with it.

all.title: Globalization Effect on Employee Welfare in Selected Oil Companies in Lagos State, Nigeria
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Globalisation has changed the financial, technological, educational, and corporate environments in which organisations operate, creating new opportunities and challenges for employee welfare. In the oil and gas industry, global integration can influence remuneration, occupational safety, healthcare benefits, working conditions, professional development, and work-life balance. However, the extent to which globalisation practices translate into improved employee welfare requires systematic investigation. This study examined the effect of globalisation on employee welfare in selected oil companies in Lagos State, Nigeria. Specifically, it assessed the effects of financial globalisation, media and communication globalisation, corporate globalisation, and educational globalisation on employee welfare. The study adopted a quantitative survey research design involving technical staff, administrative staff, finance personnel, and human resource officers. A sample of 362 respondents was proposed. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire designed on a four-point Likert scale. Frequencies, means, and standard deviations were used to answer the research questions, while regression analysis was employed to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The simulated findings indicated that financial globalisation had a significant positive effect on employee welfare (β = 0.618, p < 0.05). Media and communication globalisation also had a significant positive effect (β = 0.594, p < 0.05). Corporate globalisation demonstrated a positive and significant effect on employee welfare (β = 0.671, p < 0.05), while educational globalisation was similarly associated with improved welfare outcomes (β = 0.649, p < 0.05). The findings suggest that global financial integration may expand organisational capacity to provide competitive remuneration and welfare benefits, while modern communication systems can improve information access and employee participation. Furthermore, internationally recognised corporate practices may promote fairness and workplace safety, while global learning opportunities can enhance employees' professional competence and career satisfaction. The study concludes that globalisation can contribute to improved employee welfare when organisations deliberately translate global opportunities into practical benefits for their workforces. It recommends that oil companies strengthen employee compensation and healthcare schemes, improve occupational safety, adopt effective digital communication systems, and expand access to professional training and development. These measures may help organisations balance global competitiveness with employee well-being and sustainable organisational performance.

all.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
all.venue: International Journal of AI in Pedagogy Innovation and Learning Futures
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

all.title: Upskilling Without Burning Out
all.abstract: We are now living in an era of abundance when it comes to learning, training, and certification. There are many different kinds of microlearning platforms, including LinkedIn Learning, Coursera, Udemy, and many others. The upskilling problem today is not a lack of access. People often talk about certifications. Real capability comes from doing the work. Certifications may open doors, but proof of work keeps them open. Social proof is important. It is a noisy world. Many people claim they can do things, but few show that they can. This chapter focuses on micro-outsourcing. Use AI and small outsourcing platforms to accelerate the process. Proof of work is not limited to coding. Upskilling should not come at the cost of health, relationships, or longterm sustainability. Visibility matters. Build both an internal and an external brand. Unlearning is as important as learning.

all.title: Internal Mobility: Why Managers Unintentionally Block It
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Managers often sabotage internal mobility without realizing it. When top performers seek new roles, panic sets in instead of pride. Discover why this happens and how to become a leader who actively champions your team's career advancement. Full article: https://davidohnstad.info/internal-mobility-managers-sabotage/

all.title: Internal Mobility: Why Managers Fear Losing Top Talent
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: When your best people ask about internal opportunities, panic sets in. But David Ohnstad reveals the real problem: managers protect their teams instead of developing them. Discover how to shift your mindset and build a culture where internal growth strengthens everyone. Full article: https://davidohnstad.info/internal-mobility-managers-fear-losing-talent/

all.title: Citizenship and nativism in Nigeria: internal deportation as internal mobility governance
all.abstract: In the Federal Republic of Nigeria, some sub-national governments impose mobility restrictions that result in the internal deportation of Nigerian citizens to their so-called ‘states of origin’. Most existing scholarship frames these practices as violations of constitutional and human rights, but gives limited attention to their implications for citizenship and migration governance. This paper asks how internal deportation operates as a form of internal mobility governance and shapes citizenship and belonging in Nigeria. Focusing on two high-profile incidents in Lagos State in 2013 and 2024, it draws on nativism and the concept of governmobility, and qualitative content analysis of government press releases and national media reports. The analysis shows how sub-national states, like Lagos State, use nativist claims to legitimise borderwork, regulate citizens’ mobility and produce territorially stratified citizenship in Nigeria. It further demonstrates how formal national citizenship can be undermined in practice by ethnic citizenship rooted in indigeneity, ancestry and colonial categories of belonging. The paper contributes to debates on citizenship, migration governance, borderwork and federalism by illustrating how nativist logics are mobilised and governmobility is enacted within a federal state against citizens rather than non-citizens.

all.title: Skills Taxonomy Refresh Timing: Annual vs Biennial at 2.5-Year Half-Life
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: At a 2.5-year half-life, annual refresh is required; classify every domain by estimated half-life and refresh biennially only when half-life exceeds 3 years. Independent technical note mirroring the canonical version: https://lpi.academy/blog/skills-taxonomy-refresh-timing-annual-vs-biennial-at-25-year-half-life.php

all.title: Reskilling Versus Replacement under Technological Change and the Future of Employment Relations
all.venue: Advances in Management and Business Studies
all.abstract: Purpose: Rapid technological innovation makes skills obsolete faster and forces organizations to choose between replacing employees through external hiring and reskilling and redeploying incumbents. This article examines how these strategic workforce responses affect organizational value and employment relations outcomes under different technological, labor market, and employment relations conditions. Research Methodology: An agent based model of an organization with 500 employees was developed, in which technology depreciates skills and trust shapes effort, training participation, and turnover. Four strategies, namely passive adaptation, buy, make, and hybrid reskilling with redeployment, were compared over ten years across 48 scenarios that combine technology intensity, labor market tightness, and adversarial or partnership based employment relations. Results: Internal development strategies (make or hybrid) produced a higher Net Present Value (NPV) than external replacement in all 12 technology, labor market, and climate combinations while avoiding layoffs. External replacement achieved the highest skill fit but laid off 19% to 83% of incumbents, eroded trust, and performed worst in tight labor markets. The hybrid strategy was best under the fastest change, and a partnership climate raised NPV under all strategies. Conclusions: The future of employment relations depends on whether organizations treat reskilling as a joint investment governed by trust and social dialogue. Limitations: The parameters are illustrative, so the results are simulation based and should be validated with organizational data. Contributions: The study integrates strategic human capital theory and employment relations research in a dynamic model and offers propositions and guidance for managers, employee representatives, and policy makers.

all.title: Preparing Europe’s Transport Workforce for CCAM – The RESKILLING Employment and Skills Observatory
all.abstract: In the face of persistent challenges—including the energy crisis, supply chain disruptions, and rising living costs— the EU labour market remains resilient, with employment reaching a record 213.7 million. Within this context, the transport sector, which contributes 5% to the EU’s GDP and accounts for 3.1% of total employment, is experiencing significant transformation through the adoption of Cooperative, Connected, and Automated Mobility (CCAM) technologies. While CCAM presents opportunities for innovation, economic growth, and job creation, it also poses risks of workforce displacement and evolving skill demands. Addressing these shifts requires a systemic approach that considers not only transport-specific roles but also broader impacts across the value chain, including education, organisational transformation, and labour market dynamics. Ensuring inclusive transitions, reskilling opportunities, and the attractiveness of transport careers is essential. To this extent, the Horizon Europe project RESKILLING (G101147328) introduces the CCAM Employment & Skills Observatory, an AI-powered tool designed to identify and map evolving skill needs, detect emerging roles, and generate tailored, stakeholder-specific and evidence-based recommendations. By supporting policymakers, training providers, and industry actors with tailored insights, the Observatory fosters a socially equitable and future-ready workforce, contributing to a fair and effective transition toward CCAM in Europe’s transport sector.

all.title: Bridging the skill gap for smart manufacturing: Training and upskilling for the next industrial revolution
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Groupe de Recherche en Droit, Économie, Gestion
all.abstract: The diffusion of Industry 4.0 technologies, including artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and robotics, is transforming manufacturing by increasing efficiency, customization, and flexibility. At the same time, adoption has exposed a substantial skills gap, particularly in advanced technical capabilities and higher-order problem-solving. This study examines the sources of this gap by focusing on misalignment between educational and industry needs, organizational resistance to upskilling, and the rising demand for cross-disciplinary expertise. The study draws on 43 semi-structured interviews with industry and academic experts across 27 countries, analyzed with the Gioia methodology. The findings identify recurring barriers, including outdated training provision, underinvestment in reskilling, and weak collaboration between academia and industry. The results also point to the need to institutionalize continuous learning and to strengthen industry-led workforce transformation through coordinated partnerships and policy incentives. Building on these findings, the paper proposes the Smart Manufacturing Skills Framework (SMSF). The framework links three layers of competence to a continuous learning loop and represents the conditions under which competence is formed, absorbed, and renewed. The mechanisms connecting these conditions are stated as four propositions for future research. The paper concludes with practical recommendations centered on targeted training pathways, government support mechanisms, and lifelong learning strategies to improve workforce readiness for smart manufacturing.

all.title: Strategic Upskilling and Employees' Intention to Stay in Metro Manila's Food and Beverage Sector: The Parallel Mediating Roles of Upskilling-Supportive Transformational Leadership and Psychological Empowerment
all.venue: International Journal of Education, Research, and Innovation Perspectives
all.abstract: This study examined the relationship between employee intention to stay (ITS) and perceived strategic upskilling (SU), as well as the parallel mediating roles of psychological empowerment (PE) and upskilling-supportive transformational leadership (USTL) in several food and beverage establishments in Metro Manila. Of the 447 submissions we received, 441 were eligible complete responses from a quantitative cross-sectional survey. We used latent structural equation modeling (SEM), Pearson correlation, descriptive statistics, and supplementary composite-score mediation. All four construct scores were very high (SU M = 4.50; ITS M = 4.29; USTL M = 4.41; PE M = 4.57). SU and ITS were positively correlated (r = .853, p < .001). The USTL indirect effect in the parallel composite model was positive and significant (B = .7836, 95% CI [.6500, .9171]), whereas the PE indirect effect was not significant (B = −.0978, 95% CI [−.2170, .0215]). All latent component paths were positive, but the model fit was poor (CFI = .580; RMSEA = .219), and no latent indirect effect tests were available. The results suggest that development-specific supervisory support is the statistically more consistently supported pathway, and the independent role of empowerment remains unclear. We have developed a matrix of evidence-informed management actions to guide the design of training, the provision of supervisor support, the level of employee empowerment, and the availability of internal career pathways. Limitations: cross-sectional design, scoring, and measurement issues, which in turn limit the strength of any causal or generalizable conclusions.

all.title: Reskilling female entrepreneurs for knowledge spillovers: a KSTE perspective on SMEs in lagging regions
all.abstract: Purpose The research focuses on how territorial innovation aids the process of reskilling and training female entrepreneurs in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) through knowledge application and spillover in disadvantaged areas. Based on the knowledge spillover theory of entrepreneurship (KSTE), this study aims to investigate the role of institutional help as an essential tool tying together the development of entrepreneurial competence and application of knowledge. Design/methodology/approach The study uses quantitative research techniques based on structural equation modeling that help identify the correlations between obtaining skills by female entrepreneurs and getting managerial training and implementing innovations in their region concerning knowledge gain and usage. Findings The findings show that territorial innovation enhances entrepreneurial capabilities through reskilling and managerial education, while institutional support facilitates the translation of these capabilities into knowledge application and knowledge spillovers. Firm size and firm age significantly influence knowledge spillovers but do not significantly affect knowledge application. Practical implications The findings of this study will assist policymakers and institutions in developing inclusive reskilling and management education programs for female-owned SMEs based upon knowledge spillovers that lead to true innovations and development in the region. Originality/value The study extends KSTE by embedding it in the context of female-led SMEs in lagging regions, linking entrepreneurial education and territorial innovation to knowledge outcomes.

all.title: Workforce reskilling and training-finance optimization for Laem Chabang Port Phase 3: a scenario-based MILP framework
all.abstract: Laem Chabang Port Phase 3 is intended to increase container-handling capacity from approximately 11 to 18 million TEU while strengthening rail connectivity within Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor. This study develops a scenario-based decision-support framework that links throughput and rail-share assumptions to occupation- and region-specific workforce requirements and a policy-constrained mixed-integer linear programming model. The final reproducibility calibration uses public project and labour-market data, benchmark-derived labour-intensity parameters, explicitly labelled policy scenarios, and probability-adjusted training outcomes. Under an 80% workforce-coverage target, the corrected model requires approximately 1,612 enrollments under a 15% rail-share scenario and 1,739 under a 25% scenario over 2026–2027. Two-year training expenditure is estimated at THB 137.5–148.3 million against a THB 118 million envelope, while support expenditure reaches THB 37.2–40.1 million against a THB 22 million envelope. One-way sensitivity analysis shows that both financing gaps persist under coverage targets of 70–90%, completion-placement probabilities of ±10%, and support-cost changes of ±20%. The results indicate that workforce-transition feasibility depends on probability-adjusted labour absorption, the joint adequacy of training and post-training support finance, and transparent calibration rather than headline training capacity alone.

all.title: Barriers and facilitators to upskilling primary health care clinicians in diabetes education and management in Australia: a scoping review
all.abstract: Primary health care (PHC) is the first and most consistent point of contact for individuals with chronic conditions such as diabetes. As diabetes management and treatment options continue to evolve and clinical guidelines are regularly updated, ongoing professional development for clinicians is essential. Therefore, this scoping review aimed to identify and map barriers and facilitators influencing the upskilling of PHC clinicians in diabetes education and management in Australia, and to highlight gaps to inform future research and professional development initiatives. The protocol was registered retrospectively following completion of the review to provide a public record of the review methodology.

all.title: GESTÃO DE PESSOAS E IA GENERATIVA: REQUALIFICAÇÃO, SUBSTITUIÇÃO DE FUNÇÕES E EFEITOS SOBRE O CLIMA ORGANIZACIONAL
all.abstract: A IA generativa entrou nas organizações como ferramenta de produtividade, mas chega aos trabalhadores como decisão sobre o seu trabalho, e a gestão de pessoas responde a ela com duas estratégias principais: requalificar os trabalhadores cujos papéis mudam ou substituir as funções que a tecnologia passa a executar. O artigo pergunta como a gestão de pessoas tem tratado essa adoção e que efeitos cada estratégia tende a produzir sobre o clima organizacional. A análise, uma revisão integrativa de estudos empíricos e teóricos, compara os achados sobre requalificação e deslocamento com as dimensões em que o clima é medido. A requalificação aparece associada a confiança, informação, disposição para adotar a tecnologia e permanência, desde que conduzida com transparência sobre a evolução dos papéis, segurança para experimentar, mentoria e gestores preparados. A substituição atinge quem é dispensado, com perda de identidade e percepção de traição organizacional, atinge quem permanece, pela ansiedade que reduz a adoção, e atinge quem entraria na carreira, pela supressão das tarefas de formação. Na dimensão da igualdade, as duas estratégias concentram ganhos e perdas em grupos diferentes, porque o aumento cognitivo beneficia mais os cargos de status alto e o descarte pesa mais sobre as funções de suporte. Conclui-se, por inferência a partir da convergência entre os estudos e não de um efeito medido diretamente, que o efeito sobre o clima depende tanto da condução e da distribuição da mudança quanto da estratégia escolhida, e que os custos da substituição tendem a ultrapassar a organização.

all.title: Coaching and Inclusive Lifelong Learning within an AI-Supported Skilling System
all.abstract: This paper first explains how skilling systems improve workers' and firms' capacity to adapt to changing labour markets by helping them develop adequate skills, measure progress, and reward practice in distinct tasks. Coaching within skilling systems supports managers and employees in improving performance, managing workplace challenges and transitions, pursuing life goals, and developing leadership skills. Lifelong learning helps employees and employers remain successful within their own job and generally in the labour market. Inclusive lifelong learning within a skilling ecosystem ensures that continuous education, upskilling, and reskilling opportunities reach all people regardless of background, age, or employment status. AI-supported skilling systems, like those described in this paper, use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve coaching and lifelong learning by delivering personalized coaching and removing traditional barriers to education. This also helps to identify skill gaps and adapt educational content. Multilingual translations and real-time language conversions using AI make training more inclusive and available to marginalized groups and those with basic skill gaps. AI-based chatbots and mentors support "learning in the flow of work," continuous coaching and mentoring. AI can identify industry trends, and upskilling or reskilling programs can align with existing needs. Inclusive skilling ecosystems, which are also described in the paper, use artificial intelligence to support learning, job training, and career growth fairly and are open to all people.

all.title: AI-DRIVEN HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT: EVIDENCE FROM INTERNATIONAL COMPANIES
all.abstract: The study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) development and human capital development in the context of technological transformation. The research is based on secondary data from ten large international companies representing technology, consulting, industrial, and consumer sectors. Publicly disclosed corporate information is used to identify AI-related human capital practices, including AI and Generative AI training, upskilling and reskilling, continuous learning, career development, and AI-enabled learning. An AI-related Human Capital Development Evidence Index is proposed to systematize the breadth of documented practices. The findings demonstrate that AI adoption is increasingly accompanied by systematic workforce development and continuous learning. The study confirms the importance of AI-related skills development and organizational adaptability for sustainable human capital formation.

all.title: The Transformation of Work in the Age of AI: Organizational Transformation, Skills, and the Future of Vocational Education
all.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
all.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Generative AI (GenAI/GAI), is reshaping work, organizational processes, and the skills required in contemporary labor markets. Beyond efficiency gains, AI is changing human roles, communication, knowledge production, and decision-making, while also raising ethical, social, and educational challenges. This chapter examines AI's impact on organizational transformation, human–AI collaboration, creative productivity, workforce development, and vocational education. Drawing on recent literature, it highlights the need for critical thinking, digital literacy, ethical awareness, and lifelong learning. It also argues that effective AI adoption depends on combining technological capability with governance, institutional policy, and continuous upskilling and reskilling. By linking research and practice, the chapter shows how education can support responsible, human-centered, and sustainable AI integration in the future of work.

all.title: Training Social Workers for the AI Era
all.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of social work practice and education. This chapter explores how the profession can prepare for this transformation through training and education while remaining rooted in its mission of equity and justice. This chapter begins by defining AI literacy and fluency for social workers and the need to engage with AI and ensure responsible use critically. Drawing on frameworks such as Boetto’s EPIC model and Ahn et al.’s AI literacy framework and using the Council on Social Work Education’s (CSWE) Educational Policy and Accreditation Standards (EPAS), this chapter illustrates how AI literacy aligns with core competencies and how social work education can embed these skills into curricula. Examples are provided to demonstrate how AI literacy can be integrated across micro, mezzo, and macro practice. This chapter also addresses the urgent need for upskilling and reskilling among current practitioners through accessible professional development opportunities, such as certificate programs, conferences, and community-based learning spaces. Together, training for the profession and education programs can build a future-ready social work profession that utilizes AI as a tool for innovation while safeguarding the values and commitments that define the field.

all.title: The Competency Gap Between Graduates and Labor Market Demands: Challenges in Educational Relevance, Curriculum Transformation, and Human Resource Development
all.venue: MANTRA Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Management
all.abstract: Rapid technological change has intensified discrepancies between graduate competencies and evolving labor market expectations, raising concerns about educational relevance and workforce readiness. This study aims to synthesize evidence on graduate competency mismatch, curriculum transformation, and human resource development and propose an integrated educational–workforce alignment framework. A qualitative integrative literature review was conducted using 19 purposively selected scholarly publications published between 2021 and 2026. Data were collected through structured document analysis and synthesized using thematic coding, cross-study comparison, and conceptual integration. The findings identify recurrent gaps in analytical reasoning, problem-solving, technical proficiency, communication, and adaptability, although their severity varies by discipline, country, and stakeholder perspective. The thematic synthesis highlights five interconnected responses: labor market competency mapping, collaborative curriculum redesign, experiential learning, multidimensional competency assessment, and continuous upskilling and reskilling. These mechanisms suggest that skills mismatch reflects institutional coordination and implementation challenges as well as individual capabilities. An integrated framework links employer feedback and competency evaluation to ongoing educational and professional development to support timely adjustments as occupational demands evolve across diverse institutional contexts. The study concludes that sustained alignment requires adaptive curricula, meaningful industry partnerships, and lifelong learning. Because the framework is conceptual, its effectiveness requires subsequent empirical and longitudinal evaluation.

all.title: HUMAN CAPITAL SHORTAGE AND THE PSYCHOLOGICAL TRANSFORMATION OF MANAGEMENT: CHALLENGES FOR THE NATIONAL ECONOMY
all.venue: Actual problems of improving of current legislation of Ukraine
all.abstract: Ukraine’s persistent shortage of human capital presents a complex economic challenge shaped by demographic decline, forced migration, labour market imbalances, and the psychological strain experienced by the existing workforce. This study examines the economic and organisational implications of this shortage and develops a conceptual framework for transforming human resource management under prolonged labour constraints. The analysis incorporates labour market trends observed in 2023–2025 and highlights the growing importance of employee retention, psychological well-being, professional resilience, and skills development. The article introduces the HRC-Resilience model, designed to integrate four complementary dimensions of human capital preservation and development: psychophysiological regeneration, inclusive humanisation, psychological safety and empathetic leadership, and cognitive adaptability. The proposed framework shifts managerial priorities from the predominantly reactive replacement of missing employees towards the systematic preservation, recovery, and development of existing workforce capabilities. Its practical implications include preventing occupational exhaustion, improving the allocation of workloads, supporting the professional integration of diverse employee groups, strengthening organisational communication, and promoting reskilling and upskilling. The model is presented as a conceptual management instrument rather than an empirically validated intervention. Its potential contribution lies in supporting organisational workforce capacity and mitigating some of the adverse effects of labour shortages on Ukraine’s national economy. Further research should develop measurable performance indicators and empirically test the model across enterprises operating in different economic sectors.

all.title: AUTOMATION SYSTEM AND LABOUR FORCE TRANSFORMATION: PROGNOSIS ON POLICY INTERVENTIONS, SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC IMPLICATIONS IN SOUTH EAST, NIGERIA
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: Enugu State University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of automation and artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming labor market globally, necessitating strategic labour force preparation to mitigate job displacement and maximize economic opportunities. This study accesses the effect of automation on skill gap, determine the effect automation on public private partnership and also explores the policy interventions, social dynamics, and economic implications of automation, emphasizing the need for upskilling, reskilling, and education reform to equip workers with future-proof skills. Using a mixed-methods approach, data from policymakers, captains of industry, and employees were analyzed to assess the effectiveness of existing workforce policies and identify gaps in automation preparedness. Findings indicate that while automation enhances productivity and economic growth, it exacerbates inequality and job polarization without targeted interventions. The study highlights best practices from developed economies where public-private partnerships, digital literacy programs, and adaptive labor policies have successfully mitigated labour force disruptions. Comparative analysis with existing research confirms that a proactive approach to automation-driven labor shifts is essential for national economic resilience. This research contributes to policy discourse by proposing a multi-stakeholder framework for governments, industries, and educational institutions to collaborate in shaping an adaptive labour force. Key recommendations include regulatory adjustments, increased investment in vocational training, and inclusive digital transformation strategies to ensure sustainable economic development in the automation era.

all.title: Training in the social economy and the role of ESF in Spain
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Presentation at the Community of Practice on social innovation - European Social Fund conference 'The Role of NGOs in Up- and Reskilling: Exploring ESF+ Supported Initiatives' Madrid, 3 and 4 June 2025

all.title: Employee Training and Development in a Changing Workplace: A Critical Review of Performance, Digital Learning, and Future Skills
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Employee training and development have become important human resource management practices for strengthening workforce capabilities, improving employee performance, and preparing organisations to respond to changing workplace demands. However, the effectiveness of the former is determined not only by their availability but also by their relevance to job requirements, motivation to acquire new knowledge and skills, opportunities for their application, and the attitude of organisations to training. This paper presents a critical narrative review of 20 selected papers examining employee training and development, organisational performance, learning transfer, employee motivation, digital learning, artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management, learning culture, and workforce reskilling and upskilling. The literature was thematically analysed to determine the themes, contradictions, and gaps that unify the findings as well as the divergent conclusions, contradictions, limitations, and research question. The review indicates that training and development can contribute to employee capabilities and organisational effectiveness; however, these outcomes are not always direct or consistent across organisational contexts. The literature suggests that training does not always lead to better employee performance on its own. Support from managers and employees’ willingness to learn can make a difference in how training affects their work. Job satisfaction and the opportunity to use new skills in daily tasks are also important. Today, many organisations are using online training and AI-based tools to help employees learn new skills. However, not everyone has equal access to digital resources, and concerns about data privacy remain. Another challenge that should be addressed is that the employee might gain some knowledge in the training program and then barely apply the experience they gained in the workplace. ◷ 31 words↻ Further, there is a need for more research in various fields to establish the long-term benefits of such training for the employees It is crucial to investigate whether they can apply the learned skills in the workplace and if it allows them to meet the organisation’s future requirements.

all.title: Effect of Worker Engagement Practices on Employee Performance at the Rwanda Revenue Authority
all.venue: Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education
all.abstract: This study examined the effect of worker engagement practices on employee performance at the Rwanda Revenue Authority (RRA), Kigali, Rwanda.Three objectives guided the study: to assess the effect of value-based recognition, employee voice and open communication, and internal mobility and mentorship on employee performance.A combined descriptive and explanatory design was adopted, informed by Social Exchange Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and McGregor's Theory X/Theory Y. From a target population of 644 RRA employees, a sample of 247 was determined using Yamane's (1967) formula, covering all departments and hierarchical levels.Data were collected through questionnaires, interview guides, and documentary review, and analysed using descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression in SPSS, complemented by thematic analysis.All 247 respondents participated (100% response rate).The regression model explained about 59% of the variation in performance, and all three null hypotheses were rejected (p < .05),indicating that value-based recognition (p = .004),employee voice and open communication (p = .032),and internal mobility and mentorship (p = .001)each had a significant effect.The study concludes that worker engagement practices significantly enhance employee performance at RRA and recommends formalised recognition, structured voice mechanisms, and clear internal mobility and mentorship pathways.

all.title: The Impact of AI on the Future of Work and the Gig Economy in Nigeria
all.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
all.abstract: This paper investigate the impact of the impact of a i on the future of work and the gig economy in Nigeria. While AI technologies have the potential to improve efficiency and productivity in various industries, they also raise concerns about job displacement and the need for upskilling and retraining. In the gig economy, AI may create new opportunities for freelance workers, but it also has the potential to further exacerbate income inequality. The manuscript found that It is crucial for policymakers, businesses, and workers in Nigeria to proactively address these challenges and leverage the potential of AI to create a more inclusive and sustainable future of work. Embracing AI responsibly and with a focus on equity and exclusivity will be essential for shaping a positive future for the gig economy and work in Nigeria.furthermore, the show that the world of work is changing with a multi-generational workforce and changing employment models with more flexibility. The location is no more a constraint to acquire capable talent. The gig economy is booming, and today’s workers prefer to adopt the gig model, and employers are increasingly preferring gig workers to the permanent workforce and preferring skills and competencies over formal qualifications. They need to upskill them with a new set of competencies.

all.title: Cultural and Organizational Shifts for AI-Driven SRE
all.abstract: Replace "Fight Club" with "the AI monitoring rollout" and you have an accurate description of how most organizations handle the organizational side of this journey. Nobody talks about the SRE-data science friction. Nobody discusses who actually owns the model when it degrades at 2 AM. Nobody mentions that the "upskilling program" was two mandatory lunch-and-learns that everyone forgot by the following Monday.

all.title: Employment Relations and Labor Market Dynamics under Globalization and Digitalization, a Task Based Simulation
all.venue: Annals of Human Resource Management Research
all.abstract: Purpose: Globalization and digitalization are reshaping labor markets by relocating tasks abroad and transferring tasks from workers to machines. This article examines their combined effects on employment structure, wages, and income distribution, and the capacity of employment relations institutions to shape these effects. Research Methodology: A general equilibrium task model with three skill groups, routine biased automation, and offshorable tasks is simulated over 20 years. Scenarios separate globalization and digitalization shocks and compare five institutional regimes, namely market adjustment, a productivity indexed wage floor, negotiated technology adoption, reskilling, and a coordinated regime, using illustrative parameters for theory building. Results: The combined shocks moved 30% of tasks to automation and 4% abroad, and the share of tasks performed by middle skill workers fell from 41% to 25%, reproducing job polarization. Output doubled and real wages rose for all groups, but middle skill wages grew least (23% versus 39% and 43%), and the labor share fell to 69%. A strongly indexed wage floor created 6.6% unemployment, negotiated adoption preserved the labor share at the cost of output, reskilling raised output and compressed inequality, and a coordinated regime combined these benefits without unemployment. Conclusions: Institutions matter most through their influence on skill supply and the pace of task reallocation rather than through wage protection alone. Limitations: The model is stylized, uses illustrative parameters, and omits new task creation and employer market power. Contributions: The article links task based labor economics with comparative employment relations research and derives propositions for empirical research and policy.

all.title: Beyond the Verbal – Creative Therapeutic Approaches
all.abstract: This chapter starts to explore how to be creative when working with these clients. When we cannot rely on the verbal as a reliable and effective mode of communication, how do we begin to explore other approaches? Case studies for different approaches are offered such as drawing, nature and animals, and spirituality. It is not an attempt to train or upskill therapists in these areas, but more an exercise encouraging other ways to support clients to express their inner emotional world. At the end of this chapter, readers are encouraged to consider which, if any, approaches they might consider in their own counselling practice.

all.title: ICT employment and regional disparities
all.abstract: This chapter examines the relationship between the recent expansion of ICT employment – driven by the post-Covid-19 context and commonly referred to as the second digital revolution – and its impact on regional income levels and territorial inequalities in Spain. Through a review of academic literature and empirical correlation analysis, the study explores whether ICT diffusion fosters economic growth and reduces income disparities across regions. Findings indicate that ICT employment is strongly associated with higher income and economic dynamism, yet its effect on inequality remains ambiguous and largely dependent on measurement approaches. While sectoral ICT employment shows a modest link to reducing regional disparities, the ICT employment by occupational measures reveal no meaningful relationship. The analysis underscores the role of structural factors, institutional frameworks, and public policies in shaping the distributional outcomes of technological development. Finally, the chapter highlights the need for targeted strategies – such as digital reskilling, infrastructure investment, and sectoral decentralization – to prevent lagging regions from being left behind in the ongoing digital transformation.

all.title: Business Policy Adaptation in the Age of Industry 5.0: Challenges and Strategic Responses
all.abstract: Industry 5.0 is a shift to human-centric, sustainable and resilient industrial systems, which requires a significant change in business policies. This paper explores the major issues that arise when adapting policies and it also finds the strategic reactions to these issues by using the secondary data available. The thematic analysis is the basis of the qualitative approach, which is founded on the recent empirical study (2023-2026) and uses the thematic analysis to extract the patterns related to the policy rigidity, ethical governance, workforce transformation, and sustainability pressures. The results show that the traditional policy frameworks cannot be used to effectively handle complexity in human-AI collaboration and dynamic industrial ecosystems. The strategic responses should include agile governance, AI ethics models, reskilling of the workforce, and integrating sustainability, to help adapt effectively. The research is important as it indicates a structured structure, in which the issues are related to the policy approaches, which provides practical implications to the organizations, which are moving towards Industry 5.0. The advancements in businesses enhanced through this transformation and business management.

all.title: Implementing AI in your organisation
all.abstract: Most generative artificial intelligence (AI) pilots never reach production, and by 2026 the reason is not the technology. This chapter gives engineering leaders a practical path from interest to embedded capability, drawing on deployments at Mott MacDonald, Skanska, AECOM, Balfour Beatty, WSP and Sweco and on the author’s own experience on both sides of the procurement table. It covers how to identify high-value opportunities, how to write requirements and acceptance tests for probabilistic systems and how to choose between building, buying and partnering now that an engineer with a coding agent can build in days what used to need a development team. It then turns to evaluating vendors and to the organisational work that follows: upskilling, champion networks, pilots that become routines and governance before scale. The reader will be able to assess where their firm stands, select proportionate first projects and plan a multi-year programme.

all.title: Jesuit Business Education: Preparing Our Students for an Ai-Driven World
all.venue: Jharkhand Journal of Development and Management Studies
all.abstract: We are experiencing historic transformation of our global economy and society, propelled by AI technologies. These innovations promise extraordinary gains in productivity and convenience, reshaping how we work, learn, and interact. Yet, these benefits come with profound challenges. Foremost among them is widening inequality in access and use, as AI’s advantages remain concentrated among a limited set of actors. Other pressing concerns include environmental impacts, manipulation of public opinion, restrictions on free expression, cyber-attacks, and data privacy risks. Addressing these issues requires governance frameworks that uphold ethical principles, safeguard human rights, and ensure transparency and accountability. Equally important is a commitment to human-centric design – AI should augment human capabilities rather than replace them. We must invest in education and reskilling to prepare the workforce for this transition and foster collaboration across academia, industry, and government to shape inclusive and sustainable solutions. The opportunities and challenges posed by AI must be managed to advance human flourishing and strengthen the Common Good. I look forward to engaging with fellow participants and learning from their insights on these critical issues.

all.title: Building on the 5Cs: Digital Curation of Open Source Resources for Digital Health Innovation
all.abstract: Digital Health Innovation is by nature highly interdisciplinary and attracts people from a myriad of disciplines. These researchers often want to rapidly upskill but little time to find, judge and organise learning materials that are scattered across many organisations. This study utilises the 5Cs methodology to create a library of free educational resources for learners to develop knowledge and skills in digital health innovation. After examining the benefits and limitations of this methodology, we applied 4 of the 5 phases. Conceptualisation, the linking together of disparate artifacts to make new understandings of the content, was not applicable in this context. To evaluate the effectiveness of this free library, nine participants were interviewed and a thematic analysis of their responses conducted. Learners valued the assurance resources in the library had been selected and judged by a trusted source, but a lack of time and lack of communication limited use of the library. The 5Cs offers an effective methodology for curating open-source resources, with 4 of the 5Cs being applicable in this context.

all.title: The Hydrogen Economy and its Social Implications: Workforce Transformation and Access Inequality
all.venue: International Journal of Energy Research Science and Engineering
institutions: Federal University of Technology and Environmental Sciences
all.abstract: Hydrogen economy is accompanied by socio-economic factors, workforce transformation and access inequality in the emerging economies. Thus, the study anticipates social implication of hydrogen production and workforce transformation through the analyses of needed skill, measures of implementation as well as the integration of social justice. The literature study addressed some challenges by looking at the comparative framework that put hydrogen workforce planning at the centre of knowledge, training and labour market governance. Findings revealed that there is a need to develop a dynamic model for the planning of the hydrogen workforce, creation of the hydrogen skill structure for defining the difference in skills between the hydrogen roles and those in other industrial sectors. Also, there is a need to implement training programs for new roles within the hydrogen sector and adjustment in the level of apprenticeship to be able support the transition of workforce while it is significant to upskill the trainers to improve the capacity of the training providers. The study provides a robust insight for government, policymakers and other stakeholders that are interested in the transformation of renewable energy.

all.title: Kesiapan Komunitas Lokal dalam Mewujudkan Just Transition Berbasis ESG pada Transisi Energi di Indonesia
all.venue: CANTING Indonesian Community Development and Social Investment Journal
all.abstract: Indonesia’s commitment to achieving Net Zero Emission (NZE) by 2060 has accelerated the transformation of its energy sector through the gradual reduction of fossil fuel dependence and the expansion of renewable energy. However, the success of the energy transition depends not only on environmental targets but also on the protection of communities affected by structural economic changes. This study aims to analyze local community readiness and formulate an ESG-based just transition strategy. A descriptive qualitative case study approach was employed. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, field observations, and policy document analysis related to coal-fired power plant retirement and renewable energy development. The findings reveal that major challenges include job displacement in coal-dependent regions, weakening local economic resilience, limited public participation, and the vulnerability of women and informal workers. The study proposes mitigation strategies integrating workforce reskilling, temporary income protection, environmental restoration, and participatory governance. These findings demonstrate that ESG provides a comprehensive framework for ensuring an equitable, inclusive, and sustainable energy transition in Indonesia. Keywords: energy transition; ESG; just transition; local community; Net Zero Emission

all.title: Engaging Educators and Children in Digital Play in Early Learning Settings
all.abstract: As digital technologies become increasingly embedded in early learning settings, educator guided play is gaining attention to enhance children’s purposeful, creative, and collaborative use of digital tools. This project upskilled three fourth-year preservice teachers as Digital Ambassadors (DAs), supporting educators to engage children in meaningful digital guided play experiences to support childrens computational thinking across three Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) settings. Guided by an interpretative paradigm, data were generated by both children and adults. Children wore GoPro cameras to capture their perspectives, while iPads on Swivl systems provided a broader view of interactions. Inductive and deductive analyses were conducted on video footage, play-based conversations, and reflections. Findings revealed children demonstrated digital knowledge and competencies beyond educator’s expectations, and that guided digital co-play fostered reciprocal learning, with adults learning alongside children. The study also raised critical questions about what constitutes meaningful digital play experiences in early childhood contexts.

all.title: Modelling future dental workforce need for adults with special care needs within the UK
all.abstract: Aims Special care dentistry (SCD) in the United Kingdom (UK) provides care for a range of adults with complex needs, including physically and mentally disabled people, older adults with dementia, adults with medical, emotional, sensory, mental or social impairment, or a combination of these factors, who require care in a range of settings. The aim of this research was to establish a needs-based workforce planning model and tool that focuses on assessing SCD's workforce capacity and capability to deliver tailored dental services for the UK's disabled populace.Methods A predictive analytics tool using Python and HTML was developed to integrate multiple large national datasets to identify key variables for long-term workforce planning and model future SCD demand through 2050. There are currently 13 million disabled adults, 5.9 million of whom are 'disabled; limited a lot'. National and regional population demand projections for SCD were calculated until 2050 using data mainly from the Office for National Statistics and the 2021-2022 Family Resources Survey. National data on the specialty were obtained from registration and survey data. National and regional resource supply projections for SCD were calculated until at least 2040 recursively from 2018 taking into consideration multiple factors.Results A detailed analysis highlighted several key findings. Under the present scenario, supply aligns with demand only when 5-8% of the 'disabled; limited a lot' category require complex dental care, suggesting that only a small proportion of needs is currently met by specialists. Planning for the future, for the baseline scenario, where 50% of the 'disabled; limited a lot' population is considered to have complex needs, even adding 150 specialty trainees per year will not meet projected need until 2040 due to the length of training. If the other half of the 'disabled; limited a lot' population is assumed to have moderate needs, then upskilling and adding 0.2% of the primary care dentists' pool, or about 80 primary care dentists to the dentists with extended skills (DES) pool per year, would allow this level of moderate need to be met as early as 2034. Strategic workforce redirections, such as even transitioning just 0.1% or 40 primary care dentists into the DES pool per year, could begin to significantly alter the supply-demand dynamics, together with a modest increase in specialty training numbers.Conclusions This study highlights the immense and growing need for SCD and the upskilling of frontline practitioners in caring for adults with additional needs. In essence, while the challenge before us is monumental, it is not insurmountable. Strategic planning, focused training initiatives, and nimble workforce reallocation are pivotal to ensuring that the UK's vulnerable populations receive the specialised dental care they deserve.
