all.title: Part Introduction: From Shocks to Strength
all.abstract: This introduction presents an overview of the key concepts discussed in part 4 of this book. The part helps the reader understand how resilience is built when uncertainty, markets, relationships, skills, and technology are treated together. It focuses on practical resilience design: geopolitical exposure, freight market response, partnership governance, workforce capability, and trustworthy GenAI services. The part opens by reframing geopolitical risk as a design and governance challenge. It explains why spot-rates can serve as early signals, how forecasts can be interpreted through uncertainty bands, and how playbooks can connect market signals to contracting, routing, capacity, inventory, and stakeholder communication. The part explains why digital readiness, technological competence, project-based learning, blended formats, internal mobility, and collaboration between industry and academia are necessary to keep supply chains capable as tools and operating models evolve. It examines how logistics service providers can turn GenAI into trusted resilience services.

all.title: Preparing the Workforce
all.abstract: This chapter examines how accounting education and professional development must evolve as generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) reshape work, supervision, and judgment. It identifies five recurring capability areas: learning agility; responsible tool and data use; evidence-based review; workflow and control literacy; and communication and change leadership. The chapter distinguishes responsible individual use, professional review competence, and workflow supervision, then translates those responsibilities into instructional design for generative and agentic systems. It evaluates focused, integrated, and hybrid curriculum pathways; faculty and institutional readiness; role-based professional upskilling; credentialing; lifelong learning; and global differences in access and implementation capacity. Practical tables provide instructional objectives, a professional AI learning ladder, an AI-use disclosure structure, and an agentic workflow supervision rubric. Throughout, the chapter emphasizes approved tools, source verification, confidentiality, visible reasoning, bounded delegation, escalation, retained evidence, and accountable human judgment. It concludes that workforce readiness requires repeated practice, supported experimentation, credible assessment, and sustained institutional investment rather than one-time training or tool access.

all.title: Asymmetric impact of bribes on labour investments: Evidence from Indian manufacturing firms
Futuristic Prospects of Higher Education for Soldiers: A Study of Educational empowerment, Career Transition and Emerging Opportunities
all.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
all.abstract: India’s Armed forces are undergoing a reflective transformation under the “Decade of Transformation” and the broader vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, ambitious by rapid technological change, multi-domain warfare, and the Agnipath recruitment model. This research article examines the futuristic prospects of higher education for soldiers (including Agniveers, serving personnel, and veterans) in the Indian context. It explores how digital platforms, credit recognition frameworks, university–defence collaborations, and competency-based learning can create seamless pathways between military service and lifelong academic and professional growth. Using a mixed-methods approach with the help of secondary data and that combines policy analysis, literature review of defence and higher-education reforms, and forward-looking scenario modelling, the article identifies both transformative potential and persistent challenges: deployment constraints, recognition of experiential learning, digital access in remote postings, and the need to balance warrior ethos with academic upskilling. Findings indicate that a well-aligned higher-education ecosystem can enhance force readiness, improve post-service employability, support Atmanirbhar Bharat in defense technology, and contribute to national human-capital goals under the National Education Policy 2020.

all.title: CROSS-SKILLING, UP-SKILLING, AND THEIR IMPACT ON THE ORGANISATIONS’ PERFORMANCE: A QUALITATIVE STUDY
all.abstract: Organisations are increasingly adopting cross-skilling and upskilling, which are found to be inevitable for all businesses, irrespective of sector. Automation and digitization are the major driving forces in this lead. Objective The objectives of this research are to explore the journey of crossover leadership, discussing its motivations, tangible and intangible benefits, and the challenges it faces Methods A qualitative approach is adopted to gather detailed information. A focus group of 16 members is conducted to gather their opinions. Additionally, 18 professionals are interviewed in depth. A conceptual diagram is developed, and hypotheses are formulated. Results QualCoder software is used for the data analysis. Many employees and employers agree that cross-skilling and up-skilling are beneficial in many ways, though they have drawbacks. Conclusion It is concluded that up-skilling, re-skilling, and cross-skilling are highly essential in the wake of the current digitization and automation era. However, this research is limited by several factors, including potential biases, personal opinions, and subjective choices that may influence the views expressed during the interviews. This research can be further extended to determine the return on investment of the entire process. This study benefits organisations by aligning their recruitment processes to accommodate these practices.

all.title: Enhancing pharmacist engagement in primary care through a pharmacogenomics-guided statin toolkit
institutions: VA Great Lakes Health Care System
South Central VA Health Care Network
William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital
all.abstract: PURPOSE: We created a toolkit focused on providing the resources clinical pharmacist practitioners needed to efficiently and confidently engage in pharmacogenomics-guided statin prescribing in primary care clinics. SUMMARY: In recent years, pharmacogenomic testing is increasingly recognized as a method to improve medication efficacy and safety through personalized medication selection and management. Despite the growing body of evidence supporting pharmacogenomics-driven care, routine application in primary care practice remains low. The toolkit focused on standard methods to identify eligible patients, locating and interpreting pharmacogenomics results, and documenting interventions in the electronic health record. We also included clinical education and decision support tools to allow pharmacists to quickly upskill in or to successfully interpret and apply pharmacogenomics results to statin prescribing. A multitiered strategy was adopted for diffusion which included leadership engagement, group socialization, and individual outreach. After diffusion, we were able to see an increase in clinical pharmacist practitioner engagement through all metrics tracked. CONCLUSION: Our experience demonstrates a scalable method to foster pharmacogenomics adoption within pharmacists-led care.

all.title: Economic Prospects of Georgia, DCFTA Obligations, and Labour Market Restructuring
all.abstract: This academic paper examines the theoretical foundations, structural challenges, and synergistic effects of digital transformation and European economic integration in developing economies, with a specific focus on Georgia. Drawing upon the World Bank’s "Digital Dividends" framework and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) digital diffusion models, the study analyzes global digital asymmetry and Georgia’s transitional trajectory from basic digital adoption toward an advanced platform-based economy. Particular emphasis is placed on the implementation of regulatory commitments under the EU-Georgia Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA)—specifically harmonization with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), electronic identification and trust services (eIDAS), and cybersecurity standards (NIS2)—alongside the geo-economic significance of the EU Global Gateway initiative and the Black Sea submarine fiber-optic cable project. The research demonstrates that adopting a technological "leapfrogging" model, fostering remote online employment, digital freelancing, and cross-border e-commerce provide viable mechanisms for reducing structural unemployment, mitigating brain drain, and expanding high-value-added service exports. Finally, the paper outlines a three-pillar strategic roadmap centered on universal regional broadband connectivity, micro-credential-based workforce reskilling, and full institutional alignment with the European Union’s Digital Single Market.

all.title: Supply Chain Talent in the Digital Era
all.abstract: Talent shortages are constraining digital transformation in logistics and supply chain management (LSCM). This mixed-methods study combines a survey of 179 professionals across 21 countries (Africa-led sample), five expert interviews, and an embedded case from Kaduna State, Nigeria. Respondents view AI/ML (≈60.9%), data analytics (≈49.2%), and IoT (≈45.3%) as most impactful, yet ≈61.5% report no emerging-technology training in the past two years. Top barriers are cost (≈72.6%), limited organizational support (≈40.2%), and access to relevant programs (≈30.1%); preferred formats are blended, work-embedded approaches (≈60.3%). Professional development and career growth consistently outrank compensation as retention levers. The case evidence indicates that project-based learning with real tools/datasets, co-designed with academic/industry partners, accelerates adoption and mobility but should be generalized cautiously. We propose a practical KPI set—time-to-productivity, tech-adoption lead time, internal mobility, role-specific retention, and learning gain—to monitor impact. The findings offer actionable guidance for building a future-ready LSCM workforce.

all.title: Industrial Revolution 4.0 Adoption in Malaysian Real Estate Agencies
all.venue: Research in Management of Technology and Business
institutions: Tun Hussein Onn University of Malaysia
all.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution (IR 4.0) has significantly transformed global real estate through digital integration, yet its adoption within Malaysian agencies remains inconsistent and underexplored despite its potential to enhance operational efficiency. This study aims to identify the specific IR 4.0 technologies currently leveraged in Malaysian real estate agency practices and to examine the perceived benefits and challenges associated with their adoption from the perspective of active practitioners. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected through structured questionnaires from 61 registered real estate agents. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s Rank Correlation to accommodate non-normal data distributions. The findings reveal moderate adoption of cloud computing and drones alongside low utilisation of artificial intelligence and big data analytics. Significant positive correlations indicate that increased digital engagement concurrently heightens practitioners' awareness of both technological benefits and implementation challenges. The findings suggest that while the industry exhibits a high level of cognitive readiness for digital transformation practical adoption remains constrained by technical knowledge gaps and implementation barriers. Future research should focus on developing specialised digital readiness frameworks and targeted upskilling initiatives to bridge these gaps and support sustainable technology adoption within the industry.

all.title: **Navigating the AI-Driven Economy: Bridging the Gap Between Academic Foundations and the Future IT/R&D Workforce**
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: ## Alternative Titles* **Option A (Academic Focus):** *The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Employment Dynamics: A Study of Future Skill Requirements, Industry-Academia Alignment, and Career Pathways.** **Option B (Industry Focus):** *Machine Learning and the Future of Work: Navigating the Transition from Traditional IT Services to AI-Driven R&D.** **Option C (Action-Oriented):** *Preparing for 2026 and Beyond: Essential Skills, Emerging Job Sectors, and the Role of Continuous Learning in the AI Era.** **Option D (Regional/Contextual):** *From Classrooms to Corporate R&D: An Analysis of AI, Upskilling, and the Evolving IT Job Market.* ## Subtitle*Bridging Theoretical Pedagogy with Practical Industry Demands in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.* --- ## Detailed Description / Abstract The global job market is undergoing a profound structural transformation, shifting from traditional service-oriented models to a dynamic, data-driven economy powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This research paper synthesizes insights from recent industry forecasts, technological trends, and expert interviews with R&D leaders to provide a comprehensive analysis of the future workforce landscape. The study is anchored on three primary pillars. **First, it examines the technological shift**, wherein AI and ML are no longer merely automating routine tasks but are acting as catalysts for innovation. By analyzing data patterns to predict outcomes, these technologies are creating high-value career pathways in fields such as R&D, Data Science, Cybersecurity, Healthcare, and Green Energy. The paper explores how the demand for "smart work" is replacing traditional "hard work," requiring professionals to transition from mere task executors to strategic problem solvers. **Second, the paper addresses the critical skills gap and the imperative of continuous upskilling.** It outlines the essential technical competencies required for the 2026 job market, including proficiency in programming (Python, Java), data handling (SQL), and a strong foundation in mathematics and algorithms. Crucially, it highlights that technical expertise alone is insufficient; modern professionals must also possess strong soft skills, including adaptability, complex problem-solving, and effective communication—emphasizing the unique value of regional language proficiency in global operations. **Third, and most importantly, the research investigates the widening gap between academic curricula and the practical requirements of the corporate world.** Drawing on insights from industry veterans, the paper argues that traditional education often falls short of preparing students for the realities of AI-integrated R&D environments. It proposes a paradigm shift where academic institutions and industries collaborate closely—integrating practical, real-world problem-solving into pedagogy and fostering a culture of lifelong learning. Ultimately, this paper concludes that the future of work is not defined by mass unemployment but by massive opportunity for those who are adaptable. By bridging the divide between academia and industry, and by fostering a workforce that combines deep technical knowledge with domain-specific expertise (such as in Metallurgical or Electrical Engineering), society can effectively navigate the AI revolution. The paper serves as both a roadmap for students entering the workforce and a strategic guide for educators and industry leaders aiming to align human capital with the demands of the 2026 digital economy.

all.title: Digital Talent Development and Adoption of AI Among Higher Education Faculty
all.abstract: There has been a significant shift in the usage and adoption of AI Institutions specifically the ones providing Higher education and the AI usage has seen to be specifically in the areas of digital competency enhancement for the teaching faculty, development of course curriculum, learning and teaching methods, academic stewardship and research activities. This paper is an attempt to analyse the corelation between AI technology adoption and its impact on competency development of teaching faculty of institutions. The analysis utilises the viewpoints of existent literature, evidence from contemporary research and existing institutional case studies in this domain. The primary aim of this paper will be to focus on the usage of artificial intelligence technology as teaching tools, in faculty training beyond the classroom, and initiatives for upskilling in digital domain in higher education thus enabling better educational practices. This paper will attempt to provide a validation to digital talent development as a critical driver to be deployed in higher education institutions to ensure sustainment of their competitiveness globally. The paper will review the impact of three key factors namely faculty digital Competencies, Institutional Support frameworks, and ethical and pedagogical aspects of AI adoption. A representation of select case studies from Universities located in the United States, Europe and Asia will be considered to provide a global perspective on the subject of this paper. Lastly an analysis to accrue an understanding of issues of change resistance, data privacy and access to digital infrastructure will be included in this study.

all.title: ONA and N1 SCA: Organizational Network Analysis and Social Capital Management
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Companies study informal relationships in two ways. Organizational network analysis (ONA) is a study that captures relationships at the time data are collected. N1 Social Capital Architecture (N1 SCA) is a description of the community that is updated as work proceeds. This note explains when to use one, when to use the other, and when to combine them. It also shows how to prepare N1 SCA records for a network study and how to check its responses against the facts. A separate part of the note covers the use of ONA and N1 SCA in mergers and acquisitions (M&A), in Sections 7–9 and the appendices: why deals lose social capital and what must be preserved; how to verify, before the deal, who the business and its value depend on; how to hand over relationships after the deal and enter the acquired company's community; why handing over records of relationships is not the same as preserving the relationships themselves. The note complements AN-13, "N1 SCA in Mergers and Acquisitions." It contains no new research data and does not test whether the method works.

all.title: Duty and Fidelity: Distinguishing the Concepts in Loyalty Assessment
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: When analyzing loyalty data in projects that use N1 Social Capital Architecture (N1 SCA) and organizational network analysis (ONA), the authors have repeatedly found that clients conflate duty and fidelity. This note gives working definitions of both and shows how they differ: in their basis, their source of stability, and what a breach leaves behind. What a tie rests on determines how it behaves when roles and conditions change. The definitions are the authors' own; dictionary and philosophical sources are listed separately.

all.title: Routine-Enabled Contact and Coordination Cost: Why Contact Can Fall When a Shared Routine Ends
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Routine-Enabled Contact and Coordination Cost, a mechanism in which a shared routine supplies repeated low-cost encounters, while removal of that routine makes each later contact require fresh planning and effort. The account assesses a decline in contact by separating changed opportunity from changed feeling. Reduced contact establishes that people met less, not why. Evidence can include the routine that previously supplied encounters, the timing of its removal, comparisons with people whose routines did not change, and reports about whether participants still wanted contact. Feelings may also change, and a change of routine alone does not establish the mechanism. The discussion connects the mechanism to Feld’s account of foci of activity and examines Yang and colleagues’ study of collaboration among Microsoft employees following the shift to firm-wide remote work in 2020. The study found more static and siloed collaboration networks, fewer bridges across groups, reduced synchronous communication, and increased asynchronous communication. It does not separately identify the effects of lost incidental encounters, greater planning effort, and changes in how colleagues regarded one another. Part of the Coordination and Dependence series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines how routines make contact inexpensive and how their removal redistributes the work of maintaining connection. Its framework can inform human–AI research on collaboration systems, remote interaction, mediated social contact, and tools that alter the effort required to sustain human relationships.

all.title: Beyond Compliance: How Safety Management Practices Shape Workplace Safety Outcomes
all.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
all.abstract: Safety management practices play an important role in ensuring workplace and environmental safety. However, the practices do not rely solely on standard procedures. To prevent hazards, organizations need to provide resources, set priorities, support workers, and manage workplace conditions. The evidence on management systems and hazard prevention, leadership and employee involvement, training and communication, and the behavioural and climate pathways linking these practices to safety results is summarized in this review. Although selection effects and heterogeneous effectiveness across firm types limit causal inference, the most consistent conclusion is that organizational and group practices are associated with better safety compliance and participation. Stronger evidence for reducing injury is found for interventions that change hazards or work systems, as well as important paired observational studies of certification of occupational safety and health management systems. Safety climate is a useful leading indicator and a reliable mechanism, but it cannot be used interchangeably with injuries because studies differ in directionality, time lag, unit of analysis, and outcome source. Although training generally improves safety behaviour and knowledge, its effect on injuries varies by workplace and the controls in place. Leadership and worker involvement are important to ensure that safety practices are properly implemented. However, research evidence remains limited, particularly in studies that rely solely on questionnaires, combine different safety measures, or assess injury prevention based solely on workers' behaviour. In conclusion, safety management is more effective when different safety practices are applied together and adapted to reduce workplace risks. Worker involvement, supervision and safety performance monitoring should be given proper attention. Prolonged research periods, data from multiple sources, and consideration of differences across work sectors should be taken into account for future research.

all.title: Analysis of Labor Coefficients Based on Labor Productivity in Palembang City
all.venue: Journal of Infrastructure and Civil Engineering
all.abstract: The construction industry is a major contributor to Indonesia’s infrastructure development, covering various civil engineering works, including buildings, highways, bridges, and other infrastructure facilities. The achievement of construction project objectives depends on effective planning, appropriate management practices, and the competence of the workforce involved. Effective construction planning requires competent workers and adequate productivity. Project scheduling helps organize activities, allocate resources, and control progress, with work durations largely influenced by labor requirements and productivity. In Indonesia, labor needs are estimated using standardized coefficients from the Indonesia National standard (SNI) and Work Unit Price Analysis (AHSP), which serve as references for construction planning and cost estimation. Field data were obtained through on-site surveys conducted using interviews and questionnaire distribution. The questionnaire responses were subsequently compiled and analyzed using Microsoft Excel to identify the types of work, their respective cost value, and time required to complete each activity. The collected data were further examined to evaluate workforce productivity and establish the labor coefficients reflecting actual construction site performance. Based on the data processing result, the daily working time was established as 8 hours. For reinforcement work, 4 workers were required to complete a work volume of 65 kg within 5 days. Based on the field observations, the labor productivity of reinforcement workers was determined to be 130 kg/worker-day, with a labor coefficient of 0,0077 OH/kg. For formwork activities, 5 workers were required to complete a work volume of 1,5 m² within 5 days. The resulting labor productivity of carpenters was 0,3 m²/worker-days, with a corresponding labor coefficient of 0,3333 OH/m². Furthermore, for concrete casting activities, 4 workers were required to completed a work volume of 0,8 m³ within 5 days. The resulting labor productivity of concrete workers was 3,2 m³/worker-day, with a corresponding labor coefficient of 0,3125 OH/m³. Following the data analysis, a comparative assessment was conducted between the labor coefficients obtained from field observations and those specified in the AHSP issued by the PUPR of Palembang City. For reinforcement work, the labor coefficient obtained from the field observations was 0,0077 OH/kg, compared with 0,0070 OH/kg specified in the AHSP. For formwork activities, the field-based labor coefficient was 0,3333 OH/m², whereas he AHSP coefficient was 0,3300 OH/m². Meanwhile, for concrete casting activities, the labor coefficient obtained from the field observations concrete casting activities, the labor coefficient obtained from the field observations was 0,3125 OH/m³, compared with 0,2750 specified in the AHSP.

all.title: INCENTIVE SCHEMES AND CONSTRUCTION WORKERS’ PERFORMANCE IN BAUCHI STATE, NIGERIA
all.venue: International Journal of Earth Design and Innovation Research
all.abstract: Employee performance is a key determinant of organizational productivity and successful project delivery, particularly in the construction industry where labour plays a vital role. However, many construction firms in Nigeria continue to face challenges such as low productivity, project delays, poor workmanship, and workforce inefficiencies due to inadequate employee motivation and ineffective incentive schemes. This study examines the relationship between incentive schemes and construction workers’ performance in Bauchi State, Nigeria. The study focuses on the incentives scheme adopted by construction companies and their relationship with workers’ performance. A quantitative research approach was adopted, with questionnaire responses collected from construction workers. The findings indicate that medical benefits, safety equipment, paid leave, job security and training opportunities are among the incentive schemes reported by respondents. Workers’ performance was assessed using indicators such as efficiency in resource utilisation, teamwork, commitment, punctuality, safety compliance and task completion. Pearson correlation analysis produced a coefficient of 0.717, while regression analysis produced an incentive coefficient of 0.873 (p < 0.001), with an R-square value of 0.550. These statistics indicate a positive relationship between incentive schemes and workers’ performance. The study recommends that construction companies pay attention to appropriate financial and non-financial incentive arrangements as part of their workforce management practices.

all.title: An interplay of bricks and emotions- Role of job crafting and emotional intelligence in determining self-perceived productivity in the construction industry
all.abstract: This study aims to examine the role of emotional intelligence (EI) and relational job crafting and their association with self-perceived productivity among employees working in the construction sector. The study particularly emphasizes Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory by considering EI and relational job crafting as important resources for employees. The primary objective is to examine the role of EI and relational job crafting in enhancing employees’ psychological and social well-being and, ultimately, their self-perceived productivity. The study is explanatory and cross-sectional in nature thus the study captures only association among variables. Data was collected from construction workers using standardized scales. A sample of 689 respondents was selected using a stratified sampling technique. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was employed using AMOS to analyze the data. The findings indicate that employees working in the construction industry is linked to emotional intelligence and relational job crafting abilities to reframe their perspectives towards job demands. These abilities assist employees to maintain greater psychological and social stability, which is further found to be positively associated with self-perceived productivity. The findings suggest that construction organizations could support emotional intelligence training and encourage relational job crafting, particularly for workers experiencing physical exhaustion. Relational job crafting and emotional intelligence may help employees to cope with job demands, experience greater psychological relief, and develop a more positive outlook. This study contributes to the understanding of employee well-being in high-risk occupational sectors and advocates a shift from a purely mechanistic model towards more human-oriented management practices. Further, the study provides insights into emotional and behavioral resources associated with well-being and self-perceived productivity in a physically demanding occupational context.

all.title: AI Is Not a Safety Panacea: Evidence from Early AI Adoption
all.abstract: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) labor intensity and workplace safety violations in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry where foundational AI technologies have been incorporated into practice for decades before the emergence of generative AI. This paper hypothesizes that managers overrely on AI-enabled monitoring systems and consequently pay less attention to traditional safety-management practices. Using a novel firm-level data set of AI worker share as a proxy of AI labor intensity, it finds that firms with greater AI worker share experience significantly more workplace safety violations. The effect is stronger in AEC firms than in nonAEC firms and is concentrated in serious violations. Additional analyses show more victims, larger regulatory penalties, and weaker safety environments for AI-intensive AEC firms. However, strong board monitoring mitigates the adverse relationship between AI worker share and workplace safety violations. Overall, these findings suggest that the benefits of early AI adoption depend on complementary governance structures and sustained managerial attention to workplace safety.

all.title: Challenges to Risk Management Implementation and Perceived Strategies for Optimising Safety Performance on Construction Sites in Anambra State, Nigeria
all.abstract: Construction remains one of the most hazardous industries in Nigeria, and Anambra State has recorded repeated building collapses and site accidents that have forced emergency regulatory interventions. Yet the barriers that prevent construction firms from implementing comprehensive risk management, and the strategies most likely to optimise safety performance, have not been systematically documented for the State. This study explored the challenges faced by construction firms in implementing comprehensive risk management practices and sought to establish strategies for optimising safety performance on construction sites in Anambra State, based on the perceptions of construction professionals. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study population comprised 928 construction professionals (builders, architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and health and safety officers); a sample size of 287 was determined using the Taro Yamane formula, purposive and random sampling techniques were applied, and 198 validquestionnaires were retrieved from the 287 administered (a response rate of 69.0%) and analysed using frequencies, percentages, mean scores, standard deviations and the Relative Importance Index (RII). The findings revealed that the most severe challenges were financial constraints limiting risk management investment (mean = 4.82; 1st), inadequate knowledge and training (mean = 4.74; 2nd) and weak regulatory enforcement and political interference (mean = 4.71; 3rd), followed by workers' resistance to safety protocols (mean = 4.64), poor health and safety culture (mean = 4.56) andcorruption and bribery (mean = 4.25). All six strategies were rated agree or strongly agree by every respondent (a ceiling effect, with no undecided or disagreeing responses), so the ranking is indicative only: comprehensive safety training programmes (mean = 4.96; 1st), strengthened regulatory enforcement mechanisms (mean = 4.94; 2nd) and worker participation in safety management (mean = 4.93; 3rd) ranked highest, although all six means fell between 4.90 and 4.96.The study concludes that safety performance in the State can be optimised only through a coordinated, multi-stakeholder approach that addresses finance, capacity, regulation, behaviour and governance together. It therefore recommends a state-wide subsidised safety training programme, a dedicated and politically insulated inspection unit, low-interest financing for construction SMEs, worker safety committees with confidential reporting channels, and a simplifiedrisk management toolkit for small firms.

all.title: Traditional Workplace Surveillance
all.abstract: This chapter examines workplace surveillance before the digital age through the idea of an ‘imperfect’ ‘panopticon’, since the capitalist workplace was already ‘panoptic’ insofar as the conversion of labour-power into labour required supervision and the rendering of work visible, yet remained ‘imperfect’ because observation was constrained by the physical presence of overseers and by the episodic character of inspection. Records were fragmented and the available instruments of measurement imposed further limits on what employers could know, even as successive managerial regimes sought to reduce this opacity, beginning with the early factory system in Britain and continuing through scientific management, particularly the work of Frederick Taylor, as well as micromotion study, before taking new forms under Fordism and the later development of personnel management and human relations in the United States. None of these regimes eliminated the indeterminacy of labour, but each drew observation and temporal measurement more tightly into managerial command, allowing digital surveillance to be situated not as an unprecedented departure but as an intensification of a much older capitalist project.

all.title: Inteligência artificial e gestão algorítmica do trabalho os limites do poder diretivo do empregador e a tutela dos direitos fundamentais do trabalhador: uma revisão integrativa.
all.abstract: This study aimed to examine the transformations caused by artificial intelligence and algorithmic management in the exercise of the employer's managerial power, seeking to understand the legal limits required to protect workers' fundamental rights in employment relations. This is an integrative literature review with a qualitative and descriptive approach, complemented by a legal and normative analysis. Searches were conducted in SciELO Brasil, SPELL, and Sumários.org between August and September 2026, covering publications from the previous five years, corresponding to the period from 2022 to 2026. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 13 articles composed the final analysis. The results were organized into five thematic axes concerning algorithmic management and new forms of subordination; control, monitoring, and working time; privacy, data protection, transparency, and algorithmic discrimination; worker autonomy and health; and legal limits and protection strategies. The findings showed that algorithmic systems may be involved in recruitment and selection, task allocation, monitoring, performance evaluation, remuneration, and the organization of working time. Risks related to information asymmetry, excessive data processing, opacity of automated decisions, discrimination, and work intensification were also identified. The legal analysis showed that the use of technology does not eliminate the limits imposed on managerial power, while data protection, transparency, proportionality, nondiscrimination, the possibility of reviewing decisions, and accountability for the effects of algorithmic systems remain relevant. It is concluded that artificial intelligence may contribute to the organization of business activities; however, its use in employment relations must remain subject to workers' fundamental rights and to mechanisms capable of making technological power transparent, proportionate, and legally accountable.

all.title: The Impact of Perceived Digital Workplace Surveillance on Work Alienation: The Mediating Role of Psychological Reactance and the Moderating Role of Leader Emotional Intelligence
institutions: Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: The relationship between perceived digital workplace surveillance and work alienation of workers of higher education institutions (HEIs) in Sindh, Pakistan is examined in this study. It not only explores the mediating effect of psychological reactance but also the moderating effect of leader emotional intelligence. The proposed framework is based on a quantitative research approach where the survey data from 221 HEI employees are analyzed by using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) method to analyze the hypothesized relationships. The illustrative results suggest that perceived digital workplace surveillance is positively related to psychological reactance and work alienation. A mediating role is manifested in psychological reactance, and leader emotional intelligence is proposed to impact the relationship between psychological reactance and work alienation. The findings of the study help to further describe the psychological impact of digital monitoring, and emphasize the need for a balance of institutional responsibility and employee autonomy, privacy, and wellbeing. Empirical data must be used to confirm actual conclusions.

all.title: Worker Power, Algorithmic Management, and African Resistance in the Digital Age
all.abstract: This chapter examines the mobilizing and organizing practices of ride-hailing drivers in Africa. It draws on the labour process and power resources approaches to foreground the role of socio-political contexts in understanding how platform workers build independent self-organized solidarity networks to exert their power with variable outcomes. It argues that self-organized networks are an important outlet for worker power outside the domains of established unions. In the context of the platform economy, worker power rarely materializes into a meaningful front for resistance and instead their actions can be understood as resilience and reworking of the system to extract material and non-material rewards. This is particularly relevant for workers in Africa. Drawing on multi-country and multi-year study utilizing in-depth interviews with African Uber drivers and leaders of driver groups and digital ethnography of worker communication channels, the chapter outlines several socio-economic and political constraints faced by ride-hailing drivers which can inhibit collective resistance.

all.title: The dark side of algorithmic management: platform affordances, labour process and workers’ skills in the case of Deliveroo
Legal Regulation of Content Moderation in Social Networks: Balance of Public and Private Interests under the Algorithmic Management
all.venue: Journal of Digital Technologies and Law
all.abstract: Objective: to study current technological and legal concepts in order to determine the legal nature of content moderation in social networks, choose appropriate means of its regulatory regulation, and establish the boundaries of government interference in the activities of digital platforms. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was a set of general scientific methods of cognition (analysis, synthesis, induction and deduction) in combination with special legal methods, including formallegal and comparative-legal. The use of the comparative-legal method made it possible to compare the regulatory models of Russia, China, the European Union, and the United States. The interdisciplinary approach allowed evaluating algorithmic filtering and commercial moderation from the standpoint of public-law and civilistic doctrines. Results: it is proved that moderation of user content is an element of corporate governance of a social network and an integral part of its business model. It was established that, in legal terms, this activity is implemented in three aspects: as a public-law instrument for suppressing the dissemination of illegal content in the interests of state and public safety; as a constitutional-legal guarantee of freedom of speech and fundamental rights of citizens; as a private-law mechanism for protecting the property and personal non-property rights of users and online communities. It is proved that, under hybrid information filtering with artificial intelligence algorithms, the legitimacy of platform control is achieved by a combination of legislative regulation, corporate selfregulation and, user self-censorship. Scientific novelty: the study formulates the concept of balancing the publiclaw goals of suppressing illegal information and protecting the private interests of digital content creators while limiting the discretionary powers of platform owners. The applicability of a private-law approach to content moderation relations is substantiated, including when transferring the functions of checking and blocking materials to external contractors on outsourcing terms, where a third party is actually given public-law powers without direct contractual relations with the user. The article substantiates considering artificial intelligence in the moderation circuit as an element of a sociotechnical system that affects public trust and reliability of the information environment. Practical significance: this is due to the presence of gaps in legislation regarding the regulation of platform moderation procedures, as well as the lack of regulatory certainty of the user’s right to receive an explanation of the reasons for restricting access to content and the right to challenge the decisions of algorithmic systems or moderators. The formulated conclusions can be used by the legislator and operators of digital platforms in improving the legal mechanisms of transparency, accountability and proportionality of content moderation in social networks.

all.title: Algorithmic Management in Australian Workplaces: A Study on Transparency, Accountability and Worker Protection in AI-Driven Employment Decisions
all.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
all.abstract: AI systems are widely used in recruitment screening, job allocation, performance evaluation, remuneration decisions, promotion and dismissal. Compared with traditional human management, algorithmic management can improve information-processing efficiency and assist employers in making complex workplace decisions. This article employs doctrinal legal analysis to examine the regulation of AI-driven employment decisions under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), anti-discrimination law and the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Drawing on Mobley v Workday Inc and Houston Federation of Teachers v Houston Independent School District, it identifies the practical limitations of the existing legal framework. The analysis finds that Australian law provides partial protection, but remains fragmented and reactive. Workers generally obtain remedies only after an adverse decision has occurred, while the current framework lacks adequate pre-deployment disclosure, risk assessment, independent auditing and meaningful human review. It recommends prior disclosure, individualised reasons for adverse decisions, restrictions on solely automated decisions, clear employer accountability, algorithmic impact assessments, periodic independent audits and worker participation. These reforms would not prohibit workplace AI; rather, they would establish a more appropriate balance between technological efficiency, fairness, accountability and worker protection.

all.title: Neuroderechos y gestión algorítmica en el trabajo: riesgos laborales emergentes y redefinición del deber de prevención del empleador
institutions: Universidad Nacional del Centro del Perú
all.abstract: This article examines how algorithmic management and neurotechnologies transform occupational risks and the employer’s duty of prevention. Drawing on a legal review of publications from 2015 to 2025 and a doctrinal, functional, and comparative analysis, it examines psychosocial, cognitive, discriminatory, and other risks associated with the processing of neural data. The study compares the safeguards established under European law, International Labour Organization standards, and the Peruvian legal framework governing occupational safety and health, data protection, and artificial intelligence. It identifies difficulties in assessing risks arising from opaque systems, supervising automated decision-making, and safeguarding workers’ right to defend themselves against disciplinary measures. The article proposes clarifying preventive obligations through the provision of clear and comprehensible information, meaningful human involvement in decisions producing significant effects, participatory risk assessments, and limits on the processing of mental data. In the Peruvian context, it distinguishes existing legal obligations from proposed regulatory measures.

all.title: Perceived Unfairness in Algorithmic Management Among Gig Workers: A Grounded Theory Study of Dimensions, Emotional Responses, and Coping Strategies
institutions: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
Shanxi University of Finance and Economics
all.abstract: Online labor platforms increasingly rely on algorithmic management to coordinate labor supply and demand. Although algorithmic systems can improve operational efficiency and reduce certain forms of human arbitrariness, they also shape gig workers’ perceptions of fairness in consequential ways. Focusing on ride-hailing drivers on the Didi Chuxing platform in China, this study adopts Strauss and Corbin’s procedural grounded theory to examine how perceived unfairness in algorithmic management is structured and how it is linked to workers’ emotional experiences and behavioral coping strategies. Drawing on triangulated qualitative data comprising 19 semi-structured interviews with Didi drivers across six Chinese cities (15 model-building interviews—13 Wave-1 interviews generating 86 initial coding-sheet statements and 2 Wave-2 modeling expansion interviews—plus 4 Wave-2 interviews examined as an analytical saturation subsample for retrospective saturation verification), 38 in-depth online driver forum threads, and 14 thematic media and public commentary dossiers (totaling 422 coded raw statements and up to 482 initial label assignments), we conducted systematic open, axial, and selective coding alongside a cross-case comparison of the 15 modeling interviews. The findings indicate that while some drivers appreciate the transparency of automated metering and order matching compared to traditional taxi dispatching, perceived unfairness in algorithmic management is structured around three interrelated dimensions: distributive unfairness, procedural unfairness, and interactional unfairness (wherein interpersonal indignity and informational opacity frequently intertwine). These unfairness perceptions evoke negative emotional distress, including dissatisfaction, anger, a sense of grievance (weiqu), disappointment, helplessness, and fear. Crucially, cross-case analysis indicates that how drivers translate this emotional distress into behavior is systematically conditioned by structural and situational boundary factors—specifically exit costs under vehicle lease/loan lock-in, outside occupational or household income buffers, net margin viability, and tactical/external action resources—which orient workers toward three coping strategies: algorithmic compliance, algorithmic avoidance, and algorithmic resistance. By reconstructing how workers interpret and navigate algorithmically mediated labor control within China’s evolving regulatory regime, this study extends organizational justice and affective events theories into the platform economy and offers evidence-based implications for transparent and human-centered digital governance.

all.title: The Rise of Abstract Time
all.abstract: This chapter reconstructs the historical emergence of abstract time as a necessary condition of workplace surveillance, arguing that before labour could be systematically supervised or disciplined, it first had to become measurable in temporal terms. It contrasts pre-modern experiences organised around cycles and tasks with the abstract, linear time that develops alongside capitalist relations of production and exchange, showing how monastic schedules and urban bells, followed by public clocks and the demands of commercial coordination, prefigure a transformation that capitalism gives its decisive form: labour-power is bought for a period, so the employer’s claim over the worker becomes a claim over time itself. This history is important for the later argument because digital workplace surveillance remains organised around temporal measurement, from responsiveness and pace to productivity benchmarks, which means that the contemporary dashboard can be understood only against the longer history through which time was abstracted and commodified.

all.title: From safeguard to surveillance justification: The transformation of the right to be informed in ECtHR jurisprudence
all.abstract: This article examines the evolving function of the right to be informed in regulating workplace surveillance through a systematic analysis of the European Court of Human Rights’ case law. It asks whether workers’ prior information continues to operate as a meaningful safeguard against employer monitoring or whether its function within the Court's reasoning has progressively changed. While the Court continues formally to rely on the criterion established in Bărbulescu v Romania, a systematic examination of its subsequent case law reveals that workers’ information has lost much of its protective force. Once a safeguard whose absence weighed heavily against employers, information is increasingly treated as one criterion among others within the Court's proportionality assessment, readily outweighed by expanding managerial and property-based interests and, once formally satisfied, capable of supporting the very monitoring it was meant to constrain. The article traces this evolution through two interconnected developments. First, the circumstances in which employers may engage in covert surveillance have progressively broadened. Second, increasingly intrusive monitoring practices have been considered compatible with Article 8 despite limited, ambiguous, or delayed information being provided to workers. As a result, the threshold for complying with transparency obligations has gradually been reduced to a minimal notification requirement. Transparency therefore functions less as an autonomous safeguard protecting workers ex ante and increasingly as part of the Court's justificatory reasoning when assessing the compatibility of workplace surveillance with Article 8. On this basis, the article identifies a transformation in the legal function assigned to workers’ information. Prior information progressively ceases to operate as an ex ante constraint on monitoring and instead becomes one element within the Court's proportionality assessment capable of supporting its ex post justification. Workers’ information and transparency requirements, intended to mitigate structural power asymmetries in the employment relationship, may therefore contribute to legitimising workplace surveillance when reduced to formal transparency obligations. By reconstructing this jurisprudential evolution, the article offers a new explanation for the “ more surveillance approach ” identified in recent scholarship and shows that this development reflects a broader transformation in the Court's reasoning rather than a position confined to a limited number of cases. It further situates this evolution within a European and international regulatory landscape that increasingly reinforces transparency obligations and workers’ informational rights. Against this background, the article argues that the effectiveness of informational safeguards ultimately depends less on their formal recognition than on the weight courts are willing to accord them within their proportionality assessment. As new regulatory instruments reinforce transparency and participatory safeguards for workers, the Court may increasingly be called upon to restore the weight attributed to workers’ right to be informed of monitoring and the threshold of transparency expected from employers within Article 8 balancing.

all.title: Introduction
all.abstract: This chapter sets out the central problem of the book: the rise of workplace surveillance as a structural feature of the contemporary labour process, rather than a merely technical supplement to management or one element within the broader category of control. It argues that digital monitoring has become one of the principal means through which labour-power is rendered knowable and governable under digital capitalism, while existing research has often remained confined by a narrow sectoral focus and a preoccupation with privacy, by an empirical orientation insufficiently connected to theory and political economy or by a lack of historical depth. Against this background, the chapter brings Labour Process Theory into dialogue with Foucauldian approaches to ‘panopticism’ in order to show how contemporary surveillance reorganises the workplace by intensifying a much older capitalist effort to make labour visible and measurable, and thereby more readily subject to discipline.

all.title: ‘Datafied' Bodies
all.abstract: This chapter extends the analysis of workplace surveillance to the body by examining corporate wellness programmes and wearable fitness trackers alongside fatigue-detection systems and health-risk scoring as techniques through which employers and associated intermediaries seek to make workers’ health and bodily capacities visible. This is not a wholly new development, since capitalist workplaces have long attempted to regulate bodies and conduct, but digitalisation changes its form by integrating health-related information into infrastructures through which workers can be compared and encouraged to monitor themselves, thereby bringing disciplinary power directed at work performance into contact with ‘biopolitical’ regulation of the worker as a bearer of life processes. Read against the background of neoliberal ‘precarisation’, the language of ‘wellness and care’ can, therefore, conceal a disciplinary logic in which workers feel pressure to display good health or resilience as signs of compliance, particularly where continued employability appears to depend upon participation in these regimes.

all.title: The Context of the Rise of Digital Surveillance
all.abstract: This chapter situates the rise of digital workplace surveillance within the political economy of late twentieth- and early twenty-first-century capitalism, arguing that its diffusion cannot be explained by technological innovation alone but must be understood against the disintegration of the post-war capital–labour compromise and the erosion of the securities associated with it, as collective protections weakened and precarious employment expanded. It follows the movement from relatively stabilised employment relations towards neoliberal labour-market discipline, while locating informational capitalism and platform-based business models within this wider transformation, rather than treating them as autonomous technological developments. The chapter also qualifies accounts of ‘surveillance capitalism’ that present data extraction as an entirely new regime, proposing instead that digital surveillance extends older capitalist strategies for making labour knowable and governable; the Foucauldian concept of neoliberal ‘governmentality’ helps to explain how market discipline becomes embedded in data infrastructures and is reproduced through habits of self-monitoring, contributing to the normalisation of surveillance at work.

all.title: Regulating Workplace CCTV Surveillance to ProtectEmployees’ Privacy Rights
all.abstract: The use of Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) in the workplace places employers’ security interests alongside employees’ rights to privacy and personal data protection. This study examines the legal basis and limits of CCTV monitoring and identifies the conditions for civil liability arising from misuse of recordings. It employs normative legal research through statutory and conceptual approaches, with qualitative-prescriptive analysis. Its contribution is a framework connecting lawful grounds for data processing, proportionality of workplace surveillance, governance of recordings, and the elements of an unlawful act in the specific context of workplace CCTV. The findings indicate that workplace monitoring is not absolutely prohibited; however, processing footage that identifies employees must have a lawful basis and a specific purpose, and must be subject to access restrictions, appropriate security, and accountable retention periods. A personal data protection violation does not automatically establish civil liability in tort: a claimant must still prove an unlawful act, fault, loss, and causation. Employers should therefore adopt transparent and proportionate CCTV governance policies that preserve legitimate security interests without unduly intruding upon employees’ privacy.

all.title: The effectiveness of algorithmic information rights in the labour relationship: Lessons learnt from the Spanish experience
all.abstract: The study examines the effectiveness of algorithmic information rights in current regulation through an interdisciplinary methodological framework that integrates doctrinal legal research with in-depth interviews. The main finding of this study is that the architecture of algorithmic information rights reveals a fragmented mosaic across the European Union, with varying scopes and configurations at both the EU and state levels, resulting in uneven protections for workers. Furthermore, using Spain as a case study, the article identifies three key factors which result in a lack of company compliance and overall ineffectiveness of algorithmic information rights: an insufficient understanding of both the technology and the current fragmented regulatory landscape; company resistance to the disclosure of algorithmic information; and a reduced capacity of unions and workers’ representatives to holistically address the digitalisation of labour and engage in participatory governance of algorithmic management. These findings underscore the importance of adequate normative design to reinforce information rights for workers and workers’ representatives to increase the effectiveness of algorithmic information rights. In this sense, the study proposes the adoption of an EU Directive on algorithmic management that, following the footsteps of the Directive on platform work, regulates the use of algorithms and AI systems in the workplace from a holistic perspective, reinforcing information rights for workers and their representatives and advancing towards more transparency and accountability.

all.title: Inteligência artificial e o impacto nas relações de trabalho
all.abstract: This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

all.title: Is Algorithmic Control a Double-Edged Sword? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Perceived Algorithmic Control and Platform Workers' Well-being and Work Attitudes
all.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes quantitative studies on the association between platform gig workers' perceived algorithmic control (or algorithmic management) and their well-being, work attitudes, and work behaviors. It estimates overall associations, tests whether distinct dimensions of algorithmic control (e.g., standardized guidance, tracking evaluation, behavioral constraint) relate to outcomes in different directions, and examines contextual and methodological moderators. English-language and Chinese-language literature will be included.

all.title: Instagram as Organizing Infrastructure: New York City Immigration Delivery Workers in the Digital Economy
all.abstract: Scholarship on platform labor has documented how algorithmic management disciplines workers but has paid less attention to how organized workers use public social media to contest platform power. This article analyzes Los Deliveristas Unidos (LDU), a predominantly immigrant, mixed-status organization of app-based delivery workers in New York City, and its discursive use of Instagram as organizing infrastructure. Using qualitative content analysis of 102 systematically sampled posts from @losdeliveristasunidos_ny (2021-2025), the study develops three interrelated discursive strategies: algorithmic witnessing, victory documentation, and corporate narrative warfare. Algorithmic witnessing uses Instagram to document and archive wage theft, “digital firings,” and unsafe conditions. Victory documentation stages regulatory and legal wins to counter platform fatalism and build collective efficacy by showing that regulation of gig work is possible. Corporate narrative warfare names platform firms and city agencies as antagonists and disputes their public claims, framing policy debates as struggles between organized workers and identifiable opponents. The analysis shows how these practices reconfigure common sense about gig work by resituating the apps’ frames from individual flexibility to structural exploitation and from abstract “apps” to specific corporate and governmental actors. The article extends research on algorithmic management, migrant precarity, and worker media by demonstrating how immigrant delivery workers appropriate commercial social media platforms to generate public evidence and narrative leverage.

all.title: Raqamli iqtisodiyot sharoitida mehnat resurslarini boshqarishning zamonaviy modellari
all.abstract: The article analyzes the directions of transformation of the labor resource management system and modern management models in the digital economy. Based on the structure of Uzbekistan's labor market and the dynamics of the share of the information and communication technology sector in gross domestic product, new requirements for labor resource management are identified. The author systematizes the evolution of labor resource management models according to the stages "administrative personnel management – human resource management – electronic HRM – data-driven and algorithmic management", provides a comparative assessment of modern models by the criteria of application conditions and limitations, and proposes an approach to calculating the integral index of an organization's digital HR maturity and selecting a management model according to the maturity level.

all.title: On-Demand Labour, Counterdata, and Worker Agency: Building Data Literacies in the Platform Economy
all.abstract: This chapter examines how platform workers develop new relationships with data, both to negotiate platform working conditions and to challenge algorithmic management. The chapter examines four data-driven projects (Turkopticon, Fairwork, Worker Info Exchange, and the Workers Observatory). It argues that each project cultivates a distinct but related form of data fluency. Such fluency is not an individual technical competence but a collective sociopolitical practice through which workers actively produce knowledge and evidence of platform working conditions and platform-based harms. While none of these projects can fully erase the fundamental asymmetries of platform labour, they do demonstrate that algorithmic systems are contested spaces, and that the strategic mobilisation of data fluency can meaningfully redistribute informational power.

all.title: Algoritmo al volante: nueva organización del trabajo vs viejas condiciones laborales. Estudio de Uber y Cabify en España
all.abstract: The work of Uber and Cabify drivers in Spain is organised through algorithmic management that co-opts data from drivers and customers and turns it into the core of the platforms’ business. Drawing on fifteen semi-structured interviews conducted in 2023 within the international Fairwork project, the article analyses employment conditions (access, working time, occupational risks and autonomy) and the labour subjectivities shaped by that control. Results show that the flexibility which attracts workers is cancelled out by turnover targets and long hours, that algorithmic control is the main source of psychosocial risk and that fleet companies barely develop prevention, communication or equality policies. Subjectively, the turnover target is internalised as self-demand, an “algorithmic imaginary” guides everyday tactics, and driving is experienced as a refuge job with no professional identity attached.

all.title: Beyond Automation: Exploring Employees’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence, Job Insecurity, and Workplace Identity in The Modern Workplace
all.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a part of every organisation's day-to-day operations and is a factor in the way work is being assigned, done, directed and checked. Discussions about this change have primarily been around automation, efficiency and jobs, but also about how an employee's sense of security, competence in their role, independence and sense of identity at work is affected by AI. In this article, we delve into the interconnections between employees' attitudes toward AI, their feelings of job insecurity, and workplace identity. The study was of qualitative, interpretive, documentary design and secondary data analysis was done using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) based on peer reviewed studies, systematic reviews and reports of international organizations such as ILO and OECD. The five interrelated themes were: (1) Ambivalence about the use of AI: some experiences it as a tool to augment their work while others worry about being monitored, deskilled, and displaced; (2) Anticipatory fear of loss: fear of job loss can occur even if the number of jobs does not decrease; (3) Remediated and reinforced professional identity: when AI is used to complement their job, it enhances their sense of competence, while when it digitises their core job, it threatens it; (4) Algorithmic management reconfigures autonomy: when automating parts of their job, employees' autonomy is reassigned, while when parts of their job are kept by humans and coded into algorithms, they lose some autonomy; (5) Algorithmic management experiences depend on the organizational support, the transparency of communication, participation, and reskilling. From a theoretical perspective, the study synthesizes the concepts of job insecurity, social and/or organizational identification, technology acceptance and resistance, sociotechnical systems and human capital, and is able to articulate a framework beyond the deterministic replacement stories. The reality is that HR teams and leaders need to approach the integration of AI as a transformational journey rather than simply a technological fix, and have to do so. It concludes by proposing that although the technical difficulty is a consideration, a more important one is how well staff can feel secure, competent and valued as professionals in the context of the integration of AI.

all.title: Legal Governance of Digital Platform Practices: Reconciling Gig Economy Models With the Right to Decent Work
all.abstract: This chapter examines the legal governance of digital labor platforms, analyzing the tension between algorithmic management practices and the International Labour Organization's Decent Work Agenda. Through a comparative jurisprudential lens examining developments across the EU, UK, and US, including the UK Supreme Court's Uber v. Aslam ruling, Spain's Ley Rider, and the EU Platform Work Directive, this chapter evaluates the limitations of reactive judicial remedies and third-category labor classifications. It demonstrates how dynamic pricing, automated metrics, and algorithmic deactivation erode foundational labor rights, safety, and non-discrimination standards. To bridge this regulatory gap, the chapter proposes an integrated, rights-based governance framework anchored in a statutory rebuttable presumption of employment, algorithmic transparency, co-determination, worker data rights, competition law exemptions for collective bargaining, and portable benefit schemes to secure human dignity in platform capitalism.

all.title: Is gig work the same for everyone? Psychosocial job demands, resources, and well-being in platform work across Europe: evidence from the GIG-OSH study
all.venue: International Journal of Occupational Medicine and Environmental Health
all.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Research on digital platform work increasingly highlights unclear employment arrangements and pressures related to algorithmic management. This study aimed to describe psychosocial working conditions in web-based and on-location gig work using the job demands-resources (JD-R) model and examine associations between job demands, job resources, factors preventing resource depletion (FPRD), and health outcomes among platform workers. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Cross-sectional data were drawn from the GIG-OSH project conducted in 7 European countries (Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom). Data were collected through an online survey in November 2023 - April 2024. The analytic sample comprised 3299 platform workers (1476 on-location, 1823 web-based). A project-specific questionnaire assessed socio-demographic characteristics, employment conditions, workload, occupational safety and health hazards, psychosocial working conditions, algorithmic management, and health outcomes. Psychosocial factors were classified as job demands, job resources, or FPRD within an extended JD-R framework. RESULTS: Platform work was characterized by an imbalance between job demands and resources, particularly among onlocation workers. Compared with web-based workers, they reported greater exposure to emotionally disturbing situations, aggression, violence, discrimination, and sexual harassment. Working alone was common in both groups but more prevalent in web-based work. Factors preventing resource depletion indicators, especially absence of fines and protection against fraudulent bookings, were more favourable in web-based work. Higher job demands were significantly associated with poorer health outcomes, with emotionally disturbing situations showing the strongest effect. Job resources demonstrated modest protective associations, whereas FPRD indicators, particularly not working while ill, were consistently associated with better health. CONCLUSIONS: Platform work involves substantial psychosocial risks linked to poorer well-being and health, supporting the JD-R model. Distinct psychosocial profiles of web-based and on-location work highlight the need for targeted occupational health and platform policy interventions. Int J Occup Med Environ Health. 2026;39(5):503-22.

all.title: ‘Datafied' Employees in the ‘Gig Economy'
all.abstract: This chapter analyses platform labour as a form of work in which access to jobs and their allocation are organised through privately controlled digital infrastructures that also become instruments of discipline, so that ride-hailing and food delivery, as well as online freelancing and crowdwork, appear not merely as new markets but as organisational forms that make labour dependent upon continuous surveillance. The dominant representation of platforms as neutral ‘intermediaries’ is, therefore, incomplete: although a platform connects workers with customers, it also structures what workers can see and how they are evaluated, while shaping the conditions under which they move and earn. Platform labour remains continuous with older capitalist efforts to reduce the indeterminacy of labour-power, but its distinctive force lies in algorithmic management exercised through infrastructures on which workers depend, with legal misclassification and reputational scoring intensifying that dependence alongside continuous data capture; the argument consequently extends beyond the ‘gig’ economy to the wider platformisation of ordinary employment.

all.title: "Sindicalismo ante la Industria 4.0: Estrategias de adaptación y resistencia en España (1992-2024)"
all.abstract: This article analyses trade union strategies of adaptation and resistance to industrial digitalisation in Spain (1992-2024). Drawing on two research questions—about the alignment of the industrial regulatory framework with inclusive governance principles, and the tensions of social dialogue and collective bargaining in digitalised contexts—the study combines comparative legislative analysis, content analysis of collective agreements, and interviews with six trade union leaders from CCOO and UGT. The results reveal a central paradox: while the new normative framework, Industry Act 2024 Draft, V AENC (2023) and Digital Rights Charter (2021) opens formal spaces for participation, collective bargaining advances unevenly in incorporating clauses on algorithmic management and digital training. The Rider Law (RDL 9/2021) and pioneering collective agreements in the platform sector illustrate both the achievements and the limits of trade union action. The article concludes that a just digital transition in Spain requires converting multilevel governance into effective decision-making power.

all.title: Gig Workers and Road Safety in India: Examining Platform Accountability and Legal Protection of Delivery Partners
all.venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
all.abstract: Delivery partners in India ride to deadlines they do not set, on roads where two-wheeler riders form the largest group of fatalities and under contracts that call them independent partners. This paper examines when, and on what legal basis, platforms should answer for the road risks created by this arrangement. It examines the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 as amended in 2019, the Code on Social Security 2020 and its 2026 Rules, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, and recent state gig-worker statutes. It contends that responsibility should depend upon who controls the conditions of risk, namely time, pay, allocation and deactivation, and not on the contract. It further considers how algorithmic management of allocation, incentives and deactivation affects rider safety, an area where Indian law remains largely silent. Current law protects delivery partners mainly through welfare schemes that are not yet operational, and it says little about unsafe system design. The paper proposes reforms that can largely be made through rules and targeted amendments.

all.title: General intellect y gestión algorítmica. La regulación del trabajo en plataformas digitales
institutions: Universidad de la República de Uruguay
all.abstract: This article analyses transformations of work under cognitive and platform capitalism, placing algorithmic management at the centre as a contemporary form of labour control. Through a critical dialogue with technological determinism, it draws on Castells and Vercellone to explain how knowledge and workers’ cognitive capacities have become central sources of capital valorisation. Within this framework, algorithms operate not as neutral technical tools but as sociotechnical devices that organise, supervise and discipline labour in a continuous, opaque and delocalised manner. The article shows how platform companies condense long-term historical tendencies by articulating concentrated digital infrastructure, large-scale data capture and narratives of individual autonomy. Analysis of the mechanisms of algorithmic direction, evaluation and discipline demonstrates that control over the labour process shifts towards the appropriation of collective knowledge, that is, of the general intellect. Finally, the article examines the regulatory frameworks of Spain and the European Union, the four Latin American cases currently in force, and ILO Convention No. 193, adopted in 2026. It argues that algorithmic transparency is a necessary but insufficient condition: it becomes transformative only when accompanied by the collective capacity to contest the design of these systems, and not merely to know their effects.
