all.title: Navigating identity in platform work: sociotechnical tensions and institutional complexity
all.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the institutional logics and sensemaking perspectives within institutional theory, this study investigates how platform governance is associated with platform workers' professional identity, with a particular focus on the role of workplace depersonalization. This study also argues that these relationships are weaker when algorithmic dependence is lower and when algorithmic anthropomorphism is higher. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a three-wave field survey of 328 workers in real platform governance settings. Findings The findings show that commodified and atomized governance are positively associated with workplace depersonalization, which is in turn associated with lower professional identity among platform workers. Importantly, the negative indirect relationships between the two forms of platform governance and professional identity via workplace depersonalization are stronger when algorithmic anthropomorphism is low. However, only the negative indirect relationship between commodified governance and professional identity is stronger when algorithmic dependence is high. Originality/value This research contributes to the literature on professional identity by shedding light on the multifaceted implications of platform governance and providing practical guidance to policymakers on the effective use of algorithmic management tools in the gig economy.

all.title: Human Rights of Gig and Platform Workers in India: Social Security, Labour Rights and Legal Accountability
all.venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
all.abstract: Transport, food delivery, home services, logistics and other app-based services have transformed the way people work in India. Platform work is not just a flexible means of engagement in the labour market: it can also bring irregular income, ambiguous rating systems, unilateral termination of accounts and lower social security benefits, and so raises issues of dignity, equality, occupational safety and social protection. Through doctrinal and analytical methods, this paper explores the human rights position of gig and platform workers in light of international labour standards, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Constitution. The Code, which came into force on 21 November 2025, explicitly deals with gig workers, platform workers and aggregators: Section 113 provides for their registration, and Section 114 for schemes of life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits and old-age protection. Even with statutory recognition, registration, funding, portability and grievance redressal will remain important. The paper offers a rights-based solution which includes social security, clear algorithmic management, fair compensation, occupational security, no arbitrary disconnection, collective representation and accessible remedies, and proposes that innovation should never be secured by shifting economic and social risk from the innovator to the workers.

all.title: The Effect of Scarcity Marketing by Multinational Brands on the Purchase Intentions of Gen Z in China under a Digital Environment
all.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
all.abstract: Due to digitalization, scarcity has changed from an ordinary scarcity that limited the availability of a Good to a Multi-Dimensional Marketing Strategy. This paper will examine the impacts of the strategies using digital scarcity that multinational brands use on the purchasing decisions of China's Gen Z consumers. This study will look at the case of Nike SNKRS for this purpose. The theory of scarcity also draws on research into a number of different areas: digital consumer behaviour, perceived value, FOMO, social identity and consumer engagement. These research findings suggest that the digital environmental scarcity can lead to enhancing the perceived value of products, improving brand differentiation, stimulating continued engagement with digital content and increasing social interactivity. However, these impacts result in three risks: The opacity of algorithms may lead to distrust, standardized global marketing may misfire against Chinese culture and repeated digital gap will aggravate the FOMO and cause an impulse to buy. In order to mitigate these risks, this paper proposes a system of open and transparent digital scarcity and algorithmic management; culturally sensitive digital experience design; age-appropriate marketing regulations; and a performance evaluation framework focused on long-term brand equity. This paper contributes to the understanding of digital scarcity in cross-cultural marketing and provides insights for multinational brands looking to sustainably grow in China and promote responsible marketing and consumer protection.

all.title: O TRABALHO POR PLATAFORMAS DIGITAIS E A ATUAÇÃO DA JUSTIÇA DO TRABALHO NA ANÁLISE DO VÍNCULO EMPREGATÍCIO
all.abstract: Work carried out through digital platforms has raised an unsettled question before Brazilian Labor Courts: when should drivers and delivery workers be regarded as independent workers, and when do the facts reveal an employment relationship? This study examined the requirements set out in Articles 2 and 3 of the Brazilian Consolidation of Labor Laws, the expansion of platform-based work and decisions of the Superior Labor Court and Regional Labor Courts that reached divergent outcomes, also considering the review exercised by the Federal Supreme Court, General Repercussion Themes 1,291 and 1,389 and Complementary Bills No. 12/2024 and No. 152/2025. The research was bibliographic and documentary, followed a qualitative approach and compared a purposive selection of judicial decisions, without claiming statistical representativeness. In the cases examined, freedom to connect, reject requests or use more than one platform weighed in favor of autonomy, whereas platform-set prices, ratings, geolocation and account blocking were associated with forms of control. The study also discussed the limits of digital evidence, the dynamic allocation of the burden of proof and the review of automated decisions provided for in the Brazilian General Data Protection Law. The analysis supports the hypothesis that algorithmic management may express the employer’s directive power when it effectively shapes how the work is organized, which must be demonstrated by the facts of each case and does not allow generalizations about the courts as a whole.

all.title: The Invisible Harm Doctrine: Structural AI Harm And Neurodivergent Cognitive Liberty
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive liberty as a complementary normative formulation, not an existing legal right and not a replacement for present neurorights frameworks. It states the principal objections to the doctrine and responds to them, and it concludes by identifying research, design, and governance questions necessary to evaluate whether and how these harms can be detected, challenged, and mitigated. The article does not report new primary data, establish clinical efficacy, or propose a ready-to-adopt legal standard.

all.title: From Ujrāh to Algorithmic Accountability: Reconstructing Wage Justice and Human Dignity in the Platform Economy
all.venue: ARTHASASTRA Journal of Economics and Business
all.abstract: Digital labour platforms increasingly organise work through algorithmic systems that allocate tasks, monitor performance, determine access to income-generating opportunities, calculate remuneration, and impose sanctions. These systems may reduce coordination costs and expand market access, yet they also create distinctive problems of wage justice when workers cannot understand the rules governing earnings, verify deductions, contest adverse decisions, or identify the institution responsible for algorithmic outcomes. This article develops a critical-conceptual framework that reconstructs the Islamic concept of ujrāh for the governance of remuneration in the platform economy. It integrates scholarship on algorithmic management and platform labour, organisational justice, labour regulation, and Islamic jurisprudence on ijārah and ethical remuneration. The analysis proceeds through conceptual mapping, normative interpretation, institutional translation, and framework synthesis. It argues that ujrāh should not be confined to the nominal amount agreed for a task; its contemporary ethical assessment must also encompass the procedures and infrastructures through which work is allocated, remuneration is calculated, and payment rights are enforced. The article proposes five interdependent dimensions of Islamic algorithmic wage justice: distributive fairness; contractual intelligibility; algorithmic explainability and contestability; equitable allocation of economic risk; and protection of human dignity and worker agency. The framework contributes to platform-work scholarship by connecting distributive and procedural justice with a normative account of contractual responsibility grounded in Islamic economic ethics. It is conceptual and requires empirical testing across platform sectors and regulatory settings.

all.title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
all.venue: International Theory and Practice in Humanities and Social Sciences
institutions: Hunan Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

all.title: Who Gets Blamed for the Blackout? A Critical Incident Analysis of Clients, Reputation Systems, and Online Freelancers
all.abstract: Online labor platforms such as Fiverr and Upwork judge freelancers by how fast they reply, whether they deliver on time, and what clients say about them. In the Global South, these signals depend on electricity and internet connections that workers do not control. This paper asks how infrastructure failures, such as power outages, internet failures, and government internet shutdowns, become lasting reputational penalties in the gig economy, and how freelancers prevent or repair them. We use the critical incident technique to analyze 149 incidents from 30 interviews with online freelancers in Bangladesh, including accounts of the July 2024 nationwide internet shutdown. Most breakdowns were absorbed without lasting harm. Of the 21 that became lasting penalties, 17 passed through clients. A client who could not see the power cut or the shutdown read the worker's silence as unreliability and left, canceled, or gave a bad rating. Platform reputation systems then stored that judgment without its context. We call this two-stage process client-mediated misattribution. Freelancers responded with four repair strategies: making the context visible, making the breakdown invisible, staying visible to the platform, and reducing dependence on any single platform or client. Exposure and the capacity to repair were unequal, and urban participants were the most exposed. The study extends research on algorithmic management, attribution in distributed work, and information and communication technologies for development (ICT4D), and it proposes outage-aware design for platform rating and reputation systems.

all.title: Agent Hireability: A Working Definition for AI-Driven Management of Deep-Tech Startups
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology
all.abstract: This paper is written from practice, not from labor economics. The first author runs deep-tech startups and is moving their management toward a model in which AI agents help plan, assign, and evaluate work. That requires a shared word for a question existing vocabulary does not quite name: how likely is a given person to receive a commission for a specified paid task when an AI system takes part in selecting who does it? Optimization for AI systems has developed a rich vocabulary for brands and content: SEO, AEO, GEO/LLMO, and AAO. Related practices for individuals also exist, such as keeping one's online presence and résumé readable by machines. Separately, AI systems have taken on three overlapping economic roles: evaluating human work (algorithmic management), purchasing on behalf of users (agentic commerce), and requesting work from people. We propose Agent Hireability as a working definition for the person's side of that third role. We define the event that counts as a commission, specify the unit of analysis and the levels of delegation the definition covers, and review the public evidence, separating the decision to request human work from the decision to commission a particular person. We then offer a provisional typology of tasks for which agents may turn to people, apply the definition to research work and to team design and hiring in a deep-tech startup, and set out testable propositions with their denominators and refuting results. Two related concepts, the agent legibility of persons and the "callable human," are discussed with their prior uses. The definitions are offered as tools for internal and external communication, to be revised through use. Japanese term: 被発注力 (hi-hacchū-ryoku).

all.title: The role of artificial intelligence in green human resource management and organizational sustainability: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
institutions: Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as the technology that will allow green human resource management (GHRM) to deliver organizational sustainability, yet the evidence behind this claim is recent, scattered and largely unexamined. This study combines a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis to establish what is known, how it is known and what remains untested. A Scopus search (12 November 2026) returned 297 records; after document-type filtering and title–abstract–keyword screening, 97 journal articles and reviews formed the mapping corpus, and two further eligible articles were added to the critical synthesis (n = 99). Keyword co-occurrence, overlay, co-citation, bibliographic coupling and country co-authorship maps were produced, and every study was coded for the structural role assigned to AI, theory, method, context and outcome. The field is young (77.3% of the corpus is published from 2025–2026), geographically limited (mostly emerging Asian countries), and methodologically homogeneous, with 44 of 62 quantitative studies using cross-sectional structural equation modelling of self-reported data. Five roles for AI are discussed (enabler, amplifier, mediator, complementary resource and embedded practice), but they are often mixed up, or not well explained theoretically. The conceptual foundations are the resource-based view and the GHRM foundations and the critical literature on algorithmic management is not present in the co-citation structure. These are flanked by reports in other studies of non-significant and negative effects, as well as no environmental footprint for AI itself, meaning the current optimism is premature. The paper introduces a typology of AI roles and a socio-technical capability-conversion framework that consists of six propositions, and a research agenda.

all.title: The Illusion of Flexibility: Work-Life Balance and Time Control Among Gig Employees
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The proliferation of digital platform labor across urban India has been largely driven by the promise of schedule autonomy and temporal freedom. However, emerging empirical evidence suggests that for many platform workers, this freedom is fundamentally paradoxical. This article examines how algorithmic management, financial precarity, dynamic incentive structures, and market volatility convert promised autonomy into pervasive temporal discipline within the Indian gig landscape. Drawing on a mixed-methods investigation of 450 location-based and web-based gig employees across major metropolitan hubs in India including Bengaluru, Mumbai, and the National Capital Region (NCR), we analyze the structural mechanisms that dictate time control and severely compromise work-life balance. Our findings indicate that while gig employees experience high initial levels of perceived schedule control, their actual temporal flexibility is heavily constrained by dynamic surge pricing algorithms, target-based peak incentives, customer rating penalties, and baseline economic necessity. Consequently, gig employees suffer elevated levels of work-family conflict, unpredictable work schedules, severe physical exhaustion, and extended hours of uncompensated waiting time amidst urban congestion and climate stress. We present an empirical framework detailing the "Flexibility Paradox" in platform labor, evaluate the differential experiences between transport and freelance sectors, and provide actionable organizational and regulatory recommendations framed around the Code on Social Security (2020) and evolving state-level legislative initiatives for Indian gig employees. Paper hosted on Google Drive: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1DyVyupGjkTNPKy3qtzpv7b-C4YpRf-3k/view?usp=drive_link

all.title: Permanent Judgment, Temporary Labor: Human Feedback Work, Automated Substitution, and the Law of Platform Exit in the Global South
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Human feedback work builds the machine that replaces the rater. Across Kenya and the Philippines, generalist raters compare and rank model outputs at piece rates. The comparisons train scoring models, known as reward models, while earlier human-aligned models serve as automated judges evaluating outputs against written safety policies. Human raters disappear from that stage. Breaking the *paradox of automation's last mile*, automated systems eliminate generalist preference tasks while platforms sort the remaining human work by credential and geography. Expert evaluation pays hundreds of dollars an hour in wealthy economies, while Scale AI's labeling platform Remotasks cut Kenyan, Nigerian, and Pakistani workers in 2024 and its sister platform Outlier still bars them. Domestic labor statutes do not reach those exits. Philippine law mandates notice and separation pay for labor-saving devices, and Kenyan redundancy law imposes parallel duties, yet platform terms classify annotators as independent contractors. Both statutes leave independent contractors outside protection. Philippine Article 298 and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development disengagement standard supply a doctrinal template for advance notice and harm mitigation. International Labour Organization Convention No. 193 extends procedural coverage to independent contractors once ratified. Keywords: RLHF Labor, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback, RLAIF, LLM-as-a-Judge, AI Data Annotation, Platform Disengagement, Independent Contractor Classification, Global South Labor, Kenya Employment Act, Philippine Labor Code Article 298, Labor-Saving Devices, ILO Convention No. 193, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, Responsible Disengagement, Remotasks, Outlier, Sama, Scale AI, Data Colonialism, Ghost Work, Algorithmic Management

all.title: Impact of workplace discrimination on health worker’s employment
all.abstract: This preregistration protocol is summarizing a scoping review, focused on identifying the racism and/or discrimination-related factors (e.g., barriers or facilitators) that affect the recruitment, retention including meaningful health system participation, or advancement to leadership roles of health workers from underrepresented or underserved communities/equity deserving groups. Research Questions: The primary and secondary research questions for this scoping review are as follows: What racism or discrimination-related factors (e.g., barriers or facilitators) affecting the recruitment, retention including meaningful health system participation, or advancement to leadership roles of health workers from underrepresented or underserved/equity deserving groups are identified in the literature? (primary question) What similarities or differences exist among racism and discrimination-related barriers or facilitators affecting health workers from underrepresented or underserved/equity deserving groups, considering their occupation, role/position in the health system, race, ethnicity, gender, sexual identity, migration status, or ability level? (secondary question) Objective: The objective is to identify the barriers/facilitators related to racism and discrimination that affect the recruitment, retention, or advancement to leadership roles of health workers. Data Collection, Extraction, Analysis, Output: Searches will be conducted through six academic databases [MEDLINE (via OVID), CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar and sociological abstracts, which cover health and social topics. Selection of evidence will be according to a pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria based on PECO framework. Literature published in English language from January 2000 with a global nature search, not limited to North American Publications will be included. Journal articles, thesis dissertations and institutional reports will be accepted as primary source of evidence. Study selection process will be displayed using the PRISMA-ScR 2018. Covidence online systematic collaborative platform will be used for management of search results, evidence screening, decision-making and duplicate study removal. The title-abstracts and subsequently full text will be screened independently by two reviewers, any disagreements will be resolved by a third reviewer. Participating reviewers will take part in a pilot testing of the screening process, using a screening guidance document to maintain consistency. A tailored data extraction tool will be developed, piloted and modified as necessary during the initial stages of data extraction, based on systemic review questions. The results of this review will be presented in a structured narrative as well as tabular format, using a modified version of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2018 statement. The authors will ensure that the summary of results aligns with the reviews’ objectives and questions. The included studies will be critically appraised for risk of bias and quality by two reviewers independently, using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) (Hong et al., 2018). The results will be synthesized in a final report, which will contain information about the overall body of evidence available to answer the research questions, the details about the review methods used, the specific findings, including the results of the critical appraisal, the research gaps identified, and recommendations for practice, policy-making, and future research.

all.title: Perceived workplace discrimination and its impacts on leaders: latent class analysis
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to identify distinct latent classes of perceived workplace discrimination among leaders and examine how different patterns of discrimination perception are associated with workplace attitudes and behaviors. Design/methodology/approach Using a mixture modeling approach, this study conducted latent class analysis with data from 3,351 leaders drawn from the 2022 Korean Women Manager Panel. The study examined predictors of latent class membership, including shadow labor culture, fairness of HR practices and top management leadership and compared organizational outcomes across the identified classes. Findings The findings revealed five distinct latent classes representing heterogeneous patterns of perceived workplace discrimination among leaders. The results demonstrated that organizational contextual factors significantly differentiated class membership. In addition, significant differences were found across the latent classes in organizational satisfaction and organizational commitment. However, leadership efficacy did not significantly differ across classes, suggesting that perceived workplace discrimination may influence organizational attitudes more strongly than leaders’ self-perceived leadership capability. Originality/value This study contributes to the human resource development and workplace discrimination literature by shifting attention from directly experienced discrimination to leaders’ perceived workplace discrimination as a socially constructed and organizationally embedded phenomenon. The study also extends existing research by demonstrating that perceptions of workplace discrimination are multidimensional rather than continuous and homogeneous. Furthermore, the findings provide practical implications for developing differentiated HRD and organizational interventions aimed at fostering inclusive and supportive workplace environments for leaders.

all.title: Between promise and practice: Intelligent automation and workplace inclusion in hospitality HRM
Transforming HR practices : Integrating Diversity, Equity, and Inclusiveness for an Inclusive Workplace
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) is a comprehensive framework focusing on balancing the workforce in organizational settings that foster equitable access to opportunities and resources at the workplace. The present study synthesizes existing literature and empirical studies that highlight the significance of aligning Diversity, equity and inclusiveness at the workplace. The primary aim of this paper is to explore the essential strategies to be redefined for the successful implementation of DEI initiatives for the inclusive workplace. It had identified the spectrum of strategic HR practices, such as HR Policies & HR Practices, Leadership behaviour, Decision making process, and Sustainability workforce. The four strategic dimensions in the study provide a broader implications for organizational practices, emphasizing diversity, equity and inclusiveness are essential for an inclusive workplace.

all.title: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Employee Job Satisfaction at PT Vale Indonesia Sorowako
institutions: Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim
all.abstract: Background: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) may relate to job satisfaction, but their separate associations require examination in specific organizational settings. Indonesian mining provides a relevant context for assessing employees’ perceptions alongside formal organizational commitments. Objective: This study estimates the separate associations of perceived diversity, equity, and inclusion with job satisfaction among permanent employees at PT Vale Indonesia Tbk Sorowako. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey of 100 permanent employees used 24 items rated on a five-point Likert scale. Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling in SmartPLS estimated three reflective predictors and one outcome. No combined or higher-order DEI construct was tested. Sampling documentation and several model diagnostics were unavailable for verification. Results: Reported loadings, reliability coefficients, and average variance extracted supported internal consistency and convergent validity. Diversity (β = 0.260; p = 0.002), equity (β = 0.265; p = 0.006), and inclusion (β = 0.408; p < 0.001) were positively associated with job satisfaction. R² was 0.687. Inclusion had the largest estimated coefficient descriptively; differences between coefficients were not tested. HTMT values were below 0.85, but the Fornell–Larcker criterion was not met for job satisfaction relative to inclusion; HTMT confidence intervals and predictive performance remain unverified. Conclusion: The results support three dimension-specific associations in this sample. They do not establish causality, psychological mechanisms, or superiority over demographic representation or formal policies. Inclusive supervision, transparent opportunity criteria, and repeated perception surveys are proposed for evaluation. Single-company, cross-sectional self-reports and incomplete methodological documentation limit interpretation and generalization.

all.title: A Personal Narrative Inquiry on the Employment Journeys of Persons with Disabilities Ensuring Workplace Inclusion in South Cotabato
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

all.title: Corporate Reputation and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
all.abstract: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) are part of diversity management, which encompasses organizational actions to create greater inclusion of employees from various backgrounds into the organizational structures (Mor Barak, 2017). Research shows that the way diversity management is practiced and DEI is communicated influences an organization's reputation. Yet, organizations need to implement and evaluate their DEI initiatives and communicate their stance on DEI authentically to achieve a positive DEI reputation with their internal and external stakeholders. The current chapter outlines relations of corporate DEI reputation (e.g., corporate diversity rankings) with organizational outcomes (e.g., organizational performance and attractiveness to job seekers). It also presents organizational communication practices for creating and maintaining a positive DEI reputation and highlights emerging pitfalls in the case of poor diversity communication. Strategies to manage these pitfalls and the value of organizational authenticity in this context are also discussed.

all.title: From vocational rehabilitation to workplace inclusion: A bibliometric analysis of global trends, thematic evolution, and knowledge gaps in disability career research (1981–2025)
all.abstract: Research on the careers of people with disabilities has grown in parallel with rising attention to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), yet the field has not been systematically mapped. This study examines global trends, thematic evolution, and knowledge gaps in disability and career research through a bibliometric analysis of peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published between 1981 and 2025. Data were retrieved from Scopus due to its broad international coverage and structured metadata and analyzed using Biblioshiny. A total of 228 publications were examined through performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, influential contributors, collaboration patterns, thematic structures, and research evolution. The results indicate a steady growth in publications since 2010, with journal articles remaining the predominant publication type, alongside contributions from conference papers. The United States emerged as the most productive and influential country, followed by other developed countries, while international collaboration remained limited, highlighting geographic inequalities in knowledge production. Thematically, the literature has been dominated by career development, vocational rehabilitation, and labor market participation, with recent expansion toward workplace inclusion, organizational support, psychosocial well-being, and technology-enabled participation. Thematic evolution analysis revealed a shift from rehabilitation-oriented perspectives toward rights-based, technology-enabled, and inclusive policy approaches, particularly in the post-pandemic period. The findings also reveal important knowledge gaps, including the underrepresentation of non-Western perspectives, limited theoretical integration across psychological, organizational, and policy perspectives, and a scarcity of longitudinal and cross-cultural research. These gaps highlight the need for more inclusive and globally representative scholarship. Building on these findings, the study proposes an Inclusive Disability Career Ecosystem Framework to integrate individual, organizational, technological, and policy factors influencing career development and career success among people with disabilities.

all.title: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Practices in Global Organizations and Their Impact on Performance
all.abstract: This paper is an investigation of how Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) practices are applied to shape organizational performance across global organizations through an analytical approach based on machine learning. The study measures the impact of these variables on the performance outcomes (innovation, employee engagement, and efficiency) by integrating quantitative data on DEI dimensions, including inclusion climate, equity policies, and workforce diversity. More complex models like the Random Forest and Gradient Boosting are used and evaluated based on evaluation metrics such as accuracy, Mean Squared Error and R. These findings suggest that selection of DEI practices greatly contribute to organizational performance, with the inclusion and equity being the most significant predictors. The paper also shows how ensemble learning methods are better at explaining complicated relations among DEI variables and performance results. Overall, the results highlight that the successful implementation of DEI is a strategic contributor to sustainable competitive advantage in multifaceted and dynamic business settings.

all.title: The Racist Workplace: A Theory Emerging from Employees’ Systemic Encounters with Racism Across Professional Industries
all.abstract: Workplace racism is increasingly understood as a systemic organizational phenomenon rather than a collection of isolated interpersonal acts. Building on scholarship on racialized organizations, this qualitative study examines how employees experience systemic racism across professional industries and develops The Racist Workplace Theory to explain how multiple forms and mechanisms of racism become interconnected and mutually reinforcing in everyday organizational life. The analysis draws on 1,596 employee descriptions of workplace encounters that participants identified as racist. The submissions were collected from professionals working in 292 organizations spanning K-12 schools, higher education institutions, corporate workplaces, and other professional contexts in the United States. Through iterative qualitative analysis, encounters were organized into three empirically derived analytic categories and compared across sectors to identify recurring systemic patterns and context-specific differences. Participants reported overt racism, racial microaggressions, and racialized expectations alongside inequities in evaluation and promotion, exclusion from professional opportunities, and institutional minimization of racial harm. Cross-sector analyses revealed that racialized expectations, racist encounters, institutional gatekeeping, racialized outcomes, minimization and inaction, and normalization can operate as interconnected and reinforcing processes rather than as discrete phenomena. These processes assume context-specific expressions across K-12 education, higher education, and corporate workplaces while collectively producing and sustaining racialized workplace climates. The Racist Workplace Theory extends racialized organization theory by shifting analytic attention from the organization as a racial structure to the workplace as a lived social environment in which those structures are repeatedly enacted and encountered. The theory specifies how interconnected processes can produce, sustain, and reproduce racial hierarchy in everyday organizational life while generating racialized workplace climates that employees experience through conditional belonging, compromised credibility and safety, heightened vigilance, and other consequences. These findings underscore the need for systemic interventions that redesign organizational structures, decision-making processes, accountability mechanisms, and workplace racial climates rather than relying primarily on episodic or symbolic DEI initiatives.

all.title: Intergenerational workforce and workplaces
all.abstract: Generational cohort theory suggests that workers are categorised according to their birth years and shared characteristics – the baby boomers, Generations X, Y, and Z. Are such categorisations and assumptions applicable to societies within Asia Pacific? Are the categories adequate as a framework? This chapter explores the challenges and opportunities associated with intergenerational workforces and workplaces (IWAW) in the Philippines through the lens of the relations between generations or ‘intergenerational relations’ and investigating whether there is evidence of such workplace relations, that is, rules or norms that regulate workplace relations between older and younger workers and the parties to rule- or norm-making. Case studies and document analysis on retirement age, anti-discrimination as regards age and gender, flexible work arrangements, mental health, and diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), as IWAW related innovative policies, programmes or initiatives and legal requirements, were undertaken. One case involved ambivalent intergenerational relations in light of the intersection of the rules or norms concerning retirement ages, age- and gender-based discrimination. Another case was about negative intergenerational relations concerning returning overseas Filipino workers. Rules or norms regarding flexible work arrangements, mental health programmes, and DEI are key cases that tend to create opportunities for positive intergenerational relations in workplaces. Overall, the cases involve formal work-related intergenerational relationships informed by explicit rules of exchange. Future research can delve into cases of implicit rules of exchange.

all.title: Identity and academic hiring in sociology: race, gender, and scholarly merit
The Pillars of Islam at Work: Religious Expression and Accommodation in Professional US Workplaces
all.abstract: Drawing on data from a qualitative interview study exploring U.S. Muslim professionals’ workplace experiences, this article highlights how Muslim workers experience scheduling, workload, and space conflicts when seeking religious accommodations. These conflicts create moments of heightened visibility and interpersonal tension, as Islamic rituals are often read as signs of religious fundamentalism. The article also analyzes strategies Muslims use to avoid, confront, and prevent subtle discrimination, showing how they navigate workplaces shaped by white normative cultures. Knowledge of Muslim experiences with accommodation requests is crucial in an era where diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are under fire. Their experiences help determine whether cross-cultural diversity and inclusion initiatives are effective, maintaining a work environment where similarities and differences are valued.

all.title: Navigating Global Paradoxes: International Business Strategy and the Corporate DEI Exodus
all.venue: Journal of Teaching in International Business
all.abstract: This case examines the strategic and ethical challenges businesses face when pursuing corporate social responsibility (CSR), particularly diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), initiatives across fragmented global markets. Divergent political, social, and economic pressures often conflict sharply with financial performance objectives. Despite CSR’s mainstream status, the tension between profitability and social obligations remains under-addressed, especially in international management literature. This tension intensified significantly following the 2024 U.S. presidential election, triggering a widespread corporate retreat from DEI programs. Using a composite multinational firm (AuroraTech Inc.) grounded in empirical data from 2020–2025, the case places students in the role of CEO Maya Cooper. She must navigate declining revenues, activist investor pressure, employee attrition, and conflicting cross-border stakeholder expectations. Students are challenged to evaluate financial and non-financial metrics, assess the validity of ROI attributions for CSR investments, manage regional institutional differences, and determine how the company can uphold its core values (“Technology with Purpose”) while adapting to a polarized external landscape. This case offers a timely opportunity to explore evidence-based strategic decision-making and international stakeholder communication.

all.title: La legge n. 76/2025 sulla partecipazione dei lavoratori: osservazioni in chiaroscuro
institutions: Catholic University Our Lady of Good Counsel
all.abstract: Il saggio esamina la legge 15 maggio 2025, n. 76, che si qualifica come attuazione dell’art. 46 Cost. dopo quasi ottant’anni di pressoché totale inerzia parlamentare. Ricostruita la genesi del provvedimento, nato da un’iniziativa popolare promossa dalla Cisl, l’analisi individua la ragione determinante della sua approvazione nel carattere essenzialmente promozionale del testo, ulteriormente depotenziato durante l’iter parlamentare con la soppressione dei pochi profili cogenti originari (tra cui la rappresentanza dei lavoratori nelle società a partecipazione pubblica, l’obbligo di consultazione e il Garante della sostenibilità sociale delle imprese). Riconosciuti alla legge alcuni meriti (il superamento dell’impasse politica, la tipizzazione di quattro forme di partecipazione – gestionale, economico-finanziaria, organizzativa e consultiva –, la funzione pedagogica), il contributo ne evidenzia le numerose carenze: l’assenza di obblighi e sanzioni, di regole suppletive, di diritti di codeterminazione e di efficaci meccanismi di vigilanza. Particolare attenzione è dedicata al rapporto con la contrattazione collettiva, cui la legge rinvia in quasi la metà dei suoi articoli, rimettendo l’attuazione del principio partecipativo alla disponibilità delle parti sociali e all’autonomia statutaria, con il rischio di una partecipazione meramente eventuale e diseguale. Il confronto con l’ordinamento svedese, cui il modello italiano è stato accostato, mostra, accanto ad alcune affinità, differenze sostanziali (regole semi-dispositive, obblighi di negoziazione preventiva, un sistema sindacale centralizzato e coeso). Il saggio respinge, tuttavia, sia la tesi della sostanziale inutilità della riforma, valorizzandone le innovazioni, modeste ma reali, sia quella della sua illegittimità costituzionale, anche alla luce della sent. n. 156/2025 della Corte costituzionale. Il vero limite della legge, si conclude, non è di legittimità ma di effettività: la sua riuscita dipenderà dalla capacità di sindacati e imprese di cogliere le opportunità che essa offre per rilanciare relazioni industriali di tipo partecipativo. This essay examines Italian Law No. 76 of 15 May 2025, which presents itself as implementing Article 46 of the Constitution after almost eighty years of near-total parliamentary inaction. After tracing the origins of the law, stemming from a popular initiative promoted by the CISL, the analysis identifies the decisive reason for its approval in the essentially promotional nature of the text, further weakened in Parliament by the removal of its few original mandatory provisions (including employee representation on the boards of publicly owned companies, the duty to consult and the Guarantor of corporate social sustainability). While acknowledging some merits of the law (breaking the political deadlock, the classification of four forms of participation – managerial, economic-financial, organisational and consultative – and its educational function), the article highlights its many shortcomings: the absence of obligations, sanctions, default rules, codetermination rights and effective monitoring mechanisms. Particular attention is paid to the relationship with collective bargaining, to which the law refers in almost half of its articles, leaving the implementation of the participatory principle to the willingness of the social partners and to the company’s articles of association, risking merely optional and uneven participation. A comparison with the Swedish system, to which the Italian model has been likened, reveals some similarities but also substantial differences (semi-dispositive rules, duties of prior negotiation, a centralised and cohesive union system). The essay nonetheless rejects both the view that the reform is essentially useless, emphasising its modest but genuine innovations, and the claim that it is unconstitutional, also in light of Constitutional Court judgment No. 156/2025. The law’s real limit, it concludes, lies not in its legitimacy but in its effectiveness: its success will depend on whether trade unions and firms seize the opportunities it offers to revive participatory industrial relations.

all.title: Psychological Safety Mediates Inclusive Leadership and Organizational Support Links to Disability Inclusion in Indonesian Retail
all.abstract: This study examines the effects of inclusive leadership, organizational support, and psychological safety on workplace inclusion among employees with disabilities in the modern retail industry in Indonesia, while also investigating the mediating role of psychological safety. Using a quantitative approach with a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 220 respondents through purposive sampling and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that inclusive leadership and organizational support have significant positive effects on workplace inclusion, and psychological safety also significantly influences workplace inclusion. Furthermore, psychological safety is found to mediate the relationships between inclusive leadership and workplace inclusion, as well as between organizational support and workplace inclusion. The model demonstrates strong explanatory power, suggesting that the proposed variables effectively explain workplace inclusion among employees with disabilities.

all.title: New Guarantees of Labor Rights: The Essence and Substance of the 2026 Amendments to Labor Legislation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The article analyses the 2026 amendments to Uzbekistan's labour legislation, primarily Law No. ORQ-1150 of 11 June 2026, which regulates the right to strike, collective labour dispute resolution, part-time work for certain categories of employees and liability for violating strike legislation, as well as the 2026 provisions on workplace discrimination and sexual harassment. Practical gaps and proposals are discussed.

all.title: Pacto pela diversidade, equidade e inclusão nas empresas estatais federais: diretrizes, governança e impactos potenciais no ambiente organizacional
institutions: Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina
all.abstract: Although the literature on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) documents advances in contemporary debate, significant gaps remain regarding the systematic analysis of its institutionalization within Brazilian public enterprises and mixed-capital companies. To address this gap, this study analyzes the normative implementation of the Pact for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion among Brazilian federal state-owned enterprises, examining its guidelines, corporate execution strategies, and anticipated impacts on the workplace. Employing a qualitative approach and a descriptive-exploratory design, the research is operationalized through a document analysis of official primary sources: the Protocol of Intent, the 2024–2025 cycle Work Plan, and the official list of the 33 signatory federal state-owned enterprises. The interpretation is grounded in Triviños’s (1987) framework, synthesizing documentary evidence, specialized literature on DEI and governance, and the researchers' critical reflexivity. The results reveal that the Pact establishes a normative architecture linking distributive equity to instrumental justifications regarding corporate performance. Its operationalization is anchored in demographic assessments, leadership literacy initiatives, integrity channels, and targets for decision-making roles under a "comply or explain" regulatory model. However, tensions arise from the voluntary nature of participation ("soft law") and the absence of sanctions linked to Law No. 13.303/2016; this indicates that the reported impacts represent normative projections, the realization of which faces cultural resistance and the risk of merely cosmetic compliance. The study makes a theoretical contribution by problematizing the transposition of the DEI agenda to the state-owned productive sector, a methodological one by proposing a replicable matrix for the document analysis of corporate policies, and a practical one by providing governance insights to mitigate institutional symbolism in public administration. Key words: diversity, equity, and inclusion; public policies; federal state-owned enterprises; public administration.

all.title: Employment opportunities and discrimination faced by individuals with mental illness
all.abstract: Background: This study examines the employment experiences of peer workers with lived experience of mental illness in the Czech Republic, focusing on access to the open labour market, employment duration, and workplace discrimination. The aim was to analyse employment trajectories before and during peer work and to explore relationships between employment outcomes, discrimination, and selected sociodemographic characteristics. Methods: A quantitative survey was conducted among peer workers in health and social services (N = 101). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and chi-square tests. Results: A proportion of respondents reported experiencing discrimination during their job search and in the workplace, including rejection in recruitment, negative interactions with colleagues, and exclusion by supervisors. Most respondents reported a strong interest in employment; however, many described employment trajectories that did not correspond to their qualifications. A statistically significant association with a large effect size was found between employment duration and job position. A significant association was also found between employment duration and workplace discrimination, although this was based on a reduced sample. Conclusion: The findings suggest that peer workers with lived experience of mental illness may encounter barriers in accessing and maintaining employment prior to entering peer roles, whereas supportive peer work environments may be associated with more stable employment. The findings should be interpreted with caution due to the specific nature of the sample and should not be generalised beyond peer workers.

all.title: Beyond individual factors: a multilevel review of barriers and facilitators to employment inclusion in autism
institutions: Institute for Biomedical Research and Innovation
all.abstract: Background Employment is a key social determinant of health, shaping autonomy, wellbeing, and social participation across adulthood. Yet adolescents and adults with autism continue to experience substantial inequalities in access to work, workplace inclusion, and employment sustainability. Although the literature on this topic has expanded, evidence remains fragmented across recruitment, organizational practices, workplace culture, and broader institutional conditions. Methods This integrative review synthesized empirical studies on barriers and facilitators to employment inclusion in adolescents and adults with autism. A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted for studies published between January 2015 and March 2026. A total of 2,757 records were identified, of which 45 were retained for formal title and abstract screening. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria following full-text assessment. Given the methodological heterogeneity of the included literature, findings were examined through integrative narrative synthesis. Results Across the reviewed studies, employment inclusion emerged as a multilevel phenomenon shaped by interacting institutional, organizational, socio-cultural, and individual conditions. Reported barriers included socially demanding and inflexible recruitment procedures, limited accommodations, implicit workplace norms, low predictability, and work environments requiring sustained masking or adaptation. Reported facilitators included structured and skills-focused hiring practices, proactive adjustments, supportive leadership, clearer communication, and better alignment between job demands and the strengths of people with autism. Conclusion The available evidence suggests that employment disparities in autism are shaped by the interaction of workplace systems, organizational practices, socio-cultural norms, and individual support needs, rather than by individual characteristics alone. However, this interpretation should be considered in light of the current evidence base, which is still dominated by qualitative and cross-sectional studies and offers limited longitudinal or intervention-based evidence. Further research is needed to clarify which organizational and system-level conditions support meaningful and sustainable employment over time.

all.title: More Room for Difference, Less Room for Change: Generative AI and Psychosocial Disabilities at Work
all.abstract: The growing incorporation of generative AI into work life creates new possibilities for accommodating diverse ways of functioning while raising questions about the reproduction of existing organisational norms. Drawing on qualitative research on how people with psychosocial disabilities use generative AI at work, this article examines the reconfiguration of relations between workers, working processes, and expected outcomes in work assemblages, which are mediated through generative AI. First, generative AI serves as workplace accommodation, helping participants adapt work to their ways of functioning. Second, it mediates between diverse work processes and expected outcomes, allowing workers to work in their own ways while producing outputs that meet workplace standards. Third, generative AI helps create digital doubles that communicate and present themselves in normative ways. By mediating between diverse ways of working and standardised organisational expectations, generative AI can reinforce existing organisational norms rather than encourage the systemic changes needed for workplace inclusion.

all.title: Perceived stigma and disclosure concerns despite family support among chronic hepatitis B patients: mixed-methods evidence from India
institutions: Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences
all.abstract: This mixed-methods cross-sectional study measured enacted and perceived stigma among chronic hepatitis B (CHB) patients in India and explored lived experiences and psychosocial challenges associated with hepatitis B diagnosis. A total of 273 participants aged ≥ 18 years with chronic hepatitis B (hepatitis B surface antigen [HBsAg]-positive) were recruited from a tertiary hospital in New Delhi during 2024. Quantitative data used structured questionnaires and an 11-item hepatitis B adaptation of the Berger HIV Stigma Scale measuring four dimensions of perceived stigma: disclosure concerns, personalized stigma, public attitudes, and negative self-image, plus four enacted stigma indicators including social exclusion, workplace discrimination, family isolation, and partner abandonment. Twenty participants underwent qualitative interviews exploring diagnosis reactions, discrimination experiences, and coping mechanisms. The mean age was 41.57 years; 60.1% were male, 72.5% married, and 58.6% held graduate or higher qualifications. Most participants disagreed with the stigma statements in each of the four domains (64.5%–82.4%); the median total score was 22 (IQR 22–28) of a possible 11–44. Enacted stigma within families was uncommon (98.53% reported no family isolation), whereas 31.14% reported hesitancy about disclosing their status. Social marginalization persisted, with 15.75% excluded and 28.57% reporting career impacts. Among women diagnosed during pregnancy (n = 68), 76.5% reported concern about mother-to-child transmission. These findings provide crucial evidence supporting the Viral Hepatitis (Prevention and Control) Bill, 2025, highlighting urgent need for anti-discrimination provisions and targeted interventions addressing workplace discrimination and pregnancy-related concerns.

all.title: Barriers to female graduates' participation in Indonesia's formal agricultural sector
Higher education as a site of political reordering: the Trump-Musk phase of the second Trump administration
all.venue: Journal of Further and Higher Education
all.abstract: This article examines the higher education priorities advanced during the early months of the second Trump administration in the U.S.A., marked by the influential presence of South African businessman Elon Musk as a special government employee. As one of the first scholarly analyses of this novel political configuration, this article draws on world-systems theory to conduct an original inquiry into how the administration intensified the politicisation of higher education by systematically instrumentalising its governance for political ends. This is done through a thematic analysis of 16 national-level policy documents issued between January and May 2025. These measures, which include dismantling diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, curtailing academic freedom, and conditioning federal support on ideological alignment, have disrupted global academic mobility and challenged the hegemonic position of US-American higher education. However, while semi-peripheral nations may benefit from talent redistribution, the article argues that these shifts represent a recalibration rather than a meaningful structural transformation of global academic core–periphery relations. By situating these developments within a world-systems framework, the article contributes to theory by conceptualising higher education as a site of political reordering, informs policy by highlighting the risks of ideological conditionality, and offers insights for institutions navigating this volatile landscape.

all.title: Working in the Corporate Sector
all.abstract: This chapter examines integrative practice in the corporate sector, arguing that the complexity of contemporary workplace challenges, from burnout and trauma to interpersonal conflict and mental health, demands an approach that combines the psychological depth of therapy with the solutions-focused energy of coaching. Drawing on two practitioners’ contrasting routes into integrative practice, the chapter explores how a psychologically informed, business-savvy model can address the needs of both individuals and teams in ways that traditional performance-focused coaching cannot. Key areas explored include supporting high-performing and high-potential staff, work-related trauma, interpersonal relationships, mental health concerns, and diversity, equity and inclusion. The chapter also addresses team-level work, demonstrating how integrative practice can support dysfunctional teams, facilitate conflict resolution, and help high-performing groups navigate change. Throughout, detailed vignettes illustrate how therapeutic and coaching approaches are woven together in service of authentic, sustainable transformation.

all.title: Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Nurses’ Spoken Interaction Challenges in Finnish Hospitals: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
all.abstract: Background Migration of nurses is focused on Finland and other high-income countries, strengthening the local healthcare workforce. Working in a second language can be challenging for culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) nurses. Addressing the interaction challenges faced by CALD nurses is crucial for patient safety, workplace well-being, and nurse retention. However, little is known about CALD nurses’ speaking and listening challenges from a micro-level perspective in a Finnish hospital context. Therefore, this study aimed to explore CALD nurses’ spoken interaction challenges in Finnish hospitals. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was employed for this study. Semi-structured individual interviews were conducted from September 2024 to November 2025 with 12 CALD and 17 native nurses who worked in multiple Finnish university hospitals. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Results Two main categories and six subcategories emerged through the analysis. The main category of speaking challenges included subcategories of speaking competence challenges, challenging speaking tasks, and challenging speaking attitudes and experiences. The main category of listening challenges included subcategories of listening competence challenges, challenging listening tasks, and challenging listening attitudes and experiences. Conclusions CALD nurses faced spoken interaction challenges at linguistic, task-related, and attitudinal and experiential levels, demonstrating the complex interplay of multifaceted challenges. The findings showed the need to provide individual support and promote inclusion in workplace interactions. The findings inform the development of practices that enhance interactions, such as language mentoring, educational simulations, and diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging policies.

all.title: Leader status-leveling behavior and leadership effectiveness: the roles of warmth-based mechanism and leader gender
institutions: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Purpose In response to growing organizational efforts to promote diversity, equity and inclusion, many leaders are encouraged to adopt behaviors that reduce hierarchical distance, known as status-leveling behavior. While prior research has emphasized its benefits for employees, little is known about its effects on leaders themselves. This study aims to shift the focus to examine whether, how and for whom leader status-leveling behavior enhances leadership effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach To investigate these relationships, this study adopted a multi-method approach. This study conducted a video-based scenario experiment (n = 155) and a two-wave field survey (n = 212) to test the proposed theoretical model. Findings The video-based scenario experiment and multi-wave survey results showed that leader status-leveling behavior could promote leadership effectiveness through employee’s perceived leader warmth rather than competence. In addition, the status-leveling behavior of male leaders is more effective than that of female leaders in promoting leadership effectiveness through perceived leader warmth. Originality/value This study advances leadership research by repositioning status-leveling as a strategically effective leadership behavior. It contributes to theory by clarifying the mechanism (warmth perceptions) and boundary condition (leader gender) through which status-leveling enhances leadership effectiveness, thereby enriching our understanding of inclusive leadership practices in contemporary organizations.

all.title: Women's Participation in Transportation Services under Globalization: A Systematic Review of Workforce Dynamics
all.abstract: The phenomenon of globalization has had deep impacts on the transportation industry globally, presenting new possibilities for women even as it presents new problems in their employment. The unprecedented development of urban transportation services, logistics management, ride-sharing apps, aviation, and other forms of public transport have led to increased participation of women in occupations that were previously considered to be male domains. In countries like India, liberalization, innovation in technology, and expansion of service sectors have contributed to greater female participation in transportation-related occupations as cab drivers, aviation workers, metro staff, logistics managers, delivery executives, transport managers, among others, contributing positively to economic development. However, despite these developments, women still encounter significant daily obstacles in the form of workplace discrimination, pay inequities, security threats, sexual harassment, fewer opportunities for leadership, work-family conflict, among others. As indicated by ILO (2022), these problems impact women adversely, hampering their economic potential as well. In light of this, it is crucial that women in the transport industry be provided with a safe environment, appropriate policies, proper facilities, and attitudinal changes enabling them to thrive in their respective occupations. This study conducts a systematic bibliometric review of 1,000 academic records retrieved from Lens.org covering 2015–2026, employing R Studio's bibliometric package Key findings highlight globalization-induced challenges including wage suppression, informalisation, digital exclusion, care burden asymmetry, and gender-based violence, particularly in maritime and urban mobility contexts. The study recommends longitudinal, intersectional, and cross-border research agendas to support gender-inclusive transportation policy.

all.title: Queer inclusion in organizations: a critical review of methodologies and theoretical frameworks
all.venue: Equality Diversity and Inclusion An International Journal
all.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to critically examine how queer inclusion in organizations has been studied, with a focus on the methodological approaches and theoretical frameworks that shape this body of work. Design/methodology/approach This paper is based on a critical review of peer-reviewed literature, drawing on databases such as JSTOR, Web of Science and Scopus for their comprehensive coverage of gender and sexuality studies within corporate and institutional settings. Fifty-eight peer-reviewed publications between 2007 and 2024 are included. Findings Among the dominant frameworks in the reviewed literature – queer theory, minority stress theory and intersectionality, none adequately explains how queer claims translate into organizational change across context. Qualitative approaches dominate (50%), followed by quantitative (20.7%), theoretical and conceptual (20.7%) and mixed methods (8.6%) studies. Geographically, the literature remains heavily concentrated in a small number of national contexts, particularly the United States. The review compares the literature across shared analytical dimensions such as legal protection and enforcement, family, kinship and disclosure, intersecting axes of disadvantage, organizational form and employment informality, movement infrastructure and organizational dependencies, and business case reasoning, showing that inclusion outcomes depend on the specific combination of these conditions present in a given context. Significant gaps persist in intersectional engagement, representation beyond a monolithic “LGBT” category and longitudinal analyses of organizational change. Originality/value By connecting politics of alignment with a global–local approach, this review offers a framework for understanding not only what shapes queer workplace inclusion but the conditions under which queer claims become consequential to organizations, for whom and when the results lead to real change rather than symbolic compliance.

all.title: Not to be served but to serve: cumulative employment precarity and later-life agency among older Chinese migrants in the United Kingdom
all.abstract: Population ageing has led governments to seek ways to encourage older people to delay retirement using policy instruments such as increasing state pension ages, prohibiting workplace discrimination, and encouraging employers to recognise older workers as a source of skilled labour. Capacity to delay retirement is unevenly distributed and concerns have been raised about the impact of the Extended Working Life agenda on older people whose careers have been characterised by precarious work. This article explores the experiences of one such community: older migrants who have faced lifetimes of discrimination, language barriers, and institutional barriers to formal employment. This 2022 study examines how cumulative migration-related employment precarity shapes later-life work and retirement choices among older Chinese migrants in Manchester, United Kingdom, most of whom have spent their careers self-employed, running catering businesses. Drawing on Life-course Theory, we explore how factors such as migration timing, labour market structures, health, and economic, business and social relationships across time shape agency in later life as it relates to work and employment. Using a participatory qualitative design, researchers worked with the community radio programme Dragons Voice to conduct three four-hour workshops with seventeen Chinese migrants aged 60+ to discuss their experiences in paid employment and their perceptions of the United Kingdom government’s Extended Working Life agenda. Discussions took place in English, Cantonese and Mandarin. Findings show that while business opportunities in the catering sector provided vital access to income and stability, they also resulted in occupational confinement. Participants discussed their sense of loss regarding earlier careers and their desire to follow new vocations. Further, they discussed the impact that catering had on their mental and physical health and their scepticism about being able to continue in the sector into their sixties. However, they also described later life as an opportunity to contribute economically and socially through family care, volunteering, cultural participation, community support, and collectively organised economic activity, drawing on the ways they found work in the past as a blueprint for economic engagement in later life. We discuss the implications of the UK government’s policy agenda on older migrants.

all.title: Decoloniality and Education: Integrating the Muslim Immigrant
all.abstract: Highly skilled Muslim immigrants experience complex social and economic integration barriers during their settlement journey in Canada. These barriers include a nonrecognition and devaluation of credentials and skills, occupational downgrading, discrimination and Islamophobia in hiring etc., leading them to further accumulate educational and professional capital (Zainub, 2023). This engagement with educational institutions mirrors the many inequities they face in the labor market. Research literature continues to offer substantial evidence of integration issues in general, however, there is a need to address the barriers faced by highly skilled Muslim immigrants which emerge at the nexus of labor market and educational institutions. This chapter attempts to center the lived experiences of highly skilled Muslim immigrants who engage with Canadian education system as adult learners during their settlement journey. Through an analysis of existing literature on immigrant integration (Kazemipur, 2014; Torres-Zaragoza & Llorent-Bedmar, 2024) and the qualitative findings of my previous research (Zainub, 2023), I emphasize the use of decoloniality (Dei & Asgharzadeh, 2001; Mignolo, 2007, 2012) in educational research to bridge labor market and education system for inclusion and equitable solutions. I argue for conceptualizing a decolonial pathway for immigrant integration through “border thinking” (Mignolo, 2007, 2012; Mignolo & Tlostanova, 2006) emphasizing an intersectional analysis of gender, race, and religion. This calls for the educational system to initiate change through a renewed commitment to the existing antiracist policies, an active engagement with stakeholders (regional, community organizations, practitioners and employers) and future educational research for an epistemic shift in integration discourse and practice.

all.title: Transitions from Employment to Non-Employment After Return to Work: A Longitudinal Analysis in Spinal Cord injury
all.abstract: Background: Sustaining employment after returning to work (RTW) following the onset of chronic physical impairment remains challenging, as health-related limitations and changing work capacity may lead to employment exit. However, evidence on post-RTW employment transitions from a life-course perspective is limited. This study aimed to describe transitions from employment to non-employment after RTW among individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) and to examine socio-demographic, injury-related, work-related, and policy-related factors associated with employment exit, including whether these associations varied by time since RTW and age. Methods: We used biographical survey data from the Work-Life Study, a retrospective study investigating chronological work-life events among participants in the Swiss Spinal Cord Injury Cohort Study (SwiSCI). This study focused on working-age individuals who returned to work after SCI. Flexible parametric survival models incorporating multiple time scales were applied, with standard errors clustered at the individual level. Results: Nearly half of individuals who returned to work (n=405) experienced at least one employment exit (n=195, 48.1%). In adjusted analyses, higher hazards of employment exit were observed among women (aHR=1.43, 95%CI:1.06-1.93), persons with lower education (p=0.02), unstable living arrangements (aHR=1.52, 95%CI:1.06–2.17), a prior history of non-employment (aHR=1.39, 95%CI:1.20–1.60), lower job match regarding interests (aHR=0.83, 95%CI:0.69–0.99), lower workplace inclusion (aHR=0.64, 95%CI:0.54–0.76), frequent sick leave due to secondary health conditions (aHR=1.17, 95%CI:1.00–1.38) and comorbidities (aHR=1.83, 95%CI:1.24–2.71), residence in the Lake Geneva region (aHR=2.32, 95%CI:1.13–4.78), and absence of a disability pension (aHR=1.54, 95%CI:1.15-2.07). Gender, sick leave due to secondary conditions or comorbidities, and prior non-employment history were not associated with employment exit immediately after RTW; however, these factors showed effects several years later. The association between frequent sick-leave due to secondary conditions and employment exit became significant from approximately 54 years of age. Conclusions: This study identified risk factors for employment exit and critical time windows after RTW and across age. The findings highlight the need for coordinated multilevel interventions that address individual, work-related, and structural determinants of sustainable employment. Additionally, there is requirement for targeted and time-sensitive support for individuals at an elevated risk of exiting employment.

all.title: Limitation Period for Social Security Contributions After Reinstatement: Ten-Year Conversion
all.abstract: (English): Under Italian labour and civil law, the final judgment ordering reinstatement and the payment of social security contributions pursuant to Article 18 of Law No. 300/1970 converts the five-year limitation period into a ten-year period under Article 2953 of the Civil Code, even in favour of INPS as a third party absent from the dismissal proceedings. Examining judgment No. 27341 of 20 October 2026 rendered by the Labour Division of the Court of Cassation, this article clarifies why the public-law nature of social security obligations precludes both a split res judicata doctrine and any waiver inferred from the agency's procedural stance, while demarcating the boundaries vis-à-vis void fixed-term contracts and non-enforceable payment orders. It further analyses the partial reversal concerning restitution of the employee contribution share where the underlying payment order was swept away by termination of the dispute. Abstract (Italiano — Prescrizione dei contributi dopo la reintegra: termine decennale): La prescrizione dei contributi dopo la reintegra si converte in decennale per effetto del giudicato ex art. 2953 c.c. anche a favore dell'INPS rimasto estraneo al giudizio sul licenziamento. Il contributo esamina la sentenza della Cassazione, Sez. Lavoro, 20 ottobre 2026, n. 27341, evidenziando perché la condanna contributiva prevista dall'art. 18 l. n. 300/1970 integri un'ipotesi eccezionale a favore del terzo che non tollera la figura del giudicato dimidiato né subisce l'influenza del contegno processuale dell'ente. Attraverso il confronto con i limiti del contratto a termine nullo e del rito monitorio privo di esecutività, l'analisi indaga infine le ragioni dell'accoglimento del secondo motivo di ricorso, relativo alla restituzione della quota contributiva a carico del lavoratore incamerata in forza di un decreto ingiuntivo opposto poi travolto dalla cessazione della materia del contendere.
