This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

all.title: Phantom Networks: Window on Agency in Social Mechanisms
all.abstract: Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience—what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure in action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work. Funding: This work was made possible by financial support from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business for data-processing software and financial support from MIT Sloan for transitioning our earlier experiment to the more flexible Empirica platform and funding the experiment trials on which we report here.

all.title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
all.abstract: Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice, the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here, we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge. Funding: This research was supported in part by funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council [Grant 430-2024-01156] to M. Joshi.

all.title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
institutions: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from disruptions such as pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, or cascading partner failures, and they can rapidly reconfigure whole-network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole-network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness-resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass preshock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness-resilience perspective opens for the study of network change. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19624 .

all.title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
all.abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas. Funding: This research was supported by a research grant awarded to Y. H. Kim by Mays Business School. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19400 .

all.title: Colleagues That Work Together Move Together: How Co-Moving Among Newcomers Affects Individual and Team Performance
all.abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multitheory, and multiperiod model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience that they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, although these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: Although co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

all.title: Action-Oriented Narratives: How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
all.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers—subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources—are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call “action-oriented narratives”: simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration, while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19136 .

all.title: Multimarket Contact and Long-Term Oriented Language in Competition
all.abstract: Corporate disclosure has long served as a strategic tool for managing the perceptions of audiences that shape a firm’s access to resources. Prior research has largely focused on why firms use disclosure to engage capital-market constituents such as investors and analysts, leaving open the question of when and why firms disclose for competitive purposes. Focusing on the temporal orientation of competitive strategy communication, we examine how multimarket contact (MMC) shapes firms’ use of long-term oriented language (LTL). We argue that greater MMC raises the risk of cross-market retaliation, strengthening firms’ incentives to signal a restrained competitive posture through LTL, particularly when competitive capacity is visibly constrained by poor financial performance or analyst downgrade revisions. Using a sample of 36 U.S. manufacturing firms across six industries from 2015 to 2024, we find evidence generally consistent with our predictions.

all.title: Greenwashing in green bonds: a systematic literature review
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explain how greenwashing emerges, persists and affects credibility in green bond markets. Rather than treating greenwashing as isolated misleading communication, it examines the interaction between financial incentives, governance structures, information asymmetries, institutional arrangements and market consequences. The study also identifies the main manifestations, drivers, consequences and mitigation mechanisms associated with greenwashing in sustainable debt instruments. Design/methodology/approach The study conducts a systematic literature review following the PRISMA protocol. Scopus and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed studies addressing greenwashing in sustainable debt markets, resulting in a final sample of 46 articles. The selected studies were analyzed through inductive thematic synthesis, involving iterative data reduction, thematic organization, relational interpretation and refinement of conclusions. Categories were developed from recurring patterns concerning governance dynamics, operational mechanisms, manifestations, consequences and mitigation strategies. Findings The findings show that greenwashing in green bond markets is driven by reputational incentives, lower financing costs, weak regulatory oversight, investor attraction and the relabeling of preexisting projects. It manifests through selective disclosure, weak additionality, symbolic certification, regulatory arbitrage, limited transparency and redirection of proceeds. These practices can erode investor trust, damage issuer reputation, widen credit spreads, increase financing costs and restrict market scalability. Institutional moderators may either mitigate or reproduce these dynamics depending on their effectiveness. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by the geographical concentration of the literature, particularly its strong focus on the Chinese green bond market, and by its reliance on published academic research, which may underrepresent enforcement actions and emerging regulatory developments. Future studies should conduct comparative cross-country analyses and empirically test the proposed framework through case studies, interviews, process tracing and document analysis, particularly in emerging markets and the Global South. Practical implications The findings suggest that issuers should incorporate environmental integrity before issuance through clear eligibility criteria, measurable targets, additionality and traceability of proceeds. Investors, auditors and external reviewers should assess discrepancies between ex ante commitments and post-issuance outcomes. Policymakers should strengthen harmonized taxonomies, standardized reporting, post-issuance verification, reviewer independence and enforcement mechanisms. However, regulatory requirements should remain proportionate to avoid restricting access to climate finance for smaller issuers and emerging markets. Social implications Greenwashing in green bond markets may deepen inequalities between developed and developing economies by increasing verification and certification costs, restricting access to climate finance and concentrating capital among larger issuers. In emerging markets, exposed greenwashing cases may also increase investor distrust and widen climate finance gaps. Strengthening market credibility is therefore important not only for investor protection but also for ensuring broader access to sustainable finance and supporting progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. Originality/value This study advances the green bond literature by reframing greenwashing as a systemic and dynamic field-level process rather than an isolated organizational practice. It develops an integrative framework linking motivational drivers, operational mechanisms, empirical manifestations, market consequences, institutional moderators and mitigation responses. By connecting institutional fragmentation, governance gaps and issuer behavior to financial and societal consequences, the study provides a broader explanation of how greenwashing is produced, reproduced and potentially constrained within green bond markets.

all.title: Factors influencing FinTech adoption in the agrarian sector of developing economies: bridging technology, finance and policy for sustainable development
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the factors influencing financial technology (FinTech) adoption among Indian farmers by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with behavioral intention as a mediating mechanism. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 461 farmers across nine districts of Uttar Pradesh, India. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis. Findings Facilitating conditions and habit significantly influence behavioral intention, which strongly drives actual FinTech adoption. Behavioral intention mediates these relationships. Multigroup analysis shows that the behavioral intention–adoption relationship remains stable across gender, age and farm size, although demographic characteristics influence antecedent effects. Practical implications Policymakers, financial institutions and FinTech providers should develop intention-focused, demographically sensitive strategies emphasizing digital literacy, accessibility and enabling infrastructure. Social implications Greater FinTech adoption can reduce rural financial exclusion, strengthen economic resilience and support inclusive rural development, contributing to the Sustainable Development Goals. Originality/value This study extends UTAUT by demonstrating how behavioral intention translates enabling conditions and habitual technology use into actual FinTech adoption among farmers.

all.title: RenovaBio, environmental efficiency scores, and the cost of debt: evidence from Brazilian biofuel firms
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether the environmental efficiency scores assigned to Brazilian biofuel firms under the RenovaBio program affect their cost of debt. Specifically, it examines whether a regulated, standardized and externally verified environmental-performance metric can influence creditors’ risk assessments and borrowing conditions in an emerging economy, with particular emphasis on the highly leveraged Brazilian sugar-energy sector. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data from Brazilian biofuel-producing firms participating in RenovaBio, covering the 2020/2021, 2021/2022 and 2022/2023 crop years. Financial data were obtained from Balanços Patrimoniais and Valor Pró, while environmental efficiency scores and biofuel information came from the ANP. The relationship between RenovaBio efficiency scores and the cost of debt was estimated using panel regressions, with a random-effects specification as the main model, robust standard errors clustered at the firm level and additional robustness checks using lagged RenovaBio scores. Findings The results show that RenovaBio environmental efficiency scores are negatively associated with the cost of debt, but the relationship is not statistically significant. This suggests that creditors in the Brazilian sugar-energy sector do not yet systematically incorporate these environmental performance signals into lending conditions. Firm size and asset tangibility are associated with lower borrowing costs, while the Selic interest rate increases them. Robustness tests using lagged RenovaBio scores confirm the absence of a statistically significant effect, indicating that traditional financial characteristics remain more influential in creditors’ risk assessments. Social implications Broader access to affordable green credit could support investment, preserve jobs and generate positive spillovers in biofuel-producing regions. Audited environmental efficiency scores may also contribute to reducing local environmental harms and improving public health. However, policymakers should prevent the benefits of sustainability-linked financing from being disproportionately captured by large firms. Combining environmental certification with targeted support and capacity-building initiatives for smaller producers may help promote a more inclusive and just transition toward a low-carbon economy. Originality/value This study provides novel evidence on the financial implications of a regulated, policy-certified environmental-efficiency metric, rather than relying on voluntary ESG disclosures or composite sustainability indicators. By examining RenovaBio’s standardized, externally verified, LCA-based efficiency score and its relationship with borrowing costs, the study extends the literature on environmental performance and corporate finance. It also contributes evidence from the Brazilian sugar-energy sector, offering insights into how climate-related regulatory instruments may interact with credit markets in an emerging economy.

all.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
institutions: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
all.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Financial support from the National Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301055, 72322017, 72471244, and 72101102] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08500 .

all.title: The invisible side of the dish: the ethnic food value chain in the Amazon
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to contribute to the fields of operations management and supply chain management by demonstrating that, in the context of ethnic foods, value chains must move beyond merely symbolic appreciation of territory and incorporate recognition of actors at the base of the chain to promote social justice. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative approach, the findings demonstrate that, although fish products hold high symbolic value, structural inequalities persist throughout the value chain. Findings Artisanal fishers remain invisible and their traditional knowledge and demands are neglected in decision-making processes. The concentration of power among intermediaries, combined with the absence of effective institutional support, restricts opportunities and reinforces exclusion. There is also a lack of recognition of these workers’ social identities, a fundamental aspect in promoting a more equitable distribution of the benefits generated. Research limitations/implications This study has limitations related to the specificity of its empirical context and the territorial distances involved, which warrant caution when generalizing the findings. Some fishing villages are located in remote and difficult-to-access areas, which limited the number of participants in the first phase of the research. Practical implications Managers may invest in production verticalization, which could reduce dependence on intermediaries and improve fishers’ remuneration. Chefs can also act as bridges between producers and consumers. Finally, strengthening public policies aimed at ethnic food value chains is essential. Social implications It is essential to promote DEI-oriented public policies and initiatives that value local cultural practices, thereby increasing sustainability and ensuring a fairer distribution of resources. Originality/value This study contributes theoretically to OSCM in two ways, advancing beyond the traditional sustainable supply chain management perspective. The first contribution expands the social dimension of sustainability analyses in supply chains. In contexts characterized by institutional voids and information asymmetries, social justice should not be treated merely as a normative principle but as a prerequisite for supply chain sustainability.

all.title: Integrity, justice and diversity, equity and inclusion: a discourse analysis of award-winning Brazilian agribusiness companies’ websites
all.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to investigate how Brazilian agribusiness companies awarded the Mais Integridade Seal (Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Food Supply – MAPA – Agribusiness Integrity Recognition) discursively construct the meanings of justice and diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) on their websites. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on critical discourse analysis, the results reveal a selective narrative that frames justice predominantly as compliance and procedural integrity, while DEI is treated in a compartmentalized manner. Findings This discursive decoupling points to an instrumental logic that limits the agenda’s transformative potential. Theoretically, the study unveils discursive strategies that reproduce the status quo. Social implications At the social level, it questions the effectiveness of integrity seals and warns of the risk of global agendas being instrumentalized without promoting structural changes, a particularly relevant challenge for agribusiness in the Global South. Originality/value The study contributes by offering a model for aligning discursive practices with material actions toward justice, fostering debates on socio-environmental justice in agribusiness and to the broader agenda of the sustainable development goals.

all.title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
all.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.

all.title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
all.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan media construct divergent social evaluations of the same executive behavior through distinct narrative processes.

all.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
all.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

all.title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
all.abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

all.title: Beyond guesswork: how market knowledge and social influences impact investment decisions in Brazil
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how market knowledge and social influences are associated with investment decisions in Brazil. It examines the relationship between investment participation and two cognitive enablers – self-declared market knowledge and education – as well as three information channels: professional guidance, autonomous search and informal sources. Investment decisions are differentiated according to the complexity of financial products, classified as low, medium or high. Design/methodology/approach Annual data from the Brazilian Association of Financial and Capital Market Entities (ANBIMA)/Datafolha “X-ray of the Brazilian Investor” survey (2018–2023) are analyzed, comprising 26,428 individuals aged 16 and over across all Brazilian regions. Financial products are classified into low-, medium- and high-complexity categories. Separate binary logistic regression models are estimated for each category because respondents may hold investments across multiple complexity levels and the proportional odds assumption of ordinal logistic regression is violated. The models assess associations between investment decisions, market knowledge, education and information sources, controlling for demographic, socioeconomic, regional, temporal and pandemic-related factors. Robustness analyses are conducted by excluding the COVID-19 pandemic years. Findings Findings indicate that market knowledge is positively associated with investment participation across all product categories, with stronger effects for medium- and high-complexity investments. Professional guidance shows the strongest association with low-complexity products, whereas autonomous information search is most strongly associated with high-complexity investments. Informal sources are positively associated with participation, but their practical relevance declines as product complexity increases. Education is positively associated with medium- and high-complexity investments, while higher education is negatively associated with low-complexity products. Income, age, gender, marital status, region and the pandemic also exhibit heterogeneous associations across complexity categories. Social implications Greater financial literacy and access to reliable information can promote financial inclusion and more equitable investment opportunities. Limited familiarity with complex financial products remains an important barrier to market participation, while regional disparities reflect unequal access to financial resources and information. Educational initiatives should foster greater autonomy and confidence in navigating complex digital financial environments. Public policies should address financial misinformation and improve risk disclosure practices, particularly in regions with limited access to information. In parallel, the financial sector can support informed decision-making by developing mechanisms that mitigate behavioral biases and align financial sophistication with appropriate risk management. Originality/value The research contributes to the literature by providing a granular analysis of investment decisions according to financial product complexity in an emerging market. Rather than treating investment participation as a binary outcome or focusing exclusively on stocks, it distinguishes low-, medium- and high-complexity products and examines how market knowledge and different information channels are associated with each category. By integrating cognitive enablers and social influences within a conceptual framework, the analysis reveals heterogeneous patterns across investment categories and provides evidence on how professional guidance, autonomous information search and informal sources relate differently to investment participation in the Brazilian financial market.

all.title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
all.abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

all.title: Religiosity and consumer behaviour among Millennials and Gen Z: does gender make a difference?
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how religiosity is associated with consumer behaviour among Millennials and Gen Z in a highly religious emerging market. It proposes the spiritual cognitive consumption theory (SCCT), a dual pathway framework, and provides preliminary empirical support for its overall predictive validity. However, these two pathways were not directly measured; future experimental research is needed to isolate each mechanism. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 400 Nigerian respondents were analysed using structural equation modelling. Gender significantly moderates this relationship: women tend to show a stronger association between religiosity and relational aspects (e.g. brand trust, emotional congruity), whereas men focus more on instrumental outcomes (e.g. product functionality, religious symbolism). Findings The SCCT framework provides a nuanced understanding of the tension between spiritual devotion and market-based consumption. The findings offer marketers gender-sensitive, faith-conscious strategies and position SCCT as a robust theoretical tool for understanding spirituality, cognition and consumption in evolving digital economies. Social implications The study contributes to sustainable development goal (SDG) 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) by providing insights into inclusive, faith-sensitive marketing practices in the Global South. Originality/value The originality of this study lies in the development of the SCCT framework, which integrates spirituality, cognition and consumption into a dual pathway model. This offers a novel theoretical lens for understanding consumer behaviour in religious emerging markets.

all.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
all.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use the prediction from our theoretical model as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using the predictor derived from our theoretical model, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by roughly 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05427 .

all.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
institutions: Institute of Operations Research and Analytics
Institute of Real Estate and Urban Studies
all.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00747 .

all.title: Connectors and Influencers
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Groupe d'Analyse et de Théorie Economique Lyon St Etienne
all.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. all.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
all.abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05050 .

all.title: It’s a System: Shareholder Activism, Corporate Harm, and the Role of Regulators, NGOs, and Media
all.abstract: Research on shareholder activism has focused largely on the direct, dyadic relationship between activists and the firms they target, leaving open a broader question: When does activism actually change corporate behavior? We argue that the answer depends on the wider system of stakeholders surrounding the firm. Integrating stakeholder influence research with institutional theory, we theorize that shareholder demands more effectively motivate organizational change when other actors in the institutional environment reinforce the issues those demands raise. We test this in the context of environmental and social (E&S) shareholder proposals, asking whether they reduce firms’ stakeholder violations, which are regulator-sanctioned acts of misconduct that can harm non-shareholding stakeholders. Using data on E&S proposals at 428 U.S. firms from 2007 to 2021, we find that proposals reduce stakeholder violations, and that this effect operates through managerial receptivity, defined as a firm’s behavioral pattern of engaging rather than resisting activist demands. Critically, this relationship is amplified when firms face greater scrutiny from two institutional pillars: regulative pressure from regulators and cultural-cognitive pressure from NGOs. By showing that non-shareholding stakeholders condition whether shareholder activism translates into reduced corporate harm, we move beyond the activist–firm dyad and offer a systems-level account of when, and through what mechanisms, shareholder activism succeeds in achieving its aims.

all.title: Stakeholder Governance
all.abstract: Stakeholder governance has become central to debates about stakeholder capitalism, yet research remains fragmented about the configurations through which non-shareholder stakeholders gain authority and firms become credibly bound to stakeholder claims. We systematically review 171 articles in management and related fields to develop a framework organized around stakeholder authority (i.e., the participatory rights or recognized standing through which stakeholders can engage in governance), and firm commitment (i.e., the obligations organizations assume toward stakeholder claims in ways that are costly to reverse or ignore). We identify five recurring configurations: (a) disclosure and evaluation; (b) monitoring and verification; (c) contracting, formal rules, and adjudication; (d) governance rights; and (e) rule-making rights. These configurations generally move from informational authority and very weak firm commitment to constitutional authority and very strong firm commitment. We also identify two off-diagonal configurations—constrained authority and embedded commitment—that reveal how authority and commitment need not align. Our framework distinguishes stakeholder governance that remains largely symbolic from arrangements that create durable constraints on organizational discretion. We conclude by outlining a research agenda on institutional settings, organizational forms, transitions across governance configurations, and the implications of learning dynamics for stakeholder authority and commitment.

all.title: Learning from a Biased Sample
all.abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. RS is further supported by a NSF GRFP under grant DGE-1656518, a Stanford Data Science PhD Fellowship, and a Stanford Diversifying Academia Recruiting Excellence (DARE) Fellowship. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08073 .

all.title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
all.abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

all.title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
institutions: University of Science and Technology of China
all.abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: G. Feng acknowledges financial support from the Hong Kong Research Grants Council [Grant GRF11502023] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72203190]. G. Feng is partially supported by the InnoHK Initiative of the Innovation and Technology Commission of the Hong Kong SAR and the Laboratory for AI-Powered Financial Technologies. L. Jiang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72473027]. J. Li acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72473026]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03136 .

all.title: Drivers of electric vehicle adoption in Brazil
institutions: Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a contextual extension of UTAUT2 to explain behavioral intention to adopt electric vehicles in Brazil, where institutional signals, economic constraints and psychological barriers influence sustainable consumption. Design/methodology/approach A survey of 660 Brazilian adults assessed UTAUT2 core drivers and additional constructs, including environmental consciousness, personal innovativeness, financial self-efficacy, perceived government incentives, resistance to change and price sensitivity. Covariance-based structural equation modeling estimated structural relationships, and multigroup analyses evaluated heterogeneity across generational cohorts and gender. Findings The proposed model accounted for 79.3% of the variance in behavioral intention. Government incentives served as signals that influenced multiple perceptions, while price sensitivity remained a persistent inhibitor. The significance of effects varied by generational cohort and gender, suggesting that policy and marketing interventions do not have uniform effects across demographic segments. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design and self-reported measures limit causal inference. Future research should use longitudinal and experimental designs and incorporate behavioral outcomes. Practical implications The findings offer insights for designing targeted policies and marketing strategies that consider environmental attitudes, financial confidence and demographic differences to accelerate EV adoption. Social implications The findings inform initiatives to accelerate sustainable mobility transitions in an emerging economy context. Originality/value This study provides a contextual specification of UTAUT2 and empirically evaluates (across generational cohorts and gender) the significance of psychological, financial, and institutional determinants of electric vehicle adoption decisions in Brazil, a market the UTAUT2 literature on electric vehicles has yet to reach.

all.title: Investor sentiment, crash risk and accounting information quality
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether investor sentiment is associated with stock price crash risk in Latin American capital markets and whether lower accounting information quality strengthens this relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study analyzes an unbalanced panel of publicly traded firms from Brazil, Chile, Mexico and Peru over the period 2004–2024. The empirical analysis uses fixed effects (FE), two-stage least squares (2SLS) and System-GMM. Crash risk is measured using negative conditional skewness and down-to-up volatility. Investor sentiment is assessed at aggregate and firm-specific levels, while accounting information quality is proxied by absolute discretionary accruals. Findings The results indicate that firm-specific and aggregate investor sentiment are positively associated with stock price crash risk, with System-GMM supporting this relationship after accounting for endogeneity and dynamic effects. This study also finds partial evidence that lower accounting information quality strengthens this relationship: greater earnings management intensifies the association between firm-specific sentiment and crash risk when crash risk is measured by negative conditional skewness, but no comparable moderating relationship is observed for down-to-up volatility or aggregate sentiment. Research limitations/implications Future research could examine other institutional settings and develop more precise measures of investor sentiment. Originality/value This study provides evidence on the relationship between investor sentiment and crash risk in Latin American emerging markets. By contrasting firm-specific and aggregate sentiment, it highlights the importance of cross-sectional heterogeneity and dynamic endogeneity in assessing behavioral influences on crash risk. It also shows that the moderating role of accounting information quality varies across sentiment dimensions and crash risk measures.

all.abstract: How can humans make sense of the rapid takeoff of artificial intelligence (AI)? We studied the sensemaking dynamics of AI through an open-ended, mixed-methods study with computational text analysis of millions of AI-related newspaper articles and social media posts grounded in 57 semi-structured interviews with AI professionals in 2021 and 2023—before and after the recent surge of public interest. We identify a range of sociological frames (interpretive schemas that structure collective cognition) and show how AI professionals use frames to address significant cognitive challenges, such as assigning responsibility for societal impacts.

all.title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate
all.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent’s model of the environment.

all.abstract: I just spent two long weeks in the Middle East, Geneva, and Barcelona meeting with hundreds of companies (manufacturing, tech, airlines, defense, financial services) including a week at Workday Rising. And while I was gone Nvidia crashed, Anthropic went public, Trump went to China, Outlook and the US air space went down, and the AI-stocks took a nosedive. In today’s recap I discuss the role of greed, the immaturity of this massive market, and what pragmatic, solution-oriented companies can do to prepare for the AI transformations ahead. As I describe, we’re dealing with a very immature technology and immature market . So rather than rush into major decisions, it’s ok to take a step back and look at the AI tsunami as an opportunity for strategic problem-solving. I also saw Ethan Mollick present to a series of executives and saw first-hand how “hyping AI” can create a frenzy of FOMO (fear of missing out). My message, as you’ll hear, is to take a deep breath and recognize that we’re still in the early days of this revolution, so to speak, and a culture of problem-solving and organizational growth is the best way to proceed. So I step through HR2030® and the four big use-cases for AI in HR and business. And no, despite Dario’s ongoing claims, we are not going to wipe out the job market. sample.title: The Search for Parental Leave and the Early-Career Gender Wage Gap
sample.abstract: Gender differences in preferences for parental leave contribute to the early-career growth in the gender wage gap among highly educated millennial Americans. Estimating a hedonic job-search model, I show that, while both men and women experience wage growth by entering firms offering better pay and benefits, the wage gap increases as women accept lower wages upon receiving job offers from employers providing parental leave. The wage-gap growth could decline by 60% if preferences for paid parental leave did not differ by gender. It could also decline if mandating and subsidizing the provision of paid leave muted workers’ leave-wage trade-off.

sample.title: Who Will be Assigned Unreasonable Tasks by Supervisors: A Conjoint Survey Experiment
sample.abstract: Supervisors sometimes assign employees tasks that employees may perceive as unreasonable because they fall outside their formal job duties. Prior research has mostly focused on the negative effects of unreasonable tasks on employee outcomes, without examining the fundamental question of who is more likely to be assigned such tasks by their supervisors. To answer this question, we examined three distinct logics underlying the assignment of unreasonable tasks based on employee attributes (i.e., age, gender, task performance, helping behavior, recent workload, and relationship closeness): stereotype‐driven logic, efficiency‐driven logic, and exchange‐driven logic. In a fully randomized conjoint survey experiment, we asked 464 supervisors to allocate an unreasonable task based on evaluations of 4640 hypothetical employee profiles, with profiles varying randomly on six employee attributes. Results show that supervisors are more likely to assign unreasonable tasks to younger employees who perform better on tasks, exhibit more helping behavior, currently have lighter workloads, and maintain closer relationships with their supervisor. The relatively stronger effects of employees' recent workload, task performance, and helping behavior suggest that the efficiency‐driven logic plays the most influential role in shaping supervisors' unreasonable task assignments. We discuss the theoretical, methodological, and practical implications of our findings.

sample.title: Cognitive Ambidexterity: Balancing Algorithmic Efficiency and Contextual Judgement in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
sample.abstract: AI-enabled decision systems make algorithmic recommendations appear objective and ready for action before contextual, ethical, and stakeholder concerns are fully considered. This study examines how leaders preserve judgment under these conditions. We develop cognitive ambidexterity as a leader-level meta-cognitive capability through which managers balance algorithmic exploitation with contextual exploration in AI-mediated decisions. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first examine five U.K. procurement and infrastructure organizations and identify four mechanisms of cognitive ambidexterity. We then examine these mechanisms through vignette experiments with managers. The findings show that leaders preserve contextual judgment by treating AI outputs as interpretive cues, calibrating trust under ambiguity, slowing decisions when reflection is needed, and building supports that make algorithmic recommendations contestable. The study extends ambidexterity theory by showing how exploration–exploitation tensions are cognitively regulated when exploitation is embedded in algorithmic decision processes. It also uses leadership cognition and Upper Echelons Theory to explain why leaders differ in their capacity to enact this regulation. Together, these insights position cognitive ambidexterity as a critical leader-level capability for using AI’s efficiency gains while preserving the contextual judgment.

sample.title: Deciphering the slow adoption of HR analytics: a comprehensive exploration of individual, social, and technological factors
sample.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
sample.abstract: The growing importance of analytics in management, including Human Resource Management, supports data-driven decisions and strategic objectives. Despite its benefits, HR professionals have been slow to adopt HR analytics. This study aims to identify factors that facilitate and hinder HR analytics adoption among HR professionals, with a focus on the moderating role of organizational culture. Using an integrated model that combines the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), this study examines factors influencing HR analytics readiness and their influence on adoption behavior The validation of model was accomplished through the employment of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), which was conducted using survey data from 305 HR professionals based in India. The findings show significant positive relationships between readiness for HR analytics and factors such as attitude, quantitative self-efficacy, peer influence, superior influence, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and tool trialability, while data availability was insignificant. Individual and social factors positively influence readiness, whereas organizational culture negatively moderates the relationship between readiness and the adoption of HR analytics. The findings emphasize the need for cultural reorientation to foster innovation and effectively implement HR analytics, offering valuable insights for managers, business leaders, and policymakers.

sample.title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
sample.abstract: Pay range transparency—that is, disclosing the minimum and maximum pay for a job rather than individuals’ actual pay—has become the most prevalent form of pay transparency. Yet, existing theories explain employee reactions to pay information through present-focused, interpersonal comparisons with coworkers’ pay. We theorize that pay range transparency instead directs employees to interpret their structural pay standing—their pay position relative to the disclosed range boundaries—as a forward-looking signal of the organization’s recognition and structural room for pay growth. Drawing on expectancy theory, we propose that structural pay standing has a curvilinear (attenuated-positive) effect on job satisfaction, intention to stay, and job performance, mediated by pay growth uncertainty: pay near the range minimum offers weak evidence that contributions will be recognized, whereas pay near the maximum reveals limited structural room for further growth, a pattern we term a ceiling effect. Pay-related procedural justice attenuates these effects. Four studies—a natural experiment (n = 371), an online experiment (n = 603), a three-wave field study (n = 525), and an experimental-causal-chain study (n = 392)—support our theorizing, establishing structural pay standing as distinct from interpersonal pay standing and revealing an unrecognized trade-off of pay range transparency.

sample.title: Toward an Integrative Model of Layoff Effects: A Strategic Human Capital Resources Framework
institutions: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey
sample.abstract: Despite decades of research yielding rich theoretical insights and empirical evidence, the layoff literature remains fragmented. It lacks an overarching framework integrating findings across levels of analysis (e.g., organizational, group, and individual), stakeholder groups (e.g., layoff decision‐makers, executioners, survivors, and displaced employees), and outcomes from proximal processes to distal performance consequences. This fragmentation impedes understanding of how layoff effects unfold and why they vary across individuals and organizations. We review and synthesize layoff research and integrate insights from recent advancements in the strategic human capital resources literature. Our framework explains how layoffs first trigger an outflow of human capital and then reshape the quality, complementarity, and deployment of remaining human capital resources, while shaping the social‐psychological reactions of stakeholder groups. We further identify layoff characteristics as contingencies that determine whether layoffs produce negative or positive shifts in strategic human capital resources states, shape stakeholder reactions, and condition whether individual outcomes aggregate to the organizational level. In doing so, we delineate the organizational‐, individual‐, and cross‐level pathways through which layoffs influence individual performance and, ultimately, organizational outcomes. We offer implications for firms seeking to plan layoffs strategically, manage social and psychological processes, and leverage human capital resources before, during, and after layoffs.

sample.title: When shifts matter for hybrid teams: The moderating role of location predictability.
sample.abstract: In recent years, changes to the nature of work and evolving employee preferences have led to the rise of hybrid teams. In contrast to traditional teams, hybrid teams frequently shift between remote and face-to-face interaction. This structure raises new questions about how such dynamism impacts team engagement, an emergent state typically thought to develop under long periods of stability and face-to-face interaction. Drawing on the boundary transition theory of dynamic teamwork, we theorize that weekly downshifts in face-to-face interaction (i.e., relative decreases from the prior week) harm weekly team engagement and performance, but only for teams with lower levels of location predictability-an important yet understudied differentiator of hybrid team functioning. To test these ideas, we use a within-team, repeated-measures field survey design with a sample of hybrid sales teams at a large alcohol distributor in China. We surveyed 164 hybrid teams and their supervisors across 6 weeks (648 team-level weekly responses) to capture shifts in team work locations and examine their impact on weekly team engagement and performance. Results supported our hypotheses. By focusing on the role of weekly fluctuations in team structures and how location predictability shapes these effects, we advance our understanding of the unique and dynamic nature of hybrid teams.
