sample.title: Automation and Gender: Implications for Occupational Segregation and the Gender Skill Gap
sample.abstract: We examine the differential effects of automation on the labor market and educational outcomes of women relative to men over the past four decades. Although women were disproportionately employed in occupations with a high risk of automation in 1980, they were more likely to shift to high-skill, high-wage occupations than men in over time. We provide a causal link by exploiting variation in local labor market exposure to automation attributable to historical differences in local industry structure. For a given change in the exposure to automation across commuting zones, women were more likely than men to shift out of routine task-intensive occupations to high-skill, high wage occupations over the subsequent decade. The net effect is that initially routine-intensive local labor markets experienced greater occupational gender integration. College attainment among younger workers, particularly women, also rose signicantly more in areas more exposed to automation. We propose a model of occupational choice with endogenous skill investments, where social skills and routine tasks are q-complements, and women have a comparative advantage in social skills, to explain the observed patterns. Supporting the model mechanisms, areas with greater exposure to automation experienced a greater movement of women into occupations with high social skill (and high cognitive) requirements than men.

sample.title: Using AI to Guide Workers
sample.abstract: New research shows how LLMs can balance organizational performance with individual priorities. Listen to this article: If AI is integrated into operational and decision-making systems within organizations, it could in effect start to act like a manager. Think of AI in charge of assigning workers to tasks, sequencing work, or distributing resources. Executives who oversee […] The post Using AI to Guide Workers appeared first on Harvard Business School AI Institute .

sample.title: A new equilibrium: COVID-19 lockdowns and WFH persistence
institutions: ARC Centre of Excellence for Children and Families over the Life Course
sample.abstract: This paper documents a robust link between COVID-19 lockdowns and the uptake and persistence of working from home (WFH) practices. Exploiting rich longitudinal data, we use a difference-in-differences strategy to compare office workers in three heavily locked-down Australian states to similar workers in less affected states. Locked-down workers sustain 43% higher WFH levels through 2023  0.5 days per week  with a monotonic doseresponse relationship. Persistence is driven by adjustments on both sides of the labor market: employers downsize office space and open remote/hybrid positions, while employees relocate away from city centers and invest in home offices and technology.

sample.title: Workplace gender discrimination: key insights, emerging trends, and future research directions
sample.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
sample.abstract: Workplace gender discrimination has been extensively examined across disciplines, yet its evolving research landscape remains fragmented. This study applies Structural Topic Modelling (STM) to 1,091 peer-reviewed articles published between 1975 and 2024, identifying six major themes: wage gaps, performance evaluation bias, work-family conflict, unequal working conditions, professional inequality, and structural masculinity. Temporal analysis reveals a shift from concerns about pay and promotion towards broader discussions of identity, mental health, intersectionality, and inclusivity. Integrating these findings with related literature, the study develops the Inclusive Impact Matrix, a conceptual framework connecting workplace culture, formal policies, and everyday organisational practices to outcomes including reduced stereotyping, equitable career advancement, work-life balance, professional support, and employee well-being. The matrix illustrates how cultural, policy-based, and practice-based mechanisms can jointly address distinct dimensions of gender inequality, emphasising their alignment rather than isolated interventions. The study contributes by synthesising fragmented research streams and identifying intersectionality and women’s self-neglect under sustained workplace and care-related pressures as areas warranting further investigation. It offers organisational leaders, HR practitioners, and policymakers an evidence-informed framework for advancing workplace equity and inclusion.

sample.title: Cultivating Team Psychological Safety: A Model Rooted in Conservation of Resources Theory
sample.abstract: We examine team psychological safety (TPS), the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk‐taking, in its function as a resource caravan passageway. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, we develop a multilevel process model explaining how individual initiative, team interaction, and organizational conditions cultivate and sustain this shared climate, and how it shapes resource protection, investment, and acquisition. Our theoretical model comprises three stages: Cultivation, in which TPS is established, maintained, and nourished; Bloom, in which TPS supports participation, engagement, and sustained performance; and Harvest, in which these processes generate opportunities for resource acquisition across levels. We advance psychological safety research by specifying mechanisms connecting its development and consequences across levels and extend COR theory by explaining how resource caravan passageways are cultivated and renewed.

sample.title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
sample.abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

sample.title: The Five Stages of Becoming an AI-Native Organisation
sample.abstract: Giving people access to powerful technology is one step. Building the training, support and governance to change how work gets done is where many organisations are still catching up. In this episode of the Digital HR Leaders podcast, David Green is joined by Melissa, founder of Hyperadaptive Solutions and author of Hyperadaptive: Rewiring the Enterprise to Become AI-Native. They explore her five stages of transformation, from laying the foundations for AI to redesigning work around customer outcomes, and what each stage asks of HR. Join them as they discuss: Why faster decisions and easier access to skills are testing traditional hierarchies and functional boundaries The five stages of the Hyperadaptive model, with examples from FedEx, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota and Ping An Insurance What it means to organise around value streams, and where HR expertise fits when teams are built around customer outcomes How job architectures and career paths could evolve as people move from doing tasks to building, monitoring and maintaining AI systems Why middle managers need support to guide teams through change, and what organisations risk by moving faster than they can learn How to set a clear goal for AI, measure progress beyond usage and decide where to reinvest the time it saves This episode is sponsored by Eightfold. sample.title: Confident and Well‐Connected: The Interplay of Line Managers' HR Self‐Efficacy, Brokerage, and HRM Implementation
institutions: University of Doha for Science and Technology
sample.abstract: HRM implementation, defined as line managers' execution of core HRM tasks, has been identified as a key challenge in realizing the competitive advantages associated with HRM. Integrating social cognitive and social network theories, we investigate the joint effect of line managers' HR self‐efficacy (i.e., their confidence in their ability to effectively perform HRM‐related tasks) and their positions as brokers (i.e., their role as intermediaries between otherwise disconnected contacts) in HR advice networks on HRM implementation and establish a link to team performance. Multilevel analyses were conducted using multisource survey data from 88 line managers, their 325 subordinates, and 69 of the line managers' direct superiors across six Indonesian firms. The findings reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, with medium levels of self‐efficacy linked to more effective HRM implementation than either low or high levels. Moreover, line managers' positions as HR information brokers moderate the inverted U‐shaped relationship: The curve remains steeper at low levels of brokerage, but becomes shallower at high levels. Finally, HRM implementation mediates the joint effect of self‐efficacy and HR information brokerage on team performance. Taken together, these findings challenge the assumption of a linear relationship between HR self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, enrich understanding of the social foundations of line managers' HRM implementation, and contribute to broader discussions on the enablers and effects of HRM implementation.

sample.title: Employee Attrition Predictive Modeling Using CRISP-DM: A Supervised Learning and Workforce Analytics Framework
sample.venue: Transactions on Engineering and Computing Sciences
sample.abstract: Employee turnover represents a critical operational, financial, and strategic bottleneck across contemporary enterprise environments, frequently incurring replacement expenditures ranging between 50% and 200% of an annual salary while eroding institutional human capital. This study presents a rigorous end-to-end predictive modeling framework adhering strictly to the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) methodology to identify empirical risk factors and reliably forecast voluntary employee turnover prior to formal resignation. Leveraging a curated enterprise human resources dataset encompassing 1,270 personnel records across 35 multi-modal attributes, rigorous data sanitation, automated zero-variance filtration, and factor encoding were performed alongside Exploratory Data Analysis, Recursive Partitioning (Decision Trees), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Unsupervised K-Means clustering ( ). Supervised predictive models—specifically Binomial Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes Classification—were trained and benchmarked against an independent 30% test holdout ( ) and further validated against a 200-record unseen verification holdout. The primary institutional research goal was to determine whether voluntary attrition could be classified with an accuracy exceeding 70.0%. Experimental results demonstrate that Logistic Regression substantially outperformed Naïve Bayes, achieving a test accuracy of 88.71% (95% CI: 85.10%–91.71%), an Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.8282, a sensitivity of 98.11%, and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.4906. When evaluated against the unseen verification cohort, the model demonstrated outstanding generalization capability with an accuracy of 91.00%, a sensitivity of 98.80%, an improved specificity of 51.52%, and a Kappa of 0.6064. Key empirical predictors of attrition identified include overtime commitments, business travel frequency, tenure without promotion, distance from home, and reported environmental satisfaction. A modular production turnover pipeline and ethical governance framework are formalized to operationalize real-time individual risk stratification while safeguarding against algorithmic bias.

sample.title: From exclusive to inclusive? Exploring the barriers of i-deals for functionally diverse (FD) workers
sample.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
sample.abstract: Idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) have traditionally been granted exclusively to the ‘stars’ of organisations, promoting the ‘Matthew effect’ (the more you have, the more you get), while other workers are denied access to this contemporary HR practice that takes accommodation requests one step further. This practice has led to perceptions of unfairness among co-workers, particularly minorities, who encounter obstacles and discrimination when seeking to access or benefit from i-deals. Through a scoping review, we explore the barriers that arise when functionally diverse workers (FD workers) negotiate i-deals, shedding light on whether, and how, it is possible to move beyond an exclusionary, opportunistic approach toward an inclusive, strategic use of i-deals as a tool for inclusion. By explicitly applying a workplace dignity framework, the study supports a genuine concern for equity in i-deal negotiations, as opposed to a mere practice of ‘social washing’ and self-serving hypocrisy regarding the inclusion of FD workers in organisations. Recommendations for organizations to eliminate the barriers and the inclusive application of i-deals are discussed, as well as the paper’s theoretical and practical contributions.

sample.title: A call for rebellion: demanding justice in operations and supply chain management
institutions: Escola de Administração de Empresas de São Paulo
sample.abstract: Purpose This study aims to reflect on the operations and supply chain management (OSCM)-dominant focus on traditional stakeholders (e.g. buying firms, top managers) and its instrumental view of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) to discuss how to position excluded, marginalized and historically underrepresented stakeholders into the OSCM research stream. Design/methodology/approach Through provocative theorizing, the authors problematize how OSCM research can integrate people, especially workers and underrepresented groups, to embrace justice, reduce inequalities and promote social impact. Findings This essay offers insights into structural challenges beyond the empirical context to (re)think research choices and outcomes, recognize what needs to change in OSCM scholarship and practice and embrace novel and impactful research. Social implications This essay highlights different ways to connect OSCM with real-world problems and needs toward societal well-being. Originality/value Aiming to address existing supply chain structural injustices, the authors propose five reorientation shifts: reframing DEI, shifting the unit of analysis, rethinking the source of knowledge, changing the rules of the field and redefining impact. These shifts can transform OSCM into a more diverse, equal and inclusive field.

sample.title: Generative AI collaboration and expatriate career adaptability: a career construction perspective on sustainable career development
sample.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
sample.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.

sample.title: How remote work reshapes talent acquisition and innovation: evidence from U.S. listed firms
institutions: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade
sample.abstract: This paper examines how work-from-home (WFH) policies shape firms’ talent acquisition and innovation performance. While prior research has treated remote work as an employee benefit affecting individual productivity and retention, we conceptualise WFH as a firm-level strategic capability for overcoming geographic labour market frictions. Drawing on human capital theory, we argue that acquiring skilled talent beyond local labour markets is a key channel through which remote work enhances innovation. Using difference-in-differences with propensity score matching on a panel of U.S. listed firms, we find that firms with higher WFH feasibility achieved significant gains in talent acquisition quality following the widespread shift to remote work. This relationship is strengthened by organisational flexibility and concentrated in industries where geographic constraints were previously binding. Talent acquisition, in turn, partially mediates the effect of WFH on innovation.

sample.title: People analytics in employee performance management: A bibliometric mapping and structured content review
sample.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science- Economics and Business Administration
institutions: Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics and Finance
Ho Chi Minh City Open University
sample.abstract: People analytics is increasingly being used to measure, track and improve performance. The research in this area, however, is highly fragmented across disciplines and the results are mixed. This paper maps the thematic and intellectual structure of the field and synthesizes the evidence on the impact of people analytics on performance management. It combines a bibliometric analysis of the Scopus indexed literature with a structured content review of the full text studies. There has been a significant increase in the volume of publications over recent years with HR analytics, AI and HRM forming the core of the keyword network. Bibliographic coupling reveals four tentative theoretical streams emerging over time: from incentive economics to organizational capability, then to a more behavioral focus on fairness and finally to the more recent generative AI work which largely reuses the existing frameworks. The content review suggests that people analytics can improve measurement, prediction and feedback, but the extent of this is contingent upon the quality of the data, the design of the metrics, the presence of complementary management practices, the level of managerial support and employee trust. A number of the studies point to trade-offs between the quality and quantity of output and between the technical accuracy of the analytics and employee acceptance. The paper presents an integrative multi-level framework with testable propositions and sets out a research agenda which includes causal designs, multi-dimensional performance measures, employee voice, data governance, emerging economy contexts and human-AI collaboration.

sample.title: ‘Flying under the radar’: job crafting when menopause disrupts neurodivergent coping
sample.venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
sample.abstract: Human Resource Management increasingly recognises the importance of job crafting, which relies on personal structures of coping. This study foregrounds workplace job crafting using a critical case approach, focusing on neurodivergent individuals whose coping mechanisms may be destabilised during menopause. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 45 neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms (UK and US) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings provide insight into how intersecting vulnerabilities shape person-led workplace adaptation. Specifically, neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms were found to engage in different forms of avoidance job crafting (behavioural avoidance demand crafting, behavioural avoidance resource crafting, cognitive avoidance demand crafting). Moreover, a newly identified preservation orientation drives a combination of avoidance and approach job crafting, evidenced by crafting strategies that primarily focus preservation, or maintaining the status quo, to align personal resources within maintaining job performance. This article contributes to the job crafting literature by demonstrating distinctive job crafting practices of individuals whose life-long coping strategies (of neurodivergence) are temporarily and transitionally destabilised (by menopause symptoms). Organisations have a critical role to support potentially stigmatised employees, thereby nurturing inclusive human resources support policies that provide support to individuals experiencing multiple stigmas.

sample.title: The Rise of Multi-Agent AI in Strategic Human Resource Management: Exploring How Collaborative AI Agents Transform Talent Management, Workforce Coordination, and HR Decision Authority
sample.venue: Journal of Business Insight and Innovation
sample.abstract: This study examined how professionals in Pakistan understood the role of collaborative artificial intelligence (AI) agents in talent management, workforce coordination and HR decision authority. Guided by Socio-Technical Systems Theory and Organizational Information Processing Theory, the study used reflexive thematic analysis to interpret 20 online interviews with HR, operations and technology professionals. Six themes captured participants’ accounts of recruitment, career development, workforce planning, decision authority, procedural fairness and organizational readiness. Participants located a critical point of recruiter oversight at initial screening, when historical hiring preferences could exclude qualified applicants before human review. In development and scheduling, they identified employee aspirations, skills and personal circumstances as information that could change an otherwise plausible recommendation. They assigned responsibility for pay adjustments to compensation committees and staffing reductions to executives. Across functions, participants connected fairness with understandable reasons and access to a reviewer empowered to correct an outcome. The findings show that, in participants’ judgments, the value of collaborative agents depends on whether decision owners can inspect underlying evidence, exercise judgment and intervene when recommendations affect employment opportunities. sample.title: How and when do green HRM practices foster organizational citizenship behavior for the environment? A multilevel approach
sample.abstract: Purpose Organizational citizenship behavior for the environment (OCBE) is essential for sustainable development. This study aims to examine how and when green human resource management (GHRM) practices contribute to OCBE. Design/methodology/approach Two waves of multisource data were collected from 737 employees and 84 HR directors in the Chinese hospitality industry. Data were analyzed using robust maximum likelihood estimators in Mplus 7.4. Findings The results show that green organizational climate (GOC) and employee environmental commitment (EEC) serially mediate the GHRM practices–OCBE relationship. Moreover, line managers’ environmental support (LMES) moderates the GHRM practices–GOC relationship. Practical implications The current study suggests that organizations can improve OCBE by implementing GHRM practices and recognizing LMES’s significant role. Social implications Specifically, the authors’ findings offer actionable insights for Global South organizations to support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 12 and SDG 13) by fostering voluntary pro-environmental behaviors. Originality/value This study explains how and when GHRM practices contribute to OCBE.

sample.title: Institutional ambiguity and its dimensions in anti-enslavement arena
sample.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how institutional ambiguity enables the persistence of contemporary enslavement. The authors analyze organizations engaged in eradicating slave labor as well as those resisting such efforts. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on interviews, shadowing and documentary analysis, the authors applied Constructivist Grounded Theory to develop a framework linking ambiguity and conflict, and their manifestations within, through, over and against organizations. Findings The findings show that institutional ambiguity not only legitimizes exploitative labor practices but also undermines efforts to combat them. Social implications By addressing the Decent Work and Economic Growth Sustainable Development Goal, this study contributes to organizational theory by demonstrating how ambiguity operates as power that shapes organizational responses to contested social issues and restructures institutional fields. Originality/value This paper derives its originality from being based on previously unexplored data regarding the “Dirty List” and from within an organization that managed the National Pact.

sample.title: AI Literacy and Ethical Voice in Algorithmic Hiring: The Mediating Role of Psychological Safety and Moral Efficacy
sample.abstract: Responsible human resource management (HRM) relies on human oversight, which works only when people are willing to question problematic algorithmic outputs. Based on social cognitive theory and psychological safety theory, this study investigates whether there is a direct link between AI literacy and the ethical voice in algorithms for hiring, as well as whether there is an indirect link through psychological safety and moral efficacy. Data of the survey in the form of information was collected from 390 employees who were engaged in recruitment and selection process in four multinational companies in Pakistan (purposive sampling; 470 questionnaires were distributed). The regression and bootstrap analyses revealed that the variables of psychological safety (B = 0.31) and moral efficacy (B = 0.37) had a positive relationship with AI literacy, while the direct path from ethical voice to AI literacy showed a stronger effect (total effect B = 0.44, p < .001). Psychological safety and moral efficacy both predicted ethical voice, and there was an indirect relationship between psychological safety and moral efficacy. Indirect effects made up approximately 42% of the overall effect, and there were significant indirect paths via psychological safety, via moral efficacy, and sequentially via both psychological safety and moral efficacy, in addition to a significant direct path (complementary partial mediation). AI-literacy training in combination with a safe reporting climate and high moral efficacy might therefore be most likely to help supervise ethical use. Data are cross-sectional in nature and self-reported, so the results are interpreted in terms of associations.

sample.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
sample.abstract: Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

sample.title: Understanding the Mediating Role of Talent Retention in SMEs' Sustainability Practices
sample.abstract: Digital transformation and institutional regulation do not consistently translate into more sustainable practices in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). This study, which is grounded in the resource‐based view (RBV) and draws on institutional theory (IT) and talent management theory (TMT), emphasizes talent retention as a theoretically central mediating mechanism that links external institutional and digital drivers with embedded sustainability practices. Applying PLS‐SEM to survey data from 253 SMEs in La Rioja (Spain), our findings reveal no significant direct effects of digital management intensity or the social and regulatory framework on sustainability. However, both of these variables have an indirect effect on sustainability via talent retention. Our results suggest that regulatory and digital drivers are more likely to be effective when supported by a stable “Green Pillar” of human capital that can internalize these external stimuli. By positioning talent retention as the core conduit through which external digital and institutional pressures are converted into sustainable practices in SMEs, the study advances TMT, adds to the Digital Green Twin Transition debate, and offers practical implications for aligning talent management strategies in SMEs with digital and institutional policies.

sample.title: The power of perception: the impact of inclusivity policies and diversity climate on employee well-being
sample.venue: Equality Diversity and Inclusion An International Journal
sample.abstract: Purpose The purpose of the current study is to assess the relationship between employees' perceptions of inclusivity policies and employee well-being (i.e. life satisfaction, job satisfaction, turnover intentions and work–life balance). Moreover, we also examine diversity climate as a potential mediator of this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the model of inclusive organizations and the signaling theory, we hypothesized that positive perceptions of inclusivity policies would relate to better employee well-being through a more favorable perception of diversity climate. The sample consisted of 361 faculty and staff from a large Southeastern university. A single-level path-analytic mediation model was used to test hypothesized relationships due to the negligible between-college variance. Findings The results revealed that positive perceptions of inclusivity policies were associated with a more positive diversity climate which, in turn, enhanced certain well-being outcomes – life satisfaction, job satisfaction, turnover intentions and work–life balance. Further, diversity climate mediated the relationship between employees' perceptions of inclusivity policies and employee well-being. Our results highlight the importance of not only implementing inclusive policies but, also ensuring that employees perceive them as fair and effective. Originality/value The current study extends prior research by emphasizing employees' perceptions of inclusivity policies rather than just policy presence. Further, demonstrating the role of diversity climate as a mechanism linking inclusivity policies to well-being outcomes, offers a better understanding of how organizational inclusion initiatives can translate into employee attitudes and health.

sample.title: Where turnover contagion tips: Coworker network structure, job embeddedness, and retention targeting in an agent-based model
sample.abstract: Employee turnover spreads among coworkers, but the organizational consequences of that contagion are poorly understood. We build an agent-based model in which employees embedded in a coworker network start searching for a new job when shocks and the share of searching or vacant coworkers exceed an embeddedness-dependent threshold. Across about 63,000 simulation runs, contagion strength produced a sharp tipping point between modest amplification of turnover and a self-sustaining regime. Clustered networks tipped earlier than random ones, whereas hubs alone did not lower the tipping point. Higher mean job embeddedness delayed tipping strongly. Under a fixed budget, retention practices that reached hubs or brokers and were attached to positions rather than individuals raised the tipping point most. The model is stylized and uncalibrated, so the findings are hypotheses for empirical testing.

sample.title: Determinasi Retensi Karyawan Ditinjau dari Employee Engagement, Pengembangan Karir, dan Lingkungan Kerja
sample.venue: Jurnal Akuntansi Ekonomi dan Manajemen Bisnis
sample.abstract: This study examines the effect of employee engagement, career development, and work environment on employee retention, with organizational commitment as an intervening variable. The research was conducted at PT Parsaoran Global Datatrans, an internet service provider operating across six regional areas in Indonesia. A quantitative approach was employed using survey data collected from 96 employees, selected through proportional stratified random sampling from a population of 2,207 employees. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results indicate that employee engagement and career development have a positive and significant effect on employee retention, while the work environment does not show a significant effect. Furthermore, organizational commitment does not have a significant effect on employee retention and does not mediate the relationship between employee engagement, career development, work environment, and employee retention. These findings suggest that strengthening employee engagement and providing clear career development opportunities are more critical for improving employee retention than relying on organizational commitment as an intervening mechanism. The study contributes to the human resource management literature by providing empirical evidence on employee retention determinants in the internet service industry.

sample.title: When CSR signals fail: perceived quality as a credibility condition for consumer–brand identification
sample.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how corporate social responsibility (CSR) translates into consumer–based brand equity (CBBE) by identifying the mechanisms and conditions underlying this process. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on signaling theory, data from 172 Mexican consumers exposed to a CSR initiative were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings CSR does not generate consumer value through direct effects. Instead, consumer–brand identification acts as the central mechanism linking CSR to CBBE. Empathic concern positively influences identification, but only when perceived quality is high. Under these conditions, effects extend to trust, purchase intention, recommendation intention and engagement. When perceived quality is low, the mechanism collapses. Socially responsible consumption exhibits weak and unstable effects. Social implications Social initiatives are more likely to mobilize consumer trust, engagement and support when social purpose is accompanied by credible organizational performance. Originality/value This study advances CSR research by proposing a conditionally bounded signaling model in which perceived quality serves as the credibility condition that enables or suppresses CSR value creation.

sample.title: The effects of HRM practices on organizational performance: The moderating role of workplace safety in Bangladesh’s garment industry
sample.abstract: This study attempted to examine how Human Resource Management (HRM) practices affect the organizational performance of Bangladesh's garment industry. The moderating effects of workplace safety on the relationship between HRM practices and organizational performance were also investigated. To achieve better organizational performance, four factors have been selected in the Bangladeshi context and, more specifically, in the garment industry of Bangladesh. 400 human resource managers from several Bangladeshi garment industries took part in this study. PLS-SEM was employed in analyzing the data. It was found that recruitment and selection, training and development, performance evaluation, and rewards and benefits have a substantial influence on organizational performance in the Bangladesh Garment Industry. The results revealed that workplace safety has a significant moderating influence on the relationship between human resource management practices and organizational performance. It will help the garment factory owners and HR managers to follow the ideal and standard procedures for the recruitment and selection process, an appropriate environment and adequate arrangements for training and development, effective means and procedures to evaluate employee performance, and gratify employees and workers for their excellent performance in their respective jobs and trades. This study provides a framework and references for future HRM research on Bangladesh’s garment industry and organizational performance. It highlights workplace safety’s role in linking HRM practices, recruitment, training, appraisal, and rewards- to organizational performance, contributing valuable insights into HRM dynamics and practices that can guide future academic and industry research.

sample.title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
sample.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.17926 .

sample.title: Predictive People Analytics Using Machine Learning-Based HR Metrics for Strategic Workforce Planning in Industry 5.0
sample.abstract: As Industry 5.0 can be introduced the nature of the relationship between human capital and intelligent technological systems fundamentally changed as the workforce is now at the core of the organization strategy. In this paper, the author puts forward a Predictive People Analytics (PPA) model, which embraces the HR metrics on machine learning (ML) to provide a strategic workforce planning that is supported by evidence. The suggested architecture transforms a data convergence of private data, including HR resource planning documents, IoT sensor streams, HR Information Systems (HRIS) and workforce survey devices, into one analytical data stream. Four ML models are also trained and aggregate to predict meaningful workforce results: employee turnover, mobility within the organization, performance curves, and succession preparedness: Random Forest, XGBoost, Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN). Transparency in high stakes HR is promoted through explainability through SHAP-based posthoc attribution. Empirical test on the IBM HR Analytics dataset and an augmented synthetic workforce panel shows that the ensemble model has the accuracy of 94.7, AUC-ROC of 0.971 and F1-score of 0.938 that are better than all of the baseline models and previous benchmarks. The results affirm that industry 5.0 people analytics enhanced by ML can assist in creating proactive, people-concentrated workforce in a noteworthy way.

sample.title: AI Powered Recruitment Portal Using Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning
sample.venue: International Research Journal of Modernization in Engineering Technology and Science
sample.abstract: Recruitment teams routinely receive more applications than they can screen manually, and job seekers find it hard to locate roles that fit their skills.This paper combines a literature review with the design of an AI Powered Recruitment Portal.Four recent studies on artificial intelligence enabled talent sourcing, natural language processing based resume screening, resume to job matching and automated campus placement management are reviewed and compared.The review shows that existing work relies largely on keyword comparison, struggles with varied resume formats, offers limited skill gap analysis, explains its scores poorly and gives recruiters little control over automated outcomes.To address these gaps, the paper proposes a web platform for candidates, recruiters and administrators, organised into eight modules and built on a React frontend, a Java Spring Boot backend, a centralized MySQL database and an artificial intelligence and natural language processing engine that extracts resume features, matches them with job requirements, scores and ranks candidates and generates recommendations, while the recruiter takes the final decision.Random Forest and Logistic Regression are proposed for suitability scoring.The paper separates proposed components from components verified as implemented.It reports no accuracy figures because no experimental results were available at the time of writing, and it gives an evaluation plan instead.

sample.title: HOW JOB CHARACTERISTICS INFLUENCE THE MOTIVATION OF MILLENNIAL HOSPITALITY WORKERS IN BRAZIL
sample.abstract: This article investigates how job characteristics influence the motivation of Millennial hospitality workers in Brazil, where turnover is high and work schedules are demanding. The authors collected 137 responses from Millennials (18+) through an online questionnaire shared on LinkedIn and WhatsApp, then tested a structural model with PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4. Motivation was modeled as the outcome of five predictors: organizational culture, feedback, skill variety, organizational support, and task importance. The measurement model retained 26 indicators with acceptable reliability and discriminant validity, and the structural model explained substantial variance in motivation (R2 ≈ 0.76). Hypothesis tests showed that only feedback had a strong, statistically significant positive effect on motivation, while culture (negative), support, task importance, and skill variety were not significant. The findings suggest that frequent, clear, developmental feedback is the most actionable lever for motivating and retaining Millennial hospitality employees in this sample. It also highlights limits of culture-focused interventions alone. The study articulates job characteristics and Millennial motivation in Brazilian hospitality, a context still underexplored empirically. By testing multiple predictors via PLS-SEM, it shows that feedback surpasses culture, support, and skill variety as the main motivational factor, offering novel evidence and specific practical implications for employee retention. The study articulates job characteristics and Millennial motivation in Brazilian hospitality, a context still underexplored empirically. By testing multiple predictors via PLS-SEM, it shows that feedback surpasses culture, support, and skill variety as the main motivational factor, offering novel evidence and specific practical implications for employee retention.

sample.title: Performance Appraisal Fairness, Perceived Organisational Support, Employee Engagement and Human Resource Analytics: A Human-Centred Decision-Support Framework
sample.venue: Journal of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering
sample.abstract: This study develops a human-centred human resource (HR) decision-support framework integrating performance appraisal fairness, perceived organisational support (POS), employee engagement and workforce analytics. Drawing on the Social Exchange Theory, the conceptual component proposes that appraisal fairness and POS are positively associated with employee engagement and that POS may strengthen the positive relationship between appraisal fairness and engagement. These relationships are proposed rather than empirically tested because the secondary dataset does not contain validated measures of appraisal fairness or POS. However, an “Engagement Score” is available; its measurement provenance is undocumented. Accordingly, the analytics case is used to examine the sufficiency and governance limitations of administrative HR records rather than to test the proposed conceptual relationships. The illustrative analytics component uses the publicly available HR Analytics Dataset. The raw file contained 3,150 records and 39 variables; removal of 150 exact duplicate records resulted in a final analytical dataset of 3,000 observations. A target-leakage audit identified ExitDate, EmployeeStatus, TerminationType, TerminationDescription and exit-dependent tenure measures as inappropriate prospective predictors. Following their exclusion, a leakage-controlled Random Forest (RF) model showed essentially chance-level discrimination, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.507 and an area under the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC) of 0.528. Logistic regression produced similarly weak performance (ROC-AUC = 0.475). These findings demonstrate the importance of data provenance, temporal validity, leakage control, fairness assessment and human oversight when developing HR analytics systems. The study therefore contributes a theoretically grounded and systems-oriented framework for responsible workforce decision support while identifying direct empirical testing of the proposed moderation relationship as an important direction for future research.

sample.title: Improving Employee Performance Based On Work From Home and Work Flexibility With Job Satisfaction as A Mediation Variable
sample.venue: International Journal of Science and Environment (IJSE)
sample.abstract: This study aims to analyze the improvement of employee performance based on Work From Home (WFH) and work flexibility with job satisfaction as a mediating variable in the manufacturing industry in Jakarta. The study used a quantitative approach involving 155 respondents. Data analysis was conducted using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) method through the SmartPLS 4 application. The results showed that WFH had a positive and significant effect on employee performance (β = 0.214; p = 0.002). Work flexibility also had a positive and significant effect on employee performance (β = 0.248; p = 0.001). In addition, WFH had a positive and significant effect on job satisfaction (β = 0.384; p < 0.001), as did work flexibility (β = 0.381; p < 0.001). Job satisfaction was proven to have a positive and significant effect on employee performance (β = 0.438; p < 0.001). Mediation testing showed that job satisfaction mediated the effect of WFH on employee performance (β = 0.168; p < 0.001) and the effect of work flexibility on employee performance (β = 0.167; p < 0.001). These findings confirm that flexible work arrangements and job satisfaction are important aspects in supporting improved employee performance in the manufacturing industry.

sample.title: Models for Sustainable Human Resource Management: Combining Ethics, CSR and Data-Driven HR Analytics
sample.venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
sample.abstract: This research presents a conceptual framework for sustainable human resource management (HRM) that integrates ethical decision-making, corporate social responsibility (CSR), and data-driven HR analytics. It underscores the importance of sustainable HR practices in fostering long-term employee development, enhancing organizational resilience, and promoting adaptability in the current digital landscape. Ethical principles are emphasized as vital for creating transparent, fair, and inclusive workplaces, while CSR initiatives significantly contribute to increasing employee engagement and nurturing a mission-driven organizational culture. The paper further examines the role of HR analytics as an effective instrument for optimizing workforce planning, improving employee retention, and enhancing productivity. Proposed strategies aim to align HRM with broader sustainability goals by utilizing the interrelatedness of these components. The study concludes by providing practical recommendations for implementing this integrated model to build strong and sustainable organizations.

sample.title: The impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on employee green well-being: The mediating role of employee engagement in Vietnamese enterprises
sample.venue: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
institutions: Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City
sample.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

sample.title: HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, EMPLOYEE WELFARE, AND INDUSTRIAL STABILITY IN NIGERIA: A QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS
sample.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between HRM practices, employee welfare, and industrial stability in Nigeria, with a focus on how workplace policies shape employee wellbeing and labour relations. This is with the specific objectives to: explore how human resource management practices are perceived and experienced in relation to employee welfare within Nigerian organizations; examine the role of employee welfare in shaping workplace relations and industrial stability in the Nigerian work environment; and investigate the organizational and institutional factors influencing the implementation of employee welfare policies in Nigeria. The study adopted a qualitative research design and an exploratory–descriptive approach. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and document analysis involving HR managers, employees, labour union representatives, and organizational administrators in selected organizations in Lagos State, Nigeria. Thematic analysis was used to identify and interpret recurring patterns relating to HRM practices, employee welfare provisions, and industrial relations outcomes. Findings indicate that effective HRM practices particularly in recruitment, training, compensation, performance management, and employee relations contribute positively to employee welfare and workplace harmony. Organizations with strong welfare systems tend to experience higher employee commitment, improved motivation, and reduced industrial conflict. Conversely, poor welfare implementation, delayed salaries, weak communication systems, and adverse economic conditions were found to contribute significantly to industrial unrest and declining employee morale. The study concludes that industrial stability in Nigeria is largely dependent on the effectiveness of HRM systems and the extent to which organizations prioritize employee welfare. Strengthening institutional frameworks, improving communication, and ensuring fair and consistent welfare practices are essential for promoting sustainable labour relations and organizational stability. It was then recommended that government should strengthen labour laws, enhance enforcement institutions, and ensure strict compliance with labour standards to promote worker welfare, fairness, and sustained industrial peace and productivity in the country.

sample.title: Dataset for: Inclusive Talent Management for Border-Region MSMEs: A PRISMA 2020 Systematic Literature Review
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: This dataset supports a PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review on inclusive talent management in micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), with a focus on border regions. It contains the full Scopus search strings, record counts for each PRISMA stage, Scopus result screenshots, and the authors' coding of all 76 unique articles (2015–2026; 68 synthesised), including evidence category, inclusive-TM evidence, MSME fit, border context, text availability, primary theme, MMAT-based confidence rating, theory codes (TCCM), and coded findings. A five-year subset (2022–2026; 63 unique, 55 synthesised) is flagged in the same file. Author-keyword co-occurrence maps and a codebook are included. No abstracts or full texts are redistributed.

sample.title: Challenges to Risk Management Implementation and Perceived Strategies for Optimising Safety Performance on Construction Sites in Anambra State, Nigeria
sample.abstract: Construction remains one of the most hazardous industries in Nigeria, and Anambra State has recorded repeated building collapses and site accidents that have forced emergency regulatory interventions. Yet the barriers that prevent construction firms from implementing comprehensive risk management, and the strategies most likely to optimise safety performance, have not been systematically documented for the State. This study explored the challenges faced by construction firms in implementing comprehensive risk management practices and sought to establish strategies for optimising safety performance on construction sites in Anambra State, based on the perceptions of construction professionals. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study population comprised 928 construction professionals (builders, architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and health and safety officers); a sample size of 287 was determined using the Taro Yamane formula, purposive and random sampling techniques were applied, and 198 validquestionnaires were retrieved from the 287 administered (a response rate of 69.0%) and analysed using frequencies, percentages, mean scores, standard deviations and the Relative Importance Index (RII). The findings revealed that the most severe challenges were financial constraints limiting risk management investment (mean = 4.82; 1st), inadequate knowledge and training (mean = 4.74; 2nd) and weak regulatory enforcement and political interference (mean = 4.71; 3rd), followed by workers' resistance to safety protocols (mean = 4.64), poor health and safety culture (mean = 4.56) andcorruption and bribery (mean = 4.25). All six strategies were rated agree or strongly agree by every respondent (a ceiling effect, with no undecided or disagreeing responses), so the ranking is indicative only: comprehensive safety training programmes (mean = 4.96; 1st), strengthened regulatory enforcement mechanisms (mean = 4.94; 2nd) and worker participation in safety management (mean = 4.93; 3rd) ranked highest, although all six means fell between 4.90 and 4.96.The study concludes that safety performance in the State can be optimised only through a coordinated, multi-stakeholder approach that addresses finance, capacity, regulation, behaviour and governance together. It therefore recommends a state-wide subsidised safety training programme, a dedicated and politically insulated inspection unit, low-interest financing for construction SMEs, worker safety committees with confidential reporting channels, and a simplifiedrisk management toolkit for small firms.

sample.title: Beyond Compliance: How Safety Management Practices Shape Workplace Safety Outcomes
sample.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
sample.abstract: Safety management practices play an important role in ensuring workplace and environmental safety. However, the practices do not rely solely on standard procedures. To prevent hazards, organizations need to provide resources, set priorities, support workers, and manage workplace conditions. The evidence on management systems and hazard prevention, leadership and employee involvement, training and communication, and the behavioural and climate pathways linking these practices to safety results is summarized in this review. Although selection effects and heterogeneous effectiveness across firm types limit causal inference, the most consistent conclusion is that organizational and group practices are associated with better safety compliance and participation. Stronger evidence for reducing injury is found for interventions that change hazards or work systems, as well as important paired observational studies of certification of occupational safety and health management systems. Safety climate is a useful leading indicator and a reliable mechanism, but it cannot be used interchangeably with injuries because studies differ in directionality, time lag, unit of analysis, and outcome source. Although training generally improves safety behaviour and knowledge, its effect on injuries varies by workplace and the controls in place. Leadership and worker involvement are important to ensure that safety practices are properly implemented. However, research evidence remains limited, particularly in studies that rely solely on questionnaires, combine different safety measures, or assess injury prevention based solely on workers' behaviour. In conclusion, safety management is more effective when different safety practices are applied together and adapted to reduce workplace risks. Worker involvement, supervision and safety performance monitoring should be given proper attention. Prolonged research periods, data from multiple sources, and consideration of differences across work sectors should be taken into account for future research.

sample.title: "Sindicalismo ante la Industria 4.0: Estrategias de adaptación y resistencia en España (1992-2024)"
sample.abstract: This article analyses trade union strategies of adaptation and resistance to industrial digitalisation in Spain (1992-2024). Drawing on two research questions—about the alignment of the industrial regulatory framework with inclusive governance principles, and the tensions of social dialogue and collective bargaining in digitalised contexts—the study combines comparative legislative analysis, content analysis of collective agreements, and interviews with six trade union leaders from CCOO and UGT. The results reveal a central paradox: while the new normative framework, Industry Act 2024 Draft, V AENC (2023) and Digital Rights Charter (2021) opens formal spaces for participation, collective bargaining advances unevenly in incorporating clauses on algorithmic management and digital training. The Rider Law (RDL 9/2021) and pioneering collective agreements in the platform sector illustrate both the achievements and the limits of trade union action. The article concludes that a just digital transition in Spain requires converting multilevel governance into effective decision-making power.

sample.title: AASHA Net AI: An Offline-First, Voice-Based Health Record Assistant for ASHA Workers Using a Large Language Model
sample.venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology
sample.abstract: Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) record health information during household visits in rural India, often without reliable internet access and usually in a regional language. Typed, connectivity-dependent mobile forms make this documentation slow and error-prone. This paper presents AASHANet AI, an offline-first, voice-based health record assistant. A Flutter application stores every record on the device first and synchronises it with a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend through an idempotent, versioned three-step protocol that guarantees exactly-once server records under retries and detects conflicting confirmations instead of overwriting them. Voice notes in Kannada, Hindi or English are processed by the Google Gemini large language model, which returns a transcript, an English translation and schema-validated fields (patient name, age, symptoms and duration) that the health worker reviews before confirmation. The system was verified with 44 backend tests (5 against PostgreSQL), 41 mobile unit and widget tests, including 17 synchronisation fault-injection scenarios, and a live end-to-end run against the real services. Measurements showed that model selection dominates latency: on the same recording, processing took 3.0–3.4 s with one model and 96–302 s with another, which motivated configurable model fallback with time limit.

sample.title: Performance Assessment Tools and Employee Motivation in a South African Public Legislature
sample.venue: International Journal of Research on Multidisciplinary Studies
sample.abstract: A prominent question in performance appraisal research is whether employee motivation is related to appraisal as an integrated HRM practice. Particularly in public legislative institutions, employees' experiences with appraisals through specialized assessment procedures have received less attention. Therefore, this study investigates how employees see the performance evaluation instruments integrated within the Limpopo Provincial Legislature's performance management system in South Africa. Out of 190 employees, 130 participated in a quantitative, cross-sectional survey. A structured questionnaire with eighteen Likert-scale statements was used to gather data. The analysis concentrated on mechanisms related to assessment, such as performance-linked incentives, procedural fairness, developmental support, recognition, and the use of assessment results for training and development. The results show a significant difference: while performance-linked incentives were highly supported as motivating, a significant percentage of workers expressed concerns about fairness and transparency, anxiety about assessments, dissatisfaction with recognition, a lack of developmental support, and weak connections between assessment results and training. By demonstrating that the motivational value of assessment depends not only on the existence of a formal system but also on the configuration and implementation of its constituent processes, the study adds a tool-level perspective to public-sector performance management.

sample.title: Synergizing Quantum Computing and Blockchain for Secure Talent Management and Predictive Financial Intelligence
sample.abstract: The convergence of quantum computing and blockchain technology presents unprecedented opportunities for revolutionizing talent management systems and financial intelligence platforms. To address the growing need for secure, scalable, and predictive enterprise systems, this research proposes a novel framework that integrates quantum computing capabilities with blockchain security. The hybrid quantum-classical architecture leverages quantum machine learning algorithms, post-quantum cryptographic protocols, and distributed ledger technology, evaluated through theoretical modeling, security analysis, and performance benchmarking. Findings indicate a 340% improvement in predictive accuracy for talent performance metrics and a 280% enhancement in financial forecasting precision compared to classical approaches, while achieving resistance against both classical and quantum attacks and improving processing speeds by up to 450% for complex analytical tasks. These results highlight the transformative potential of quantum-blockchain synergy in delivering next-generation enterprise solutions with unmatched security, computational efficiency, and predictive intelligence.
